items.title: Courtois puts Belgium career on hold until September 2027
items.summary: Real Madrid goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois announces he will put his Belgium career on hold until 2027, missing the upcoming Nations League campaign. Read More: https://punchng.com/courtois-puts-belgium-career-on-hold-until-september-2027/
items.body_text:
Goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois said in quotes published on Wednesday he has decided to put his Belgium career on standby until September 2027.
The 34-year-old made the last of his 115 international appearances at this summer’s World Cup but will only return to the Red Devils set-up for Euro 2028 qualifiers next year.
The Real Madrid ‘keeper will miss the upcoming Nations League campaign under new boss Mark Van Bommel starting with a game against Italy on September 25.
Van Bommel told Courtois beforehand he was unable to guarantee him the starting No. 1 shirt.
“I have made the choice not to play the entire Nations League campaign with the Red Devils,” Courtois told Belgian newspaper Het Laatste Nieuws after Madrid’s 2-1 Champions League win over Inter Milan on Tuesday.
“Unless the national coach runs into injury problems; then I can be called up exceptionally,” he added.
Options for Van Bommel in goal in Courtois’ absence include Manchester United’s 24-year-old Senne Lammens and Chelsea’s 21-year-old Mike Penders.
“I am making myself available again for the European Championship qualifiers,” Courtois said.
“If the goalkeeper playing in the Nations League performs well, Van Bommel might continue with him.
“However, I want to fight for my place. I want to prove that I can be the first-choice keeper again,” Courtois added.
AFP

items.title: FG moves to end ‘make-believe’ accreditation in tertiary institutions
items.summary: …Plans digital tracking of lecturers, equipment, facilities By Joseph Erunke, Abuja ABUJA — The Federal Government has moved to overhaul the accreditation system for Nigerian universities, polytechnics and colleges of education, warning institutions against presenting a false or temporary picture of their academic and infrastructural capacity during accreditation exercises. The Minister of Education, Dr Tunji […] The post FG moves to end ‘make-believe’ accreditation in tertiary institutions appe
items.body_text:
•Dr Tunji Alausa, Minister of Education
…Plans digital tracking of lecturers, equipment, facilities
By Joseph Erunke, Abuja
ABUJA — The Federal Government has moved to overhaul the accreditation system for Nigerian universities, polytechnics and colleges of education, warning institutions against presenting a false or temporary picture of their academic and infrastructural capacity during accreditation exercises.
The Minister of Education, Dr Tunji Alausa, gave the warning in Abuja on Tuesday while inaugurating a Ministerial Committee on Strengthening the Accreditation and Quality Assurance System for Tertiary Institutions in Nigeria.
Alausa said the era of temporarily assembling lecturers, equipment and facilities ahead of accreditation visits must end, stressing that institutions should be assessed on resources that are genuinely available and sustainable.
He said the government would deploy digital technology, identity-management systems, geospatial mapping and other verification mechanisms to ensure that what institutions present to accreditation teams reflects their actual capacity.
“An institution should not be able to prepare a temporary picture of itself simply for the purpose of an accreditation visit. Sadly, this is what we see in a majority of instances,” the minister said.
Alausa expressed concern over the temporary movement of academic and non-academic personnel between institutions, as well as the borrowing or relocation of laboratory equipment, workshop resources, library materials and other facilities solely to impress accreditation teams.
He said such practices undermined the integrity of the tertiary education system and denied students access to the resources and personnel used to secure approval for academic programmes.
“We must ensure that when an accreditation team visits an institution, what it sees and verifies should represent the actual and sustainable capacity of that institution, not an arrangement assembled for the accreditation exercise,” he said.
Digital tracking of facilities, equipment
To close the loopholes, Alausa directed the National Universities Commission, NUC; National Board for Technical Education, NBTE; and National Commission for Colleges of Education, NCCE, to progressively move away from predominantly manual and episodic accreditation procedures to a digital, data-driven and continuously verifiable system.
He said geospatial mapping, geotagging and digital identification technologies should be considered for physical infrastructure, laboratories, workshops and major equipment presented during accreditation.
Under the proposed system, critical equipment used to secure accreditation would have unique digital records linked to the institution and its physical location, making it difficult for institutions to borrow or move resources merely to pass accreditation.
The minister said the same principle should apply to lecturers and other personnel.
He called for a comprehensive digital identity-management and staff-verification framework capable of establishing that individuals presented as employees of an institution were genuinely affiliated with it.
Alausa said the government would explore collaboration with the National Identity Management Commission, NIMC, including the use of the National Identification Number, NIN, alongside other appropriate and secure technologies.
“The objective is straightforward: one individual, one verifiable identity and an accurately declared institutional affiliation,” he said.
He added that the system should be capable of detecting cases where an individual was improperly presented as full-time personnel in more than one institution.
The minister also said the proposed reforms would ensure that the actual composition of academic departments, including junior academic staff and other personnel who genuinely constitute the workforce, was captured digitally.

items.body_text:
By Henry Umoru
ABUJA — Four court cases challenging the candidacy of the All Progressives Congress, APC, governorship candidate in Ogun State, Senator Solomon Adeola, have been discontinued by the respective litigants.
Adeola, who chairs the Senate Committee on Appropriations, is seeking the APC ticket ahead of the 2027 governorship election in the state.
His Media Adviser, Kayode Odunaro, disclosed this in a statement on Wednesday, describing the development as coming at the commencement of the governorship campaign.
According to Odunaro, the four suits were discontinued voluntarily by the litigants, with the first case withdrawn on August 24, 2026, and the remaining three discontinued on September 7, 2026.
He said the cases were discontinued in open court, with the various defendants and their counsel duly informed through notices of discontinuance.
The first suit, No. FHC/AB/CS/87/26, was instituted by Professor Awolola Awoniyi under the Freedom of Information Act 2011 against Adeola, the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, APC, Guardian Newspapers Limited and the Inspector-General of Police.
Another suit, No. FHC/ABJ/CS/844/26, was instituted by Arc. Akerele Abiodun John, Ogun State Chairman of the Booth Party; Mr. Adeyemi Solomon Oluwaseyifunmi, Ogun State Chairman of the Young Progressive Party, YPP; Mr. Ola Olamide Emmanuel of the Action Democratic Party, ADP; Mr. Ayinde Oluwayemisi Abiola, an ADP member; and Mr. Fesomade Gbadebo, a member of the Labour Party, LP.
The suit also listed Adeola, INEC and APC as defendants.
Odunaro said the other two discontinued cases were suits Nos. FHC/ABJ/CS/989/2026 and FHC/ABJ/CS/884/26, instituted by some of the aforementioned party officials and members, as well as Dr. Olufemi Soluade, Ogun State Chairman of the African Democratic Party, ADP; Mr. Oluwabukola Soyoye Temitope, a member of the Labour Party; and Mr. Ogunremi Abiodu Oluwaseun.
He said no reasons were publicly given by the litigants for discontinuing the cases.
However, Odunaro claimed that the litigants had been convinced of the merit of Adeola’s candidacy and had decided to support his ambition ahead of the 2027 election.
Adeola, according to his aide, welcomed the development and said it would allow him to focus on delivering what he described as the dividends of democracy to the people of Ogun State.
He added that the senator would continue his mobilisation and campaign across the state ahead of the 2027 general election.

items.body_text:
By Kingsley Omonobi
ABUJA — The Chief of Army Staff, Lt. Gen. Waidi Shaibu, has approved the redeployment of senior officers to key command, operational and staff appointments across the Nigerian Army as part of efforts to enhance operational effectiveness.
Under the new postings, Maj. Gen. Ibikunle Ajose has been appointed Theatre Commander, Joint Task Force North-East, Operation Hadin Kai, while Maj. Gen. JE Osifo becomes Chairman of the Military Pensions Board.
Acting Director, Army Public Relations, Col. Appolonia Anele, disclosed this in a statement, saying the exercise was aimed at strengthening leadership and aligning the Army’s command structure with the country’s evolving security environment.
She said the postings prioritised critical operational theatres and strategic appointments to ensure that officers with the requisite leadership experience and expertise were positioned to deliver on the Army’s mandate.
Ajose, who was serving at Army Headquarters, Department of Army Operations, is taking over as Theatre Commander, Operation Hadin Kai, from Maj. Gen. AE Abubakar, who has been redeployed to the Nigerian Army Heritage and Future Centre as Dean, Faculty of Operational Research.
Maj. Gen. AM Alechenu has also moved from Defence Headquarters Garrison to the Nigerian Army Heritage and Future Centre, while Maj. Gen. RT Utsaha moves from the Army Headquarters, Department of Army Standards and Evaluation, to Defence Headquarters Garrison as Commander.
Similarly, Maj. Gen. AM Umar moves from the Army Headquarters, Department of Civil-Military Affairs, to the Army War College Nigeria as Commandant, while Maj. Gen. UM Alkali moves from the college to the Department of Civil-Military Affairs at Army Headquarters.
Maj. Gen. GS Muhammed has been redeployed from the Office of the National Security Adviser to the Nigerian Army Finance Corporation as Director-General.
Osifo, who was previously at the Nigerian Army Finance Corporation, moves to the Military Pensions Board as Chairman, while Maj. Gen. IE Ekpenyong has been redeployed to the Department of Defence Logistics at Defence Headquarters as Director, Engineering Services.
At the operational level, Brig. Gen. AA Bello moves from 6 Division Garrison/Sector 3 Joint Task Force South-South, Operation Delta Safe, to the Department of Defence Operations at Defence Headquarters.
Brig. Gen. MS Adamu has been redeployed from the Nigerian Army Women Command to the newly established 8 Brigade as Commander, while Brig. Gen. MS Sule moves from Operation Enduring Peace to 27 Task Force Brigade as Commander.
Brig. Gen. I Sule moves from the Directorate of Recruitment Management to 6 Division Garrison as Commander, while Brig. Gen. E Azenda moves from the Land Forces Simulation Centre to 2 Division Garrison as Commander.
Brig. Gen. AS Bugaje, who was at 2 Division Garrison, has been redeployed to the Land Forces Simulation Centre as Director, Administration.
The COAS charged the newly appointed officers to justify the confidence reposed in them through exemplary leadership, operational innovation, professionalism and commitment to duty.
Shaibu urged the officers to remain focused on the constitutional mandate of defending Nigeria’s sovereignty, protecting its territorial integrity and supporting civil authorities in maintaining peace and security.
According to the statement, the Nigerian Army would continue to strengthen its leadership and force-employment framework to improve operational outcomes, joint and inter-agency coordination, and its capacity to respond to contemporary and emerging security threats.

items.body_text:
Security forces killed 11 terrorists and recovered 2.9 tonnes of explosives in separate intelligence-based operations (IBOs) in Balochistan’s Kharan and Washuk districts, the military’s media affairs wing said on Wednesday.
According to a statement by Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the security forces conducted the IBOs in Kharan and Washuk on September 6 and 7, respectively, on the “reported presence of terrorists belonging to Indian proxy, Fitna al Hindustan and neutralised 11 Indian-sponsored terrorists”.
The state has designated Balochistan-based groups as Fitna-al-Hindustan to highlight India’s alleged role in terrorism and destabilisation across Pakistan.
ISPR said terrorists attempted to establish a roadblock in Kharan and disrupted local traffic on Sunday. “The security forces promptly intercepted and engaged the terrorists, whereby, killing eight Indian-sponsored terrorists,” it added.
The forces conducted another “deliberately planned” IBO in Washuk district on Monday on reports of the presence of terrorists, the statement said.
“During the conduct of operation, own troops effectively busted terrorists’ hideout and after an intense fire exchange, three terrorists were sent to hell,” ISPR said, adding that security forces recovered 2.9 tonnes of explosives being used for preparing improvised explosive devices (IEDs).
It further said that sanitisation operations were being conducted to eliminate “any other Indian-sponsored terrorist” found in the area.
ISPR reaffirmed that the security forces and law enforcement agencies would continue the “relentless counterterrorism campaign” under Azm-i-Istehkam, approved by the Federal Apex Committee under the National Action Plan, to wipe out the “menace of foreign-sponsored and supported terrorism from the country”.
President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif paid tribute to the security forces for killing terrorists and recovering the explosives.
“The nefarious designs of terrorists who are active under Indian patronage will be thwarted at all costs,” the president was quoted as saying in a statement.
“Operations will continue until the complete eradication of terrorists belonging to Fitna al Hindustan network,” he added.
PM Shehbaz also commended the security forces for foiling the attempt to block a road and disrupt traffic in Kharan and praised the professional capabilities of the forces for destroying a terrorist hideout in Washuk.
He reiterated the government’s aim to eradicate “terrorism conducted under India’s patronage” and pledged that operations against terrorist elements would continue with full force.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi lauded the security forces’ professional skills for thwarting the “nefarious designs” of the terrorists, his ministry said.
He saluted the security forces for eliminating the terrorists and said they were determined to eradicate the Indian-sponsored terrorists, the interior ministry said in a post on X.
“The brave sons of the security forces are a source of pride for the nation and it stands with them in the fight against terrorism,” Naqvi was quoted as saying.
Terrorism surge
Balochistan has witnessed a surge in terrorist attacks in recent weeks, prompting security forces to intensify counter-terrorism operations.
On the night of Aug 31-Sept 1, Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) terrorists launched a coordinated attack on the Customs House, located at Ziarat Cross on the N-50 National Highway, in Pishin district.
While security forces responded effectively and killed 10 terrorists, two officers were among six martyred in the fire exchange, ISPR said.
Also on August 31, 11 terrorists belonging to Fitna al Hindustan, who had blocked the N-40 Quetta-Taftan highway by establishing an illegal checkpoint for extortion in Chagai’s Nokcha area, were eliminated following an intense exchange of fire.

items.body_text:
Defence Minister Khawaja Asif has cautioned that the tripartite Makkah Defence Alliance between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye could become operational if there was a “spillover” of the conflict in Yemen into Riyadh.
The development comes as Yemen’s Houthi rebels launched attacks on oil installations in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday, injuring 73 people.
Meanwhile, the defence pact, signed on Aug 7, aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empower its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them.
On the Geo News show ‘Aaj Shahzeb Khanzada Kay Sath’ on Tuesday night, host Shahzeb Khanzada mentioned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and asked Asif whether the strategic pact could be operationalised.
Asif answered in the affirmative, saying there was no “ambiguity” as the pact stipulated that aggression against one party was equivalent to aggression against all.
“This is a joint defence pact. And unprovoked aggression or spillover of whatever is happening in Yemen into Saudi Arabia, definitely, the pact will become operational; there should be no doubt in this,” he said.
“We are bound by the terms and conditions of this pact and we will honour them in case there is a need,” he said.
Asked if Saudi Arabia and Pakistan had been in contact following the attacks, Asif said he was not aware of any engagement. However, he reiterated that Pakistan “is bound to react under the pact because it is [aimed at] joint defence and collective help in case of aggression”.
Asif further stated that the pact was not “aggressive in nature”, adding: “If there is aggression against one member state, then all three member states will respond in kind.”
The defence czar went on to say, “This is a trilateral pact [..] but even if it were bilateral, we would have responded.”
At the same time, Asif expressed hope that the situation will “come under control and die down”.
He also hoped that “the Houthis will realise that if [..] they attempt to export their internal matters, then the clauses of this pact over confronting aggression will become operative”.
“They should keep this in mind,” he said. Asif also noted that the Houthis were “non-state actors” and that Yemen’s government had responded to their attacks.
“There is sympathy for Iran around the Muslim world. There is no doubt about that, but exploitation of a bilateral dispute by non-state actors, I believe they are doing it at their own peril,” he said.
Asif observed that the pact could serve as a deterrent and went on to say that three countries “did not need to respond to aggression with aggression”, but held that the member states had established their respective strengths.
The defence minister added that the conflict in Yemen had been ongoing since 2014, recalling a visit he made to the country at the time in his capacity as the defence minister.
“At that time too, we helped Saudi Arabia,” he recalled, adding that Pakistan and Saudi’s long-standing ties and the “sanctity” of the Gulf country’s land “warrant that whenever there are testing times, we help them”.
On the stalemate in negotiations between the United States and Iran, the defence minister voiced optimism that “all doors have not closed”.
“I will not abandon hope that the process has ended or that all doors have closed. There is a stalemate, but I will say the situation is better than that,” he said, adding there was “indirect engagement”.
He noted that Pakistan walked a tightrope given its “brotherly relations” with countries on both sides of the conflict. Hoping that peace would prevail, Asif warned: “Israel will want that the conflict should continue and (Gulf) countries should be drained.”
He said Israel was not incurring any expenses in the war, as the funding “was coming from overseas”.
“In fact, I believe they are profiting off of it,” he said. He noted that people in Gaza, the West Bank and Lebanon were paying the price for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s “lust for power”. Ho

items.body_text:
Iran’s Revolutionary Guard (IRGC) said it fired ballistic missiles at a base in Jordan used by the US military and attacked 10 ships on Wednesday, after the US said it had destroyed five Iranian oil tankers, in a sharp escalation of the six-month-old war.
Increased attacks by both the US and Iran have shattered a month of relative calm, hitting military, shipping and energy assets, sending oil prices surging and drawing in regional allies in recent days.
The US military’s Central Command posted video of the strikes, which it called a response to IRGC targeting a US Navy warship twice with ballistic missiles over the previous two days. No Americans were harmed, the US said.
“Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters during a visit to Colombia.
Iran then carried out a ballistic missile attack on a base used by US forces near Al Azraq in Jordan, according to an IRGC statement on state media.
Although Iran said its missiles inflicted heavy damage, Jordan said its air defences intercepted 18 of the 20 Iranian missiles, with two falling in unpopulated areas, and that there were no casualties.
A US official said Iran’s strikes in Jordan were ineffective and all American troops were accounted for.
The IRGC said on Wednesday it also attacked 10 ships, including two US Vessels and eight oil tankers, attempting to cross a “prohibited and unsafe” area of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital energy conduit largely choked off by Iranian attacks.
Iran has targeted US assets and allies in the region throughout the war, including in Jordan several times, killing at least two US military personnel during one strike in July.
Iran has also threatened oil tankers in Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports, according to a statement carried by state media. A maritime security source reported a liquefied natural gas tanker was damaged in the Emirati port of Khor Fakkan, though it was unclear who was responsible.
Oil prices extended gains in early trade on Wednesday with Brent crude nearing $100 a barrel on market concerns over the disruption of oil tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz.
Recent attacks by Yemen’s Houthis on top energy producer Saudi Arabia have added to supply concerns.
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
On Tuesday, Houthis launched an attack on several cities in Saudi Arabia, further undermining regional stability.
The Houthi attacks wounded 73 people and set oil installations ablaze in what appeared to be a major expansion of the conflict, which began on February 28 with joint US-Israeli attacks on Iran.
The Houthis, who control most of Yemen’s populated areas, including the capital, have further pressured US allies by periodically disrupting shipping on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula, at the entrance to the Red Sea.
They said they had launched a broad operation deep into Saudi territory, using drones and missiles to strike a Saudi air base in the southern city of Khamis Mushait as well as Saudi state oil company assets in the cities of Abha, Najran and Jazan.
Saudi authorities reported blazes at the sites and said women and children were among the wounded.
The wider war in the Gulf has turned into a test of wills between the US and Iran, with each side hoping that economic pressure from competing blockades will force the other to yield.
Washington is trying to increase the flow of oil to world markets by guiding ships through the Strait of Hormuz, while cutting off Iran’s exports with a blockade.
Central Command said the tankers it destroyed on Tuesday were part of a shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies.

items.body_text:
Published September 09, 2026
Ben and Casey Affleck lost both of their parents earlier this year.
Casey, 51, revealed heartbreaking news while promoting his new film, Company, at the 2026 Venice International Film Festival on Tuesday, September 8, per Page Six.
The Oscar-winning actor, who directed, co-wrote and stars in the new movie, dedicated the project to his late parents, Timothy “Tim” Byers Affleck and Chris Affleck. Chris died at 83 on June 2 after battling pancreatic cancer, while the exact date of Tim’s death remains unclear.
“It’s dedicated to my parents because I lost both my mom and my dad this year, and they were very important to me,” Casey said.
The Manchester by the Sea star — who shares sons Indiana, 22, and Atticus, 18, with ex-wife Summer Phoenix — said the loss has also shaped how he approaches his work.
“The good thing about being an artist, the best thing maybe, is that you can take all of the hardest experiences in your life and put it into your work, and it just makes you better,” he said.
He added, “If you’re willing to face it all, be honest about it all and show up vulnerably with those feelings and allow for the fact that you might not be able to really fully understand them, but you’re willing to put them into what you’re making, it’s a blessing.”

items.title: Rescuers comb the seas for missing Indonesian journalists on volcano mission
items.summary: Officers from Banten Basarnas, wearing personal protective equipment, prepare alongside Water Police officers for the second day of the search operation, at Pelindo Regional 2 Port, in Cilegon, Banten, on September 9, 2026, to locate the five missing journalists.— AFP <p...
items.body_text:
Published September 09, 2026
Indonesian rescuers combed the waters and islands around an active volcano on Wednesday for a missing speedboat carrying eight people, including five journalists sent to cover a volcanic eruption.
The second day of the search has come up empty-handed, the Basarnas national search and rescue agency said.
The group set out on a speedboat from an area west of Jakarta on Monday afternoon, but the crew lost contact with the boat owner soon after, according to rescuers.
The five Indonesian journalists were on a mission to capture photos and video of the eruption of Mount Anak Krakatau, which for days paralysed several airports and blanketed cities including Jakarta in volcanic ash.
They were accompanied by two boat crew members and a guide.
The search effort launched on Tuesday afternoon but paused hours later due to high waves and poor visibility.
Rescuers have combed through an area of more than 270 nautical miles, including islands near the volcano, in an operation involving dozens of police officers, soldiers, fishermen, and volunteers, the Basarnas agency said in a statement.
"So far, the search result is zero," local Basarnas head Al Amrad said on Wednesday afternoon.
The operation has been suspended for the day and will resume on Thursday, he told AFP.
Rescuers were proceeding cautiously as Anak Krakatau continued to spew thick volcanic ash, he added.
"The search will continue to be carried out according to conditions on the ground," Al Amrad said.
The agency said it had deployed high-speed search and rescue vessels, inflatable boats, and thermal drones in the search.
The journalists are employed by local and international media, including the state news agency Antara, the Turkish state-run news agency Anadolu, and the local website iNews.
One of the journalists contacted a colleague and shared his location at 3pm on Monday, but has not been heard from since, the rescue agency said.
Marine accidents are a regular occurrence in the Southeast Asian archipelago, due in part to lax safety standards and inclement weather.
In January, three Spanish tourists died when their boat sank off eastern Indonesia, and a 10-year-old boy was listed as officially missing, presumed dead, after authorities ended the search.

items.body_text:
Published September 09, 2026
A senior Anthropic researcher sounded the alarm with a stark warning, claiming there’s more than a 10 percent chance artificial intelligence could wipe out humanity.
This alarming revelation comes from Evan Hubinger, who responded to an X thread shared by another Anthropic researcher, Jacob Coxon, on Tuesday, September 8, who announced his resignation from the company over AI safety concerns.
Coxon, whose role revolved around specializing in training new AI models, alleged that the company’s AI labs are “gambling with our lives.”
“They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon wrote in a post on X (formerly Twitter).
“Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources,” Coxon added.
“We have all witnessed the progress in each of these domains, and progress is not slowing,” Coxon warned.
Responding to his former colleague, Hubinger not only endorsed Coxon’s statement but also revealed that the company doesn't have a plan B for this scenario.
“Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we don’t yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to,” Hubinger added in his X post.
Evan Hubinger is an Anthropic researcher who leads the company's alignment efforts.
The growing concerns over AI safety have become a topic of discussion among policymakers and industry giants.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has been sounding alarms with repeated statements that AI has the potential to pose a serious threat to humanity.
Those concerns were only multiplied when in July an OpenAI model went out of control and hacked Hugging Face, a leading platform for open-source developers.

Netanyahu races to unify Israel's right wing in bid to avert election defeat
- By Reuters -
- Sep 09, 2026
JERUSALEM: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is seeking to consolidate Israel’s fractious right-wing parties ahead of a Tuesday deadline in order to avoid an election loss forecast by opinion polls.
Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, is seeking a record seventh term in the October 27 election, but he has faced pressure over the Hamas-led 2023 attack on Israel and subsequent wars in Gaza, Iran and Lebanon, and surveys have for months been pointing to a defeat for his nationalist-religious coalition.
Netanyahu has therefore been pressing allies to merge their candidate lists and raise their chances of gaining parliament seats, so far with only partial success.
Their deadline, when running parties must submit their final lists of candidates, expires on Tuesday night.
“When we unite, we win. When we splinter, we lose,” Netanyahu said in an August 30 interview on Channel 14, a pro-Netanyahu television station. “I am doing all I can, as I did in the previous election, to unite these parties.”
RIGHT-WING NEWCOMER WORRIES NETANYAHU
No single party has ever won an outright majority in the 120-seat Knesset, Israel’s parliament, making coalition governments the norm and sometimes giving as many as a dozen parties a chance of winning seats.
To do so, they must pass a 3.25% vote threshold, equal to four seats, meaning smaller parties risk drawing votes without gaining a seat.
Polls suggest Netanyahu’s Likud party stands to lose a third of its parliamentary power. Though it may still remain the largest party, winning 20-23 seats, Netanyahu would likely need his coalition allies including the far-right Jewish Power and Religious Zionism parties to remain in office.
Religious Zionism, headed by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, has been polling between zero and six seats, down from seven currently.
With Netanyahu’s blessing — and his help, according to two political sources — it merged its list on September 1 with that of Zehut, a small party headed by former far-right libertarian and Likud member, Moshe Feiglin.
But National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has rebuffed Netanyahu’s calls for his Jewish Power party, which currently holds six seats, to run with Religious Zionism, as it did at his behest in the last election. Ben-Gvir has argued that the parties would be stronger running separately.
Feiglin’s views on the Palestinians are similar to those of Ben-Gvir and Smotrich, whose calls to annex the occupied West Bank and depopulate Gaza have drawn international ire.
Though such foreign criticism may have little impact on the vote, another worry for Netanyahu is political newcomer Ofer Winter, a right-wing former brigadier general whose views are largely aligned with those of Smotrich.
But Winter has rejected calls to merge his party, saying he will not run with anyone who may be responsible for the security failure that allowed for the 2023 Hamas-led attack.
Read Also: Netanyahu’s main challenger accuses him of prioritising survival over security
Winter has cast the election as a protest vote and says he will draw right-wingers who are seeking a fresh start. Latest polls show him at four seats or none.
“He chose to go separately and we are now in danger,” Netanyahu told Channel 14, arguing that he risks “wasting” crucial right-wing votes if he does not win enough seats to enter the Knesset.
HAWKISH IMAGE SHATTERED
The parliamentary system delivered a decisive victory for Netanyahu in the previous 2022 election, when a splintered centre-left was knocked out by a unified right-wing alliance.
Now, however, Israel’s most dominant politician of his generation is in a far weaker starting position.

items.title: Putin, Trump discussed idea of trilateral summit with Xi: Kremlin
items.summary: Putin, Trump discussed idea of trilateral summit with Xi: Kremlin
items.body_text:
Putin, Trump discussed idea of trilateral summit with Xi: Kremlin
- By AFP -
- Sep 09, 2026
MOSCOW: Russian President Vladimir Putin and his US counterpart Donald Trump discussed the idea of holding a trilateral meeting with China’s Xi Jinping at an upcoming summit in November, the Kremlin said Wednesday.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) is scheduled to hold a summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen between November 18-19.
Russia has indicated Putin will attend, although the White House has not yet announced whether Trump will be there.
Asked whether Trump and Putin discussed the idea of a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen during their phone call on Tuesday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said: “Undoubtedly.”
“This potential possibility has been mentioned before, and there will be such an opportunity,” Peskov told reporters, including AFP.
APEC is an intergovernmental forum that dates to the 1980s.
The group, which includes Russia, China and the United States, is among the most important forums for economic cooperation in the Asia Pacific.
The November summit comes as Washington pushes Russia for an end to the Ukraine war, and amid deepening ties between Moscow and Beijing.
US envoys visited both Moscow and Kyiv last week, but did not announce a breakthrough in talks to end the war in Ukraine.

items.title: JI submits petrol price reduction plan to govt, says Hafiz Naeem
items.summary: JI submits petrol price reduction plan to govt, says Hafiz Naeem
items.body_text:
JI submits petrol price reduction plan to govt, says Hafiz Naeem
- By Faiz Ullah Khan -
- Sep 09, 2026
KARACHI: Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) chief Hafiz Naeemur Rehman on Wednesday said the party had handed over a comprehensive working plan to the government on reducing the prices of petroleum products.
Speaking at a press conference in Karachi, Hafiz Naeem said the JI had held negotiations with the government, during which the government’s representatives sought suggestions on how petroleum prices could be reduced.
“We have formed a technical committee that has been working on the issue,” he said, adding that the JI was only providing assistance to the government to reduce petrol prices, while controlling the prices was ultimately the government’s responsibility.
Hafiz Naeem said the JI had taken the issue seriously and prepared detailed proposals because it was a party of educated and technically qualified people.
“We have given the government parties a complete working plan. Now it is up to the government to decide what steps it takes,” he said.
He criticised the government for increasing petroleum prices despite ongoing negotiations with the JI, saying the authorities should not have raised fuel prices while talks were underway.
Read Also: Jamaat-e-Islami may march towards Islamabad, Hafez Naeem says
Hafiz Naeem said he had also spoken with Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) Chairman Barrister Gohar, who had assured him of support. He said a resolution on the issue had also been passed by the Sindh Assembly.
Warning of Islamabad March
Hafiz Naeem warned that the JI would announce a plan to march on Islamabad if the government failed to withdraw the petroleum levy.
Call for end to interest-based economic system
Hafiz Naeem also called on the government to reduce the policy rate and reiterated the JI’s demand for an end to interest-based economic practices.
Referring to a 1990 decision of the Federal Shariat Court on the issue of interest, he said successive governments had failed to eliminate the system despite repeated calls for its abolition.

The post Yemen rebels report fresh Saudi strikes as conflict deepens appeared first on Iraqi News.
items.body_text:
Yemen rebels report fresh Saudi strikes as conflict deepens
Sanaa – Yemen’s Houthi rebels reported dozens of Saudi airstrikes on Wednesday as daily attacks continued in a conflict that has reignited during the Middle East war, with hundreds of people killed in fighting near the Red Sea.
More than 40 attacks targeted several regions including the flashpoint areas of Taiz and Hodeida, scene of fierce clashes between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government, the rebels said.
The latest salvos in Yemen’s previously dormant conflict come a day after the Iran-backed Houthis set oil sites ablaze and wounded 73 in their heaviest missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia in years.
The Yemen fighting is taking place against the backdrop of the Middle East war, which erupted in late February with US-Israeli strikes on Iran.
On Wednesday, Iran said it attacked 20 American vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and targeted a US military base in Jordan in retaliation for US strikes on Iranian oil tankers.
The Middle East war has sucked in Yemen, the energy-rich Gulf and others across the region while roiling the world economy, as oil prices returned to $100 a barrel on Wednesday.
More than 500 people have died since the Houthis launched a major offensive last week to seize territory around the Bab al-Mandab strait, gateway to the Red Sea shipping route.
The rebels, who have been attacking Saudi oil tankers, are trying to tighten their squeeze on the shipments, analysts say — a lifeline for exports after Iran’s blockade of Hormuz.
– ‘Dangerous escalation’ –
Saudi airstrikes targeted “various areas across the governorates of Marib, Al-Jawf, Taiz and Hodeida over the past few hours”, the rebels’ Almasirah TV said on Wednesday.
There was no official comment from Saudi Arabia.
The Saudi civil defence later issued a warning for the southern governorate of Khamis Mushait, near Yemen, but quickly lifted it.
On Tuesday, Saudi authorities vowed to respond to the Houthi attacks, saying they caused fires and temporary shutdowns at oil sites.
The Houthis triggered the return to hostilities in July, when they let an Iranian plane land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace.
The government retaliated by striking the airport, an attack the rebels blamed on its sponsor, Saudi Arabia.
The ongoing exchanges risk returning Yemen to a conflict that left hundreds of thousands of people dead and sparked one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.
The Houthis, after seizing Yemen’s capital and forcing out the internationally recognised government, fought a Saudi-led coalition from 2015 until a United Nations-brokered ceasefire in 2022.
On Tuesday, the European Union urged the Houthis to end their attacks, calling them a “dangerous escalation”.
“We call on the Houthis to immediately end all attacks inside and outside Yemen, including attacks against commercial shipping in the Red Sea,” said Anouar El Anouni, a spokesman for the bloc’s diplomatic service.

items.title: ‘They’re playing with our lives’: AI researcher quits Anthropic
items.summary: An artificial intelligence researcher who left OpenAI to join Anthropic has decided to leave the industry, accusing both US companies of "playing with our lives" in the race to... The post ‘They’re playing with our lives’: AI researcher quits Anthropic appeared first on Iraqi News.
items.body_text:
‘They’re playing with our lives’: AI researcher quits Anthropic
San Francisco – An artificial intelligence researcher who left OpenAI to join Anthropic has decided to leave the industry, accusing both US companies of “playing with our lives” in the race to develop AI models capable of self-improvement.
Jacob Coxon, 27, spent the past three years pretraining AI models, first at OpenAI and then, this year, at its rival Anthropic, which he considered more cautious in its approach.
Pretraining is the stage where AI models absorb vast quantities of data.
“Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon said on Tuesday.
“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” he said in a post on X.
“This is not a marketing stunt,” he added.
Superintelligence is the theoretical point when AI’s capabilities exceed human intelligence.
Anthropic safety executive Evan Hubinger backed up Coxon on X.
“We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” he said, adding that he estimated that risk at more than 10 percent over the next decade.
Hubinger said Anthropic is “trying its best”, but does not yet have a plan to ensure an AI system that surpasses human capabilities would obey its creators. He said there was a “low” risk of that happening with current models.
Coxon’s resignation comes as Anthropic prepares for its market debut, following a summer marked by unauthorized hacks carried out by AI tools during testing.
The two companies did not immediately respond to AFP requests for comment.
AI leaders say so-called “recursive self-improvement,” a stage where AI systems could essentially design and train the next generation of AI with little human involvement, is drawing near.
Coxon considers Anthropic’s efforts genuine but said he believes no company can responsibly develop an AI that surpasses humans without government intervention or a coordinated slowdown.
“At Anthropic, the stakes are well-understood, but they are locked in a race to get there first — they believe no one else will act responsibly, so they must do it themselves, despite the risk,” he said.
In February, Anthropic removed a pledge from its safety charter to halt the development of its models if it failed to control their risks.
It argued that if it unilaterally paused its work, its less cautious rivals would dominate the industry, making it less safe overall.
At the end of July, more than 1,000 tech industry employees, including Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei, called on Washington to support a coordinated slowdown in the development of the most advanced AI systems.
OpenAI halted training of its latest models for two weeks in August before resuming it under tighter controls.
On Sunday, OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, called for “extreme caution.”
“International coordination on future AI development needs to become a top priority for governments around the world,” he said in a blog post.
AI models are not regulated by federal law in the United States.
In September, Senator Bernie Sanders and Democratic Representative Greg Casar introduced a bill seeking to suspend AI development until a federal regulator is created.

items.body_text:
EU helps cities tighten screws on Airbnb, holiday rentals
Brussels – European cities will gain more leeway to curb short-term rentals such as Airbnb under plans aimed at bringing down housing costs in tourism hotspots put forward by the EU Wednesday.
The European Commission laid out conditions under which local authorities can limit short lets, as part of an “affordable housing” package seeking to address what commission vice-president Teresa Ribera called a “terrible crisis”.
“When the market fails to deliver something as fundamental as an affordable home, public authorities have a responsibility to act,” Ribera said as she presented the measures.
Though hugely popular with visitors, short-term lodgings are blamed by residents in many popular travel destinations for depriving locals of apartments for long-term rent and pushing up prices.
From New York to Tokyo and Barcelona, a growing number of cities worldwide have imposed or considered restrictions on tourist flats in recent years.
But curbs have often been followed by court challenges from rental providers and tourism operators, resulting in legal uncertainty.
The commission’s Affordable Housing Act — which still has to be negotiated with lawmakers and EU countries — aims to provide cities with legal cover, clarifying when authorities can take action without falling foul of EU single market rules.
Cities and other relevant authorities will be allowed to limit holiday rentals as well as the purchase of property for short-term letting purposes in areas deemed “under housing stress”.
The law lays out a series of parameters that need to be met for an area to be defined as under stress, such as the ratio between house prices and incomes there.
Before introducing restrictions, authorities must demonstrate that short-term rentals have had a significant adverse effect on housing affordability or availability for at least three years.
Population and housing supply and demand trends will also need to be taken into account and any measure will have to be non-discriminatory, proportionate and limited in duration to a maximum of five years, according to the proposal.
– ‘Structural solutions’ –
The legislation will not affect landlords who rent out their own primary residence for short periods of time — nor rules cities brought in before it is adopted.
Housing affordability has become a growing issue across the 27-nation bloc in recent years, with 51 percent of European city dwellers telling a 2025 survey it was “an immediate and urgent problem”.
Property prices have surged by 60 percent, while rents have climbed by 20 percent over the past decade, leaving millions struggling to find a home they can afford, according to Brussels.
The EU says this is mainly driven by insufficient housing supply, but short-term lets add extra pressure in certain areas.
“Short-term rental activity” grew 93 percent across four major letting platforms between 2018 and 2024, according to the EU.
While such lets account for only about 1.2 percent of the European Union’s housing stock, according to EU data, the share can be much higher in popular districts of some tourist destinations.
In central Madrid for example there are around 40 short-term rentals for every 100 homes in the long-term rental market, Brussels said.
Yet rental providers dispute that holiday lets are to blame for rising house prices.
“For the great majority of cities, the claim that short-term rentals are driving housing stress does not survive contact with this evidence,” tech lobby group CCIA wrote in a letter to the commission this month.
In some cities with restrictions, rents and hotel prices have gone up, the letter added, noting that Lisbon recently overturned some of the curbs it had previously imposed.
“Europe’s housing crisis needs structural solutions, and the implementation of this act should focus on increasing the supply of homes,” said an Airbnb spokesperson.

items.summary: Britain, France, and Canada on Tuesday announced measures to ban imports of goods originating from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. The three nations said that this aims to support the two-state solution amidst growing international concern over settlement expansion, Reuters reported. The move comes part of a series of measures against Israel’s settlement … The post Three western nations move to ban imports of Israeli products from West Bank settlements appeared first on Egypt Inde
items.body_text:
Britain, France, and Canada on Tuesday announced measures to ban imports of goods originating from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The three nations said that this aims to support the two-state solution amidst growing international concern over settlement expansion, Reuters reported.
The move comes part of a series of measures against Israel’s settlement policy, and follows as ten other countries have joined a joint statement affirming their commitment to protecting the two-state solution and pursuing a just and lasting peace through negotiations.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said that his country could no longer simply condemn what he described as injustice and suffering, emphasizing the need to take action against settlement expansion—a practice he views as a threat to the viability of a future Palestinian state.
Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand affirmed that settlements in the West Bank undermine efforts to achieve a long-lasting peace based on the two-state solution.
And France said that the acceleration of settlement expansion and escalating violence in the West Bank forced it to take this step.
Backlash from Israel and the US
These measures drew criticism from Israel and the US.
Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for the expulsion of the British ambassador, while National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir demanded the closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem.
These moves coincided with Israel’s announcement of plans to build 1,000 new housing units in the West Bank, amidst growing international concern regarding the “E1” settlement project near Jerusalem—a project viewed one of the most significant threats to the territorial contiguity of Palestinian lands.
Although settlement exports account for only a small fraction of Israel’s total trade, the bans carry political and diplomatic significance, forming part of broader efforts to press for the preservation of the two-state solution.

items.title: Egypt, Kekkilä-BVB review plans for alternative soil factory in SCZone
items.summary: Egypt is exploring the establishment of a local factory to produce alternative soil, aiming to cut imports, lower agricultural production costs and support the expansion of modern, high-value farming and agri-exports. Industry Minister Khaled Hashem had talks with Pekka Tennilä, CEO of Kekkilä-BVB, on the company’s plan to establish a factory in Egypt in partnership … The post Egypt, Kekkilä-BVB review plans for alternative soil factory in SCZone appeared first on Egypt Independent.
items.body_text:
Egypt is exploring the establishment of a local factory to produce alternative soil, aiming to cut imports, lower agricultural production costs and support the expansion of modern, high-value farming and agri-exports.
Industry Minister Khaled Hashem had talks with Pekka Tennilä, CEO of Kekkilä-BVB, on the company’s plan to establish a factory in Egypt in partnership with Egyptian agritech company Agriventure. The facility is planned for the Suez Canal Economic Zone and will produce alternative growing soil for precision farming.
Hashem said localizing alternative growing-soil production is a strategic priority for supporting modern and protected agriculture and increasing value added in agro-industrial manufacturing.
He added that agricultural manufacturing technologies are among the ministry’s priorities for linking scientific research with industrial outputs, meeting export requirements, reducing production costs and narrowing the import gap.
The minister also highlighted the importance of deploying advanced technologies and innovative solutions across productive activities, particularly those that help conserve water and improve resource efficiency in agriculture.
Such solutions, he said, can support the growth and competitiveness of agro-industrial projects and strengthen their export potential.
Kekkilä-BVB company officials said alternative growing media account for around 30% of the cost of precision farming, underscoring the importance of local production in reducing agricultural costs. The planned factory will serve the domestic market while expanding exports to European, African and Arab markets.
Hashem also said Agriventure could participate in the ministry’s “Productive Village” initiative, particularly in villages with a competitive edge in medicinal and aromatic plants and export-oriented crops.
The initiative aims to support balanced industrial development and curb illegal migration and population movement from the regions by leveraging the comparative advantages of each governorate and village. It includes providing small industrial workshops and complexes, concessional financing for small investors, and technical support to connect small businesses with medium- and large-scale factories and strengthen supply-chain integration.
The minister added that Egypt’s industrial map will help identify the comparative advantages of each village and potentially allocate sites for precision-farming projects, particularly in villages known for producing medicinal and aromatic plants and export-oriented crops.

items.title: Beyond useless guilt and insatiable victimhood
items.summary: In search of a new language around privilege The post Beyond useless guilt and insatiable victimhood first appeared on Mada Masr.
items.body_text:
In 2018, my first year living in Amsterdam, studying for a master’s degree in the arts, I went to a museum to attend a performance by a group of queer artists addressing questions of injustice. The setting seemed familiar enough until one of the presenters announced that anyone who did not belong to specified “marginalized identities” should leave the room. They began reading a list of those identities aloud.
For a moment, I just listened, suspended, trying to locate myself in the list. Then it became clear: the list excluded non-queer, white people. I, therefore, “belonged.” I found that the category I best fit in was “woman of color,” a definition I had never once used for myself at that time.
I stayed. The conversation turned to safety in the Netherlands, to harassment and violence connected to skin color, gender identity, sexual orientation. The others spoke from experience I could hear but not share. Amsterdam, for me, had been something else entirely: quiet nights walking alone through streets I did not know, a strange lightness I had no name for yet. No one had stopped me. No one had read me by my color. I am not denying that such violence exists, only that it had not, at that point, been my story.
And so, I said nothing.
That moment stayed with me. It crystallized something I had been sensing since arriving in Europe: a pressure, felt everywhere in public discourse, to read every experience through the lens of identity. To locate yourself on a map drawn by others and then speak only from that location.
What unsettled me was not the artists’ choice to create a protected space. It was the underlying logic, one I kept encountering: in seminar rooms, in cultural institutions, in the language of activist circles. A logic by which identity is constructed entirely on the axis of oppression: one group over another, history compressed into a single narrative, and every human being assigned a fixed position within it. You are either a victim or a perpetrator. There is no third position. The space between is simply erased.
When pain becomes a pass
When being a victim is the only position that confers moral authority, the only place from which you are permitted to speak without being immediately questioned or condemned, then victimhood stops being a condition and starts becoming a currency. And currency, by nature, is something people reach for.
But to understand why this happens so readily today, you have to look at the broader cultural atmosphere in which identity politics operates.
We live, as sociologist Frank Furedi argued in Therapy Culture: Cultivating Vulnerability in an Uncertain Age (Routledge, 2004), in a society that has undergone a profound redefinition of what a person is. Clinical language such as trauma, triggers, nervous system dysregulation, safe spaces and emotional damage has migrated out of the therapy room and into everyday speech, political discourse and social media. The effect is that vulnerability has become the defining feature of how people understand themselves and others. To be a person, in this framework, is first and foremost to be at risk, to be potentially harmed, to be in need of recognition for your wounds. The self is constituted around its injuries.
This matters because it explains the ease with which therapeutic self-diagnosis feeds into political victimhood. When the culture already teaches you to understand yourself primarily through the prism of what has damaged you, and when the cultural framework simultaneously grants moral authority only to those who have been damaged, the two systems reinforce each other seamlessly. It offers people a coherent identity, a community, a moral position and a language, all at once. What it does not offer, and what it actively erodes, is agency. Therapeutic culture places people in a permanent state of recovery rather than transcendence: you are instructed to acknowledge your wounds endlessly and to identify yourself with and through them. Sudan Nashra: Hemedti in Addis Ababa | Buildup at Ethiopian base fuels concerns over RSF corridor toward Blue Nile capital, military sends massive reinforcements | RSF fortifies West Darfur capital with berms, reinforces troops | RSF commander in North Kordofan defects, arrives in capital with 200 fighters          
        When Rapid Support Forces Commander Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo quietly touched down in Addis Ababa last week, the Blue Nile State front was raging along Ethiopia’s border and reinforcements for the fighting were amassing on both sides. Ethiopia, meanwhile, was contending with renewed tensions of its own.
For the RSF, keeping channels open with Addis Ababa is particularly important given that its border is part of the security environment surrounding the fighting in Blue Nile. Operations and troop movements along the border were among the main subjects of Hemedti’s talks, according to an RSF leadership source and an Ethiopian government source who spoke to Mada Masr. For the Ethiopian source, Addis Ababa’s immediate concern is keeping Sudan’s war from spilling across the border.
But Sudanese intelligence sees another layer to Ethiopia’s interest in the RSF. Ethiopia could factor the paramilitary group into its own military arrangements as it manages conflicts with domestic opponents, particularly amid renewed tensions with Tigray, a Sudanese intelligence source said. Such a relationship could also give Addis Ababa greater room to operate on the Sudanese side of the border, they added.
The Sudanese military is watching that possibility from an increasingly exposed position. It has lost the strategic border towns of Geisan and Kurmuk in Blue Nile and is now trying to stop the advance from the border toward Blue Nile’s capital, Damazin.
And there is a new reason for concern — a significant buildup since July at an Ethiopian military base in Asosa, located in the Benishangul-Gumuz region bordering Sudan. The area has been repeatedly used to launch major operations by the RSF and its allies into Blue Nile. But an intelligence source in the state said the recent buildup could make the cross-border corridor into Kurmuk and Geisan harder for the military to penetrate and could facilitate the unimpeded movement of supplies and forces to the RSF and its allies.
With the border towns secured, the RSF and its allies are now pushing against the military positions guarding Damazin. They captured Bakori in the Geisan locality and Sirkum in Kurmuk last week, triggering a rush of military reinforcements into the state capital and the positions around it.
While the military is shoring up Damazin, the RSF is fortifying Geneina, the capital of West Darfur. Military operations this week secured another position near the city, part of an offensive that has been underway since July and has brought military and allied forces within reach of the RSF-held capital.
The RSF is now digging around the city, extending sand berms and trenches as a defensive measure against a possible surprise attack. This week, it brought in large numbers of fighters in what a military field source described as preparation for attacks on military positions in West Darfur and neighboring North Darfur.
Kordofan, the war’s critical faultline between an RSF push east and a military push west, saw its second major defection this week. Abu Bakr Dahloub, the RSF’s intelligence chief for special missions in North Kordofan’s Hamra al-Sheikh and the Egypt-Libya-Sudan border triangle, defected to the military with around 200 fighters.
After securing major gains in North Kordofan weeks ago, the military continues to target RSF supply and gathering points in neighboring West Kordofan. items.body_text:
What’s behind the US sanctions on Banque Misr UAE?                    
                For Egyptian officials, the singling out of Banque Misr UAE in American sanctions was shocking, even if there are multiple rationales through which the move could be read.
The announcement of sanctions that came on Friday was the latest move in America’s new strategy to suffocate Iran. In mid August, United States President Donald Trump let it be known that he was fed up. After months of negotiations with Iran over an end to a war, a war that the US and Israel started, had failed to materialize, it was time to change tactics.
This time, it wouldn’t be a new naval blockade on an existing naval blockade. It wouldn’t be more military action. This time, Trump wrote on his social media account, the pain would come in the form of the “MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY.”
Essentially, the plan, dubbed “Economic D-Day,” a reference to the US invasion of Nazi-held France during World War II, would see Washington DC impose secondary sanctions on any country that “allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran.”
Swooping in to take up the messaging of the plan, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent began to beat the war drum of economic sanctions.
“If you insist on doing business with [Iran], then the US Treasury and U.S. government will put its full might and force against you,” Bessent said on August 20. “It’s time for our allies and the rest of the world to make a decision.”
The media was awash in speculation. Turkey and the United Arab Emirates are among Iran’s largest trade partners. Would the US really consider sanctioning such key allies?
And then the decisive day came. On Friday, the US treasury announced its first salvo.
First to be sanctioned was Reza Mohammad Taeedi, the manager of the Iranian commercial bank Bank Melli’s Dubai branch.
It made sense: an Iranian bank operating in Dubai surely must be part of a shadow banking operation.
Next was Kameng Trading Limited, a Hong Kong-based exchange company that has allegedly helped launder funds for a sanctioned Iranian exchange house.
Again, the proximity to China, which is known to have relations with Iran, made the move legible.
But the last entity included in the sanctions notice was a surprise. The United Arab Emirates branches of Banque Misr, the Egyptian state-owned bank and the second largest in Egypt, holding assets worth US$83 billion, could see its banking access to US financial institutions revoked, the US treasury announced.
Describing the five branches of what is Egypt’s second largest bank, the US treasury note called the bank “a critical node for the Iranian regime’s access to US dollars. Treasury estimates that between January 2024 and June 2026, Banque Misr UAE processed approximately $1.8 billion for 103 companies that are potentially part of Iranian shadow banking networks.”
“Banque Misr UAE’s customers include apparent front companies used by Iran’s Ministry of Defense and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to evade US sanctions, as well as to launder money on behalf of Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei,” the statement read.
The US treasury has given Banque Misr 30 days before the sanctions take effect. In the meantime, it is accepting comments from the public, industry experts and financial institutions about the proposed sanction.
While the reasons are still unknown, the decision did not materialize out of thin air.
Since around 2023, Egypt has faced a new difficult reality.
A $23 billion deal with Saudi Arabia inked in 2016 had expired, and while the initial deal had been greased with the handover of Tiran and Sanafir islands, Egypt and Saudi relations had taken a turn for much rockier shores. items.title: Ilham Ahmed: The SDF Has Entered a New Phase; We Await Direct Channels with Turkey
items.summary: Ahead of her expected entry into the Syrian People’s Assembly, Ahmed expressed interest in joining the Foreign Relations and Constitutional committees. The post Ilham Ahmed: The SDF Has Entered a New Phase; We Await Direct Channels with Turkey first appeared on The Syrian Observer.
items.body_text:
Ilham Ahmed affirmed in an extensive interview with Turkish journalists that the integration of the Syrian Democratic Forces into the Syrian army marks the beginning of a new political chapter for the Kurdish question in Syria. She explained that the priority in the coming period will shift toward securing Kurdish rights within the constitution, alongside completing the incorporation of civil and security institutions into the state’s administrative framework.
Military Integration and the Shift Toward Politics
Ahmed stated that the military integration process has now reached its conclusion following recent meetings in Damascus. The SDF has been absorbed into the Syrian army in the form of brigades and no longer operates as an independent force.
With armed struggle giving way to political engagement, she noted that administrative arrangements remain under negotiation. Internal security personnel are registering with state security bodies, and institutions of the Autonomous Administration are being folded into government structures. Logistical complications related to staff registration slowed the process, yet government security officials have already entered Hasakah under the unified framework.
Education Disputes and the Future of the YPJ
Language policy and institutional restructuring continue to generate tension. Ahmed expressed dissatisfaction with the educational framework agreed upon with Damascus, noting that Kurdish has been designated a “national language” rather than an official state language. Under the current arrangement, Kurdish instruction is limited to three hours per week, alongside subjects such as history, geography and philosophy. This represents a significant reduction from the previous curriculum, in which most subjects were taught in Kurdish.
Regarding the Women’s Protection Units, Ahmed revealed that initial proposals to integrate the YPJ directly into the Syrian army were rejected during negotiations. Current discussions focus on transferring the units to the Ministry of Interior, where they would operate as a specialised operations force.
Constitutional Ambitions and Prospects in Parliament
Ahead of her expected entry into the Syrian People’s Assembly, Ahmed expressed interest in joining the Foreign Relations and Constitutional committees. She said that deliberations on a new constitution will begin once parliament is fully convened. Key priorities include securing linguistic and cultural rights for Kurds, Armenians, Assyrians and Turkmen, and exploring forms of administrative decentralisation that would grant provinces broader self-governing authority.
Regional Dynamics and Relations with Turkey
Ahmed acknowledged Turkey’s decisive influence on the dialogue with Damascus and on the ceasefire that followed. She confirmed the existence of communication channels with Turkish security institutions, although no formal link with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs has been established.
She voiced a clear desire for direct channels with Ankara and expressed readiness to visit Turkey and Imrali in pursuit of peace. In her view, Turkey remains a central interlocutor in the broader Kurdish question, and any durable settlement will require sustained engagement with Ankara.

items.title: UN Commission of Inquiry Highlights Fragility of Syria’s Political Transition
items.summary: Nearly a year after the adoption of the Suweida roadmap, critical human rights concerns remain unresolved, Ultra Syria writes. The post UN Commission of Inquiry Highlights Fragility of Syria’s Political Transition first appeared on The Syrian Observer.
items.body_text:
The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Syria reported that the country is undergoing profound political and institutional shifts despite formidable challenges. In its latest assessment, the panel noted the return of more than 1.7 million refugees and nearly two million internally displaced persons, alongside continued progress in integrating the Syrian Democratic Forces into state institutions.
A Transition Still in Delicate Balance
The commission cautioned that Syria’s transitional phase remains fragile, shaped by the difficulty of establishing institutions that are both legitimate and accountable. While acknowledging government efforts to address post-2025 violence in the coastal region, central-western Syria and Suweida, the panel urged the newly formed People’s Assembly to place fundamental human rights at the core of its legislative agenda.
Israeli Incursions and Violations of Sovereignty
The commission identified Israeli military operations as a major obstacle to Syria’s stability and territorial integrity. Following the fall of the Assad regime, Israeli forces expanded their presence through temporary checkpoints, permanent military installations inside and beyond the 1974 buffer zone, and routine ground incursions.
These actions, the panel said, severely restrict civilian movement, undermine agricultural livelihoods and inflict significant environmental damage. By September 2026, investigators had documented the detention of forty-nine individuals, including two children, by Israeli forces on Syrian soil. Several detainees were transferred to Israel or held in incommunicado detention.
Suweida: Persistent Tensions and Unresolved Rights
Nearly a year after the adoption of the Suweida roadmap, critical human rights concerns remain unresolved, contributing to heightened insecurity across the governorate. Friction between local authorities and the national government, compounded by ongoing Israeli interference, has left large areas effectively isolated.
Key grievances include:
- Unresolved cases involving missing and detained persons.
- Armed groups preventing students from sitting for state-administered examinations.
- Delayed accountability for grave violations committed in March and July 2025, despite limited trials beginning in July 2026.
Displacement, Property Disputes and Civil Liberties
The commission continues to investigate reports of kidnapped women and girls, the ongoing displacement of Druze, Bedouin and Alawite families, and allegations of property seizures targeting Alawite and Shiite communities in Hama and Homs. These concerns compound extensive property disputes inherited from the previous administration.
Although freedom of expression has broadened, the panel warned of a troubling rise in arrests under the 2022 Cybercrime Law targeting activists who criticize the government. Investigators also noted increasing reports of online hate speech, harassment of minority communities and threats of violence against women.
Regarding displacement camps, the commission stressed that the closure of the Roj camp is long overdue. The facility still houses more than two thousand women and children with alleged ties to ISIS, a violent extremist organization responsible for severe human rights abuses and mass atrocities.

items.title: Syrian Oil Refinery Workers Suspend Protests After Mass Layoffs and Mounting Health Risks
items.summary: Between 1,200 and 1,300 workers lost their jobs despite having served for twelve to fifteen years under companies affiliated with the Autonomous Administration. The post Syrian Oil Refinery Workers Suspend Protests After Mass Layoffs and Mounting Health Risks first appeared on The Syrian Observer.
items.body_text:
A surge of unrest has swept through the oil refinery belt surrounding Rumeilan in Hassakeh Governorate, after more than one thousand workers were abruptly dismissed from the Awdah, Al-Taflah, Al-Suwaydiyyah and Karzero fields, as well as the Tal Adas pumping station. In early September 2026, dismissed workers blocked international transit routes used by oil tankers, bringing long-standing grievances over labor exploitation, severe health risks and political transition to the surface.
Mass Layoffs and a Breakdown in Institutional Integration
Between 1,200 and 1,300 workers lost their jobs despite having served for twelve to fifteen years under companies affiliated with the Autonomous Administration. After the integration agreement between the Syrian government and the Syrian Democratic Forces, workers received state-stamped identification cards from the Rumeilan fields, leading them to believe they had been incorporated into the new institutional structure. Instead, they were met with sudden dismissal notices.
Protesters rejected proposals by local officials to send a four-person delegation to Damascus for negotiations, insisting that authorities address the crisis directly at the work sites.
Hazardous Operations and Alarming Mortality Rates
Workers described conditions in the region’s primitive refineries as perilous and devoid of basic safety standards. Crude oil processing in these facilities produces only three fuels—gasoline, diesel and gas—while remaining derivatives are released as toxic vapors.
Continuous exposure has resulted in an estimated mortality rate of twelve per cent among the workforce, with between 150 and 170 deaths attributed to cancer and severe respiratory illnesses. The highest risks are concentrated in three roles:
- Furnace and Crude Operators: Exposed directly to burning processes and raw crude.
- Gas Technicians: Handling volatile vapors where minor errors can trigger catastrophic explosions.
- Fuel Handlers: Discharging highly flammable fuel at temperatures between 300°C and 360°C into covered pits for transport.
Additional dangers confront filling yard inspectors who mix crude with hazardous chemicals and clean asphalt residues after incineration.
A Conditional Truce and Threats of a Full Shutdown
Although protesters reopened roads to oil tankers on 4 September 2026 after receiving administrative assurances, the suspension remains tentative. Workers are demanding permanent contracts, comprehensive health coverage and safe working conditions.
They warned that if these commitments are not honored, they will escalate their actions by relocating sit-ins directly to oil pumps and storage tanks, a move that could shut down the region’s energy infrastructure entirely.

items.body_text:
Who should be in charge of the war?
This article is based upon my experiences in MOD UK and Army and Joint staff during the first Gulf War, Bosnia and with NATO in Kosovo. I turned for support to my US defence academic friend and author Dr Thomas Durell Young a former member of staff at the US war college, and a former Policy Director in MOD Bulgaria Retired Colonel Vladimir Milenski. We all worked variously together with MOD Ukraine in 2014 and 2015 and between us on reform in over 15 other countries worldwide. I apologize in advance to my female military friends for using he throughout this article, but it reflects simplicity of writing before translation not denigration of your amazing contribution to the national war effort.
Introduction: War Does Not Suspend Democratic Defence Governance, it severely tests it
In a democratic state at war, the defence system must be able to fight effectively while remaining politically controlled, legally accountable, strategically coherent and operationally agile. War increases pressure on institutions, but the defence system must not become insular or a power on its own. War does not remove the need for clear authority, lawful responsibility and public accountability. On the contrary, the greater the stakes, the more important it is to know who governs defence, who advises government, who generates forces, who plans strategy and campaigns, who commands operations, and who answers for results. Today this is not totally clear in Ukraine.
The institutional question is therefore not primarily one of terminology. Different democratic states use different titles for organisations and posts. What matters is whether these offices form a coherent system in which authority, responsibility, military advice, operational command, force generation, political control and accountability are clearly separated where necessary and integrated where useful – and most importantly society can see who is in charge and responsible for each task. There is no doubt that to achieve a well-oiled, well-managed system the key requirement is outstanding teamwork. The fastest and best process is always two friends working together with a common purpose. Lack of trust, institutional arrogance, poor teamwork, bureaucracy or unclear tasks lead to delay - and delay kills.
In this regard the Minister and senior commanders, MOD, General Staff (GS) and Joint Staff (JS) must function as a single organism, working closely together not in opposition. I have been lucky to work in a combined MOD/General Staff in UK with teams of officers and civil servants serving together. Meetings contained staff from all relevant HQs from MOD to units and many key decisions could be made and implemented immediately without need for bureaucracy. The civilian component came with different, less narrow thinking and skills, and added to achieving results hugely. Sharing work openly is vastly better than strict ownership.
In Ukraine, the main headquarters are the MOD and the General Staff (GS) (Most countries would call this HQ, Defence Staff as it is more than just army). We suggest a third strand is needed as Joint Staff, which should manage the fighting. UK and many NATO countries have an operational Joint Staff HQ and US have the regional combatant commands (COCOMS) reflecting their world view. Together, these three HQs would form a leadership triangle with clear and separate tasks. I have worked variously at all three levels. Depending on the issue in need of resolution, one headquarters leads the staff work, while the others support it. The next day the task and leadership requirement may be totally different. States that inherit command structures from the Soviet military tradition and then introduce institutions associated with modern democratic and NATO ways of defence management are always challenged in who does what, how and when.
