items.body_text:
134th IPRM Meeting Held in Ergneti
The 134th meeting of the Incident Prevention and Response Mechanism (IPRM) took place on September 8 in the village of Ergneti, near the occupation line in Georgia’s Russia-occupied Tskhinvali region.
The meeting, which brought together the representatives of Georgia’s central government and de facto authorities of Tskhinvali/South Ossetia, was co-facilitated by Bettina Patricia Boughani, Head of the EU Monitoring Mission in Georgia (EUMM), and Christoph Späti, Special Representative of the OSCE Chairperson-in-Office for the South Caucasus.
During the meeting, Tbilisi again raised the issues of illegal detentions and so-called borderization, as well as the need to hold accountable those responsible for the killing of Georgian citizen Tamaz Ginturi. Representatives of Tskhinvali’s de facto authorities, meanwhile, again called for the removal of the Chorchana/Tsnelisi police checkpoint and raised concerns about the well-being of Tamaz Goloev, a Tskhinvali resident currently in custody in Georgia proper on espionage allegations.
The next IPRM meeting is set to take place on October 22.
The Incident Prevention and Response Mechanism (IPRM) was established in 2009 within the framework of the Geneva International Discussions that followed the 2008 Russo-Georgian war. It serves as a forum for the regular discussion of security-related incidents and developments on the ground. IPRM meetings have been held regularly in Ergneti, near the Tskhinvali occupation line, with the participation of representatives from Tbilisi and the Tskhinvali de facto authorities. In contrast, meetings in Gali, in occupied Abkhazia, have been suspended multiple times, from 2012 to 2016, and again since 2018. The meetings are co-facilitated by the OSCE and the European Union Monitoring Mission in Georgia (EUMM).
SSSG Statement
Georgia’s State Security Service (SSSG) said that participants discussed “all significant” incidents recorded in the occupied Tskhinvali region and areas adjacent to the occupation line since the previous IPRM meeting. The discussions also addressed restrictions on freedom of movement and the operation of the so-called crossing points.
“The representatives of the State Security Service again strictly raised the issue of bringing to justice and ensuring the enforcement of law against the representative(s) of the Russian occupation force responsible for the murder of Georgian citizen Tamaz Ginturi,” the SSSG said.
The Georgian side also condemned the continued process of so-called borderization and highlighted what it described as a “growing trend of fundamental human rights violations” in the occupied Tskhinvali region.
Representatives of the central government also “strictly demanded the immediate release of all individuals in illegal detention,” the SSSG said.
EUMM, OSCE Statement
According to the co-facilitators, restrictions on freedom of movement remain in place, although they welcomed the more frequent opening of crossing points.
The co-facilitators “underlined that greater opportunities for cross-ABL [Administrative Boundary Line] movement can improve the daily lives, livelihoods and sense of security of conflict-affected women, men and children, and encouraged further steps towards the full reopening of the crossing points,” the OSCE press release said.
According to the press release, “detention cases remained an important part of the discussions,” noting that the EUMM and OSCE “reiterated their concern over continued detentions and called for a humanitarian approach to resolving all existing cases.”
“All participants reaffirmed the key role of the EUMM-managed Hotline in facilitating the timely exchange of information and contributing to stability along the ABL,” the release said, adding that “the Hotline continued to address a range of practical, security and humanitarian issues, including detentions, “borderisation” and socio-economic issues.”

items.body_text:
NBG Keeps Refinancing Rate Unchanged at 8.25%, Expects 5.2% Inflation in 2026
The National Bank of Georgia (NBG) decided to keep the key refinancing rate unchanged at 8.25% following a September 9 meeting of its Monetary Policy Committee (MPC). The Central Bank expects inflation to average 5.2% in 2026 before gradually converging with its 3% target over the medium term.
Noting that annual inflation stood at 5.6% in August, it attributed the deviation from its target to “supply-side shocks,” including rising energy prices, as “renewed geopolitical tensions” in the Middle East have increased “uncertainty” surrounding energy supplies and “heightened volatility in international prices.” It also noted that “inflationary pressures stemming from international food markets have intensified.”
While saying that core inflation was 3.6%, and services inflation amounted to 4.4%, it noted that such developments suggest that, despite the supply shock, “its impact on inflation expectations remains moderate,” though cautioning that “a prolonged shock increases the risk of its transmission to inflation expectations, making second-round effects an important factor to monitor.”
According to the NBG’s assessment, “recent inflation dynamics remain broadly in line with the central forecast,” and under its central scenario, “average annual inflation is projected at around 5.2% in 2026, before gradually converging to the 3% target over the medium term.”
It also said that Georgia’s “economic activity remains strong,” citing 8% economic growth in July and noting that “high-productivity sectors continue to make a significant contribution to economic growth, partly offsetting inflationary pressures stemming from strong aggregate demand.”
As uncertainty surrounding the evolution of geopolitical tensions and their economic impact “remains high,” the MPC considered both high- and low-inflation risk scenarios in making its decision.
Under the high-inflation scenario, the NBG assumes that “a prolonged period of heightened geopolitical tensions,” coupled with “an increase in international food prices due to adverse climate conditions,” would affect inflation expectations and “amplify second-round effects.” In such a scenario, the Bank said, “inflation would be higher,” requiring “a tighter monetary policy stance.”
Under its lower-inflation scenario, the NBG said “structural changes in the economy” have increased the contribution of higher-productivity and less import-intensive sectors, strengthening productive capacity and improving Georgia’s “external position.” If these trends persist, the bank said, “stronger productive capacity would moderate demand-driven inflationary pressures,” while an improved external position and lower sovereign risk premium “would support a stronger fundamental exchange rate.” In that case, “headline inflation would converge to the target faster.”
“Taking into account the current macroeconomic environment and prevailing risks,” the MPC therefore decided to keep the monetary policy rate at 8.25%. It added that if “prolonged supply-side shocks lead to an upward trend in inflation expectations” and amplify second-round effects, “the MPC will continue to increase the monetary policy rate moderately.”
The next Monetary Policy Committee meeting is scheduled for October 21, 2026.

items.body_text:
EU Representative Raises Human Rights, Justice Concerns Over Georgia at UN
Michele Cervone d’Urso, the EU’s Deputy Permanent Representative to the UN, raised concerns over Georgia, recalling its obligation to “uphold fundamental freedoms” and urging the “repeal or substantial revision” of legislation that undermines human rights and targets dissent.
“The EU recalls Georgia’s obligation to uphold fundamental freedoms and urges the repeal or substantial revision of recent legislation that undermines international human rights standards,” Cervone d’Urso said while speaking at the 63rd session of the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva.
The EU representative said the bloc is “deeply concerned” by what he described as the “politically motivated use of the justice system against civil society organisations” and the adoption of “repressive measures targeting opposition figures, human rights defenders, and independent media.”
He added that the EU “strongly condemns arbitrary arrests and increasing repression,” including “the imprisonment of opposition leaders, independent journalists, media workers, and civil society actors.”
Cervone d’Urso emphasized the need for Georgia to “address these issues, align its policies with international standards, and engage in constructive dialogue to restore trust in its democratic institutions.”
The relations between Georgia, which became an EU candidate country in 2023, and Brussels worsened amid the Georgian Dream government’s anti-democratic moves and anti-EU discourse. The EU said in November 2025 that Georgia is a candidate country “in name only” and moved to suspend visa-free travel for Georgian holders of diplomatic and service passports.

items.title: Armenia downgrades foreign espionage charges against opposition figure
items.summary: While not explicitly mentioned, details in the previous charge implied Tevanyan was spying on behalf of Russia.
items.body_text:
The charges against Armenian opposition figure Andranik Tevanyan have been changed from espionage to publishing state secrets. While not explicitly mentioned, the earlier charge – filed days before Armenia’s June parliamentary elections – implied Tevanyan was spying on behalf of Russia and appeared to be the country’s first-ever investigation into Russian-backed espionage since independence.
The change was revealed roughly a week before the start of Tevanyan’s trial on 8 September. The proceedings are being held behind closed doors, which the court has justified on the grounds that the case purportedly contains state secrets.
During the first session, Tevanyan’s pre-trial detention was extended for another three months.
In a voice message, Tevanyan addressed the change in charges, describing the case as ‘fabricated’. His lawyer, Aram Orbelyan, later confirmed the new charge in an interview with RFE/RL.
A conviction of publishing a state secret carries a prison sentence of up to six years, but it depends on the specific provision applied.
The most recent indictment submitted to the court also no longer contains the Investigative Committee’s earlier claim that Tevanyan had been recruited by the special services of a foreign state – which was widely presumed to be Russia. Instead, the indictment reportedly refers to a public organisation.
He was initially accused of acting on the instructions of a foreign intelligence representative described as the director of the ‘Russia Caucasus’ geopolitical centre. OC Media could not find any publicly available information about the organisation.
The indictment also no longer mentions the allegation that Tevanyan transferred information containing a state secret to a representative of a foreign special service in exchange for $622,000. According to Orbelyan, the figure was based on a budget estimate for a grant obtained during the preliminary investigation from a company which Tevanyan headed, but did not actually receive the money.
The lawyer did not specify which grant programme or organisation the estimates had been prepared for.
The Investigative Committee’s statement in May claimed Tevanyan ‘illegally’ collected and transferred ‘information containing state secrets — namely, information translated into Russian regarding the course and results of hearings held during a closed, classified session of the parliament in April 2024’.
His case also includes Aregnaz Manukyan, a member of Tevanyan’s Mother Armenia party, who has been in pre-trial detention since July. She is accused of disclosing information constituting a state secret that she had access to as an MP, which she allegedly passed to Tevanyan.
Both Tevanyan and Manukyan maintain their innocence.
The earlier allegations were first made public by Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan amid the election campaign and Tevanyan was charged shortly after.
The case against Tevanyan came amid heightened tensions with Russia as Moscow gradually imposed restrictions on Armenian imports. Many saw this move as an attempt to influence the election outcome.
Tevanyan has denied the allegations and described the case as an attempt to obstruct his political alliance’s election campaign. Tevanyan was a candidate on tycoon and opposition figure Gagik Tsarukyan’s electoral list for the June parliamentary elections.
Two days after the original charges were announced, Pashinyan said at a press briefing that Armenia and Russia had an agreement not to engage in espionage activities on each other’s territory, adding that the investigation would establish whether the agreement had been violated.

items.title: Azerbaijan begins mining in gold reserves formerly controlled by Armenia
items.summary: The territory had been under Armenian control until the Second Nagorno-Karabakh War of 2020.
items.body_text:
Azerbaijan’s state-owned mining company AzerGold has begun drilling and blasting at the Soyudlu (Zod) gold deposit in the Kalbajar District, on the border with Armenia.
The project has a complicated legal and political history. The site was under Armenian control until the Second Nagorno-Karabakh War in 2020, after which it was handed back to Azerbaijan.
According to RFE/RL, the deposit was discovered in 1951 on the border between Azerbaijan’s Kalbajar District and Armenia’s Gegharkunik Province. It has been reported that the majority of the deposit — 75% of its gold reserves, or 17 of its 25 gold-bearing shafts — was located on Azerbaijani territory.
However, by order of the Soviet Ministry of Geology, management of the deposit was transferred to Armenia’s geological administration. Industrial exploitation of the deposit reportedly began in 1976, and 27.6 tonnes of gold were extracted from it by the early 1990s.
Following the collapse of the Soviet Union, the deposit was operated on the Armenian side for many years by the Russian company GeoProMining Gold. After Azerbaijan gained control of the territories after the 2020 war, GeoProMining withdrew.
In 1997, Azerbaijan signed a production sharing agreement with the US-based RV Investment Group Services to develop mines in the area.
Anglo Asian Mining later took over from RV Investment Group Services as the legal successor to the development rights.
However, because the Soyudlu deposit was under Armenian control at the time, the company was unable to carry out actual operations in Azerbaijani-controlled areas.
In 2022, the Azerbaijani government restructured the legal framework of the development agreement, listing the Ecology and Natural Resources Ministry as a party in 2022.
Subsequently, the state designated AzerGold as its representative under the agreement in June 2024.
Since August 2025, large-scale geological studies, topographic planning, and drilling operations with a total depth of 18,000 metres have been conducted at the deposit. Based on the results of geological research and exploration, the recoverable remaining reserves of the Soyudlu gold deposit have been estimated at 1 million ounces (28 tonnes).
At the current stage of the Soyudlu project, a total of 236 people, including employees of contractor companies, are employed. Of these, 55 reside in the Kalbajar District.
During the initial development and construction phase of the project covering 2026–2029, approximately 700 people are expected to be employed directly and indirectly. Once the Soyudlu mine reaches full-scale production, the project is expected to employ over 1,300 people.
Aliyev ‘bails out’ his daughters
AzerGold has been linked to reports of corruption associated with President Ilham Aliyev’s family.
In 2016, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP) published an investigation based on the Panama Paper leaks, which suggested that President Ilham Aliyev granted the mining rights to six gold deposits, worth billions of dollars, to a consortium allegedly owned by his daughters through offshore companies.
As part of the undisclosed arrangement, the daughters were to receive 70% of the future mining profits, while the state would receive the remaining 30%.
The investigation suggested the mining operations were largely unsuccessful and unprofitable, citing an official working in a company under the consortium as saying its managers ‘clearly did not understand the mining business and were making costly mistakes’.
Aliyev ordered the state-run AzerGold to buy out the consortium in 2016. The OCCRP has framed this takeover as something that would ‘likely rescue the daughters’ investment’.
‘It is not clear how much money the family will recoup from the failed venture because the terms of the deal are not yet finalised’, the OCCRP wrote in May 2016.
At the time, the OCCRP said that Azerbaijan has not responded to its requests for comment.

items.title: Georgian court upholds years-long sentences against four involved in Chiatura mine protests
items.summary: The four protesters were first sentenced in January 2026.
items.body_text:
The Kutaisi Court of Appeals has upheld a lower court’s ruling that had sentenced four labour protesters from the mining town of Chiatura to multiple years in prison on violence-related charges. Prosecutors have accused all four of attacking the director of a local mine in April 2025.
Judge Tamar Mazanashvili announced the decision on Tuesday, leaving Giorgi Neparidze and Merab Saralidze to serve six years and three months in prison for ‘organising and participating in group violence’, while Tengiz Gvelesiani and Archil Chumburidze were left to serve four years and three months jail for ‘participating in organised group violence’.
All four were first detained on 29 April 2025 and charged over an alleged attack on Tengiz Koberidze, the director of Shukruti mine of the Chiatura municipality.
The detentions occurred during the active phase of a strike in Chiatura demanding improved labour conditions. As other participants of the strike reported at the time, Koberidze insulted protest participants, calling them a ‘herd of cattle’, which triggered the scuffle.
The sentences against the four were announced by the Kutaisi City Court — the administrative centre of the Imereti region where Chiatura is located — in January 2026.
Saralidze and Chumburidze are miners who have been long employed by the mining company Georgian Manganese. Saralidze participated in protests and strikes for better labour conditions for several years, including in the mass hunger strike in the summer of 2023.
Gvelesiani, originally from Chiatura but living in Tbilisi, was an active supporter of protests in Chiatura and often joined strikes and other protests organised by locals.
Neparidze is a resident of Shukruti, a village heavily affected by manganese mining. Since 2019, Shukruti residents have considered Neparidze to be their leader. They have been protesting damages caused by mining operations to their houses on and off since.
The first-instance court had already handed down the prison sentences when Neparidze was tried once again in July 2026, this time on charges of insulting a judge during the proceedings, and was sentenced to an additional 18 months in prison.
His lawyer, Nino Andriashvili, told OC Media on Wednesday that the court had not considered — and therefore has still not clarified — whether the longer sentence imposed in the original case would absorb the shorter one, as is generally provided for under Georgian law.
According to Andriashvili, the Court of Appeal also did not address this issue on Tuesday when it upheld the verdicts in the violence-related cases. The lawyer now plans to raise the issue of absorption during the appeal of the 18-month sentence.
During the court proceedings, the now-convicted men said they were being punished for protesting in defence of their rights. They also told the court that the problems they were protesting against would not be resolved by imprisoning them.

items.title: Finland closes investigation into stray Ukrainian drones
items.summary: Four warhead-carrying drones strayed into Finnish territory in separate incidents during the spring.
items.body_text:
Finnish authorities have concluded their investigation into separate incidents during the spring when drones carrying warheads strayed into Finland.
The incidents were jointly investigated by the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) and the Finnish Border Guard.
In a statement, the authorities said that all four drones originated from Ukraine, were similar models and were manufactured for military use. Each drone was carrying explosives, the statement confirmed.
The drones were discovered during March in Kouvola, Luumäki and near Parikkala, and in April near the town of Iitti.
Finnish authorities believe that one of the drones exploded while in the air, while the other three were detonated in controlled explosions shortly after they were discovered.
The Finnish Border Guard investigated the incidents as violations of Finnish territory, while the NBI probed the potential charge of aggravated endangerment.
"The preliminary investigations have not revealed any evidence that would have justified continuing the pursuit of criminal liability," the press release stated, adding that the cases are now closed.
Finland not a target
In its statement, the NBI and the Finnish Border Guard emphasised that Finland was not the intended target in any of the incidents where the drones strayed into Finnish territory.
Instead, the devices were likely "hijacked" in mid-air while flying towards targets in Russia, and redirected westward.
UK newspaper The Telegraph uncovered evidence in the spring that a transmitter in the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad uses GPS jamming and spoofing to redirect Ukraine's drones away from Russia and towards the airspace of Nato member states.
The investigation by Finnish authorities also noted the impact of the prevailing weather conditions as a key factor.
"The wind direction at the time of the incidents was almost directly from the south. These factors are assessed to have affected the aircraft's navigation and their deviation from their original route," the press release stated.
None of the four drones that ended up in Finnish territory caused any personal injury or damage to property.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky issued an apology to Finland in the aftermath of the drone find near Kouvola and emphasised that Ukraine was not targeting Finland under any circumstances.
Yle News' All Points North podcast heard from UK security expert Keir Giles about the phenomenon of drones straying into Finnish airspace. You can listen to the episode via this embedded player, on Yle Areena, via Apple, Spotify or wherever you get your podcasts.

items.title: Google announces €13bn additional investment in Finland
items.summary: The money will be used to develop data centres as well as supporting infrastructure, and represents the search engine giant's largest single investment in Europe to date.
items.body_text:
Search engine giant Google has announced plans to invest an additional 13 billion euros in Finland over the next two years.
The operations will be focused on the municipalities of Kajaani, Muhos, and Vaala — where Google has previously purchased land from the Finnish state — as well as expanding the existing centre in Hamina.
In a statement to Yle, Google's parent company Alphabet said that the money will be invested in data centres and related artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, as well as in the company's overall operations in Finland.
In a press release, the firm noted that the deepening of its "long-term commitment" to Finland also marks its biggest investment in Europe to date.
"This is Google’s largest single investment in Europe and a testament to Finland’s leadership in responsibly building AI infrastructure — demonstrating what is possible through strong partnerships to create long-term community value and world-class environmental sustainability," the statement said.
Finnish Country Manager Antti Järvinen also noted that the outlay is one of the largest investments in Finland's industrial history.
The investment will also support clean energy projects, the statement added, as well as providing community funds to "support local biodiversity, education, research, and workforce development".
Google has been steadily expanding its operations in Finland since converting an old paper mill into a data centre in Hamina, on the southeast coast, in 2009.
Investment means thousands of jobs, Google CIO says
Google previously announced the expansion of its data centre infrastructure in Finland, involving the same municipalities, in 2024.
Those plans were later put on ice as the firm said it was awaiting more details about the government's proposed removal of a tax benefit.
Wednesday's announcement confirms that the plans to build data centres in these three locations of Kajaani, Muhos, and Vaala will now go ahead.
Google's Chief Investment Officer Ruth Porat said at a press conference on Wednesday morning that the construction phase of the data centres will lead to the creation of over 37,000 jobs. The operational phase will see thousands more jobs opening up, Porat added.
Finland has become a magnet for data centres in recent years, with companies such as Microsoft and TikTok owner ByteDance recently announcing planned investments.
Companies are attracted to Finland because of the country's climate — which helps reduce the costs associated with the heat produced by data centres — as well as Finland's large supplies of low-carbon electricity.
PM Orpo defends data centres
Speaking at the same press conference on Wednesday morning, Prime Minister Petteri Orpo (NCP) noted the announcement of new data centre projects is not always warmly welcomed in Finland.
"In public debate in Finland, the impact of data centres on employment is often underestimated. I find this peculiar in a country that has struggled with high unemployment for a long time," he said, adding that "this means jobs, many jobs for Finns all over Finland".
PM Orpo further noted that the expansion of Google's operations in Finland will "generate significant tax revenues for municipalities and central government".
The criticisms of data centres focus on their potential to drain local resources as well as concerns that their rapid expansion exacerbates the climate crisis.
Edit note: Article updated at 11:31 on 9.9.2026 to include more background on Google's operations in Finland as well as quotes from the press conference.

items.title: Finnair cancels UK flights as air traffic disruption continues

items.body_text:
A technical glitch affecting the air traffic control provider Nats has caused widespread disruption to flights to and from the UK.
According to flight tracking website FlightRadar24, up to 1,000 flights have been cancelled, affecting tens of thousands of passengers.
Finland's national airline Finnair cancelled or re-routed a number of flights on Tuesday.
For example, Finnair flight AY1335 from Helsinki to London landed at Stansted Airport instead of Heathrow, while the return to Helsinki was cancelled.
The airline also cancelled two evening Helsinki-London flights on Tuesday.
According to information from Finavia, Finland's airport services provider, the disruption is continuing into Wednesday as the first London-Helsinki flight of the day has been cancelled.
A spokesperson for Finnair told Yle that the airline will be in contact with passengers affected by any possible cancellations or delays.
According to FlightRadar24's latest data, at least 180 flights to and from the UK will be cancelled on Wednesday, with more disruptions likely.
Nats, the aviation service responsible for air traffic control at British airports, said on Tuesday evening that the fault had been identified and resolved.

items.title: Swedish election blog: More than 2 million voters have already cast their ballot
items.summary: With less than a week to go until Election Day in Sweden, follow The Local's blog to help you navigate the world of Swedish politics.
items.body_text:
1.30pm. Election Day isn't even here yet, but almost 2.1 million voters have already voted, up from almost 1.6 million at the same time before the 2022 election. Just to remind you, here's how to vote in advance.
And with that I'm putting the blog to bed for today. I'll be back again tomorrow morning with the latest updates. Thanks as always for reading!
1.15pm. I've been getting a lot of questions today about what the various parties stand for, so I thought I'd point you in the direction of our in-depth guides. In order of size:
12.20pm. I am, as usual around this time of the day, live in the comments under our Members Q&A article to answer your questions about the Swedish election. Join me there?
11.40am. Did you watch the immigration debate on SVT on Sunday? The Local's James Savage did, and he writes it showed that immigration isn't a straightforward vote-winner any longer. But by focusing almost entirely on refugees, the debate managed to ignore the people who actually migrate to Sweden in the 2020s. Here's an excerpt from James' analysis, but I recommend reading the whole thing:
Immigration policy is no longer just a fight about who can be toughest – that's a big change. But the debate was stuck in a misconception of what immigration to Sweden looks like today.
About 23,500 people came to Sweden last year on a work permit or as a dependant of someone on a work permit. 3,500 came as asylum seekers, excluding the 9,300 Ukrainians who came under the EU's temporary protection directive. Around 25,000 came as family members, many of them family members of Swedish citizens (some of them Swedish citizens with immigration backgrounds, many not).
You wouldn't have guessed this by listening to Sunday's debate, which barely discussed any other form of immigrant than refugees, or the families of refugees.
And as readers of The Local know too well, labour immigration hasn't been plain sailing these past few years: these immigrants have been hit by their teenage children being deported, by retroactive changes to work permit salary threshholds and to citizenship rules, that have made some reconsider their choice of moving to Sweden. They also pay significant amounts in tax. The Centre Party's Niels Paarup-Petersen briefly managed to squeeze in a line about how Sweden needs to "bring people here who make us richer", but he was practically alone in doing so.
The immigration debate might be more nuanced than before – but it's a surreal debate badly in need of an update.
11.00am. Following the dramatic drop in the Pisa test results for Swedish pupils, the Liberal Party wants to put a total stop to individual screens in schools.
They're calling for an end to personal laptops and iPads, where pupils are given their own device to use as they please.
The party is also inviting all parties on the parliament's education committee to cross-party talks.
10.30am. We've been interviewing foreigners voting in the Swedish election for the first time in a series of articles. Here's the latest interview with Karolina Pudlo from Poland, who explains why she left the Moderate party over transitional rules for citizenship.
9.42am. Marcus Öhrn, the singer who fronts Jimmie Åkesson's election campaign dansband Åkezzonz, sells anti-Semitic white power music through his record label "No Shame", the Dagens ETC newspaper has reported.
"This is a huge hypocrisy from a party that claims to have come to terms with its Nazi past," the Social Democrats' party secretary Tobias Baudin told TT.
Through the company, Öhrn sells Nazi music, both used CDs and new releases. Over the weekend, the company has, among other things, posted several titles on Tradera that, according to ETC, are so grossly hateful that they are prohibited from being sold on the international music site Discogs.
As well as fronting Åkezzonz, Öhrn played in a band with Åkesson, played at his wedding, and co-wrote the Fröken Snusk song Så länge mitt hjärta slär with the Sweden Democrat leader.

items.title: Swedish government considers U-turn on 'Denmark solution' for rejected Brexit Brits
items.summary: Swedish Migration Minister Johan Forssell is considering a second chance for deported Brexit Brits – three years after The Local brought the issue to the government's attention.
items.body_text:
Forssell told public radio broadcaster Sveriges Radio that the government is considering following Denmark's lead on letting Brits who had their post-Brexit status rejected reapply.
"That's the kind of thing we're going to look into, whether it's possible and how it has worked in Denmark," he said, after several cases of Brits being handed deportation notices despite having lived in Sweden for decades sparked headlines in Sweden and internationally.
The Danish government in 2023 announced that hundreds of British nationals who had missed the deadline for post-Brexit residency status would be allowed to apply or reapply.
But a spokesperson for Forssell's predecessor, Maria Malmer Stenergard, told The Local at the time that a similar reprieve was not being planned in Sweden, months after the minister was shocked to learn from our reporter about the high number of expulsions of Brits.
It appears that the government may now be changing its mind.
"As migration minister I am completely focused on helping the Brits. We want things to be as good as possible for Brits in Sweden, of course," Johan Forssell told Sveriges Radio.
"But you also have a personal responsibility. If you have received several reminders from the Migration Agency to apply for a residence permit but still didn't, of course it's a very sad situation, and one I'm truly sorry about," he added.
Forssell's claim about people receiving several reminders from the Migration Agency is false. While the agency did publish information on its website and social media, and spoke about it in several other channels, Sweden, unlike many other countries, never contacted Brits directly.
Sweden's unusually high deportation rate of Brits post-Brexit, which The Local has been covering since at least 2023, has received widespread media attention in recent months.
The Withdrawal Agreement, under which Britain left the EU, was intended to protect the rights of British people living in the EU, giving them the legal right to stay in the EU country they lived in. Implementation was left up to individual countries.
While most countries let Brits stay – on average only 4 percent of applications were rejected across the EU – Sweden is an apparent exception. Fully 27.5 percent of applications from British citizens were rejected by the Swedish authorities. Sweden accounts for roughly one-third of all deportation or removal orders issued to British nationals across the entire EU post-Brexit, according to statistics from the UK-EU committee on citizens' rights.
They include people like John Sellers, who has lived in Sweden since he was ten and is now stuck in the UK with no clear route back to his Swedish wife; George Mason, who requires 24-hour care for Alzheimer's; or 78-year-old widow Joyce Thomas.
A rejected application is not the equivalent of actually leaving Sweden (some may have received other permits or been able to stay in other ways), but the Migration Agency confirmed to The Guardian in September 2026 that 458 British citizens have been deported or forcibly removed by police since Brexit.
In Denmark, at least 350 British nationals who lived in Denmark at the time of Brexit failed to apply to remain in the country before the deadline of the end of 2021, after designated letters to remind them were not sent out due to a technical error. Many of them were subsequently given orders to leave.
But after criticism from rights groups, who accused Danish immigration authorities of not correctly applying the rules of the Brexit Withdrawal Agreement, the Danish government announced that the deadline would be extended until the end of 2023.
The Local's editor, Emma Löfgren, argued in an opinion piece in 2023 that Sweden should follow Denmark's lead.

items.title: Why is Berlin failing to build more bike lanes?
items.summary: Berlin had millions available for cycling projects last year but only spent a fraction of its budget. With less than six percent of a planned bike network completed since 2017, here’s how local politics have put the brakes on a more bikeable capital.
items.body_text:
Recent arrivals from the UK or the US might think Berlin is already bike-friendly, but the German capital is far from meeting its own ambitions for making the city more bikeable.
These are set down in a legally binding plan and supported with dedicated funding and clear targets. Yet the latest figures show the city moving further away from its goals rather than closer to them.
According to the Senate’s latest progress report, around €82.4 million was available for cycling infrastructure in 2025 but only about €27 million was actually spent.
At the same time, just 21.2 kilometres of new cycling infrastructure were completed, down from 32.4 kilometres in 2022 and continuing a three-year decline.
Of the roughly 2,400 kilometre cycling network envisaged for Berlin by 2030, only a little over 140 kilometres had been completed between 2017 and 2025 – or around 5.8 percent of the planned total according to official figures.
Why is so little being built when the money exists and the targets are legally binding?
The answer lies in a long-running political struggle over the future of Berlin's streets – and one which has become a battleground ahead of this month's state election.
READ ALSO: 'No promises' - Decoding the political slogans plastered all over Berlin
How Berlin promised itself a cycling revolution
As with the Deutsche Wohnen & Co Enteignen campaign, citizens' initiatives sometimes deliver results in Berlin which the city’s elected representatives are reluctant to put into practice.
The roots of today's dispute lie in the Fahrradentscheid, a grassroots campaign launched by cycling activists in the mid-2010s. Given its strong public support, Berlin politicians chose not to force a citywide vote and instead incorporated many of the campaign's demands into the city's Mobility Act, which was passed in 2018.
The law created a legal framework for transforming how people move around the city. It was followed by the Cycling Plan, which specified standards and targets for a connected citywide cycling network of roughly 2,400 kilometres to be completed by 2030.
The plan includes protected cycle lanes on major roads, priority routes across the city, safer junctions and better bicycle parking.
The intention was not only to make cycling safer, but also to encourage people to switch some journeys from cars to bikes.
INTERVIEW: How being hit by a car in Berlin revealed the 'scariness' of German bureaucracy
Change of government
The political climate in Berlin changed in 2023 when a CDU-SPD (Black-Red) coalition took power in the capital. Soon after taking office, then transport senator Manja Schreiner (CDU) ordered a review of cycling projects.
In June 2023, district authorities were instructed to freeze projects involving the loss of parking spaces or road lanes, or extensive new 30 km/h zones while the new administration developed different criteria for assessing transport projects.
Later that year, the Senate began replacing the blanket pause with new guidelines that placed greater emphasis on maintaining road capacity for cars, commercial traffic and deliveries.
The decision triggered fierce criticism from cycling organisations and opposition politicians.
Speaking in June 2023, Changing Cities activist Ragnhild Sørensen accused the new administration of looking backwards rather than forwards. The ADFC cycling association argued that the Mobility Act already established clear priorities and standards, making the review unnecessary.
Schreiner defended the changes by arguing that Berlin needed to balance the needs of all road users. She said major roads needed to remain capable of handling commuter, commercial and delivery traffic.
The initial freeze and subsequent review process have created a backlog, which is one reason why funds available for cycling improvements aren’t being converted into completed projects.

items.title: INTERVIEW: 'Remigration could not be implemented by a state government'
items.summary: Many of the AfD's headline proposals for Saxony-Anhalt are either beyond state authority or unconstitutional, but the party can be expected to test the limits of the law. Lawyer and political scientist Joschka Selinger unpacks what's possible.
items.body_text:
Nine years ago, when the Alternative for Germany (AfD) first entered the Bundestag, a major question around the party was whether it could ever gain enough support to govern, even at the state level.
Now, especially following the AfD's biggest victory to date in Saxony-Anhalt, the question is no longer if the far-right party could win, but what it could do if it actually takes a leading position in a governing coalition.
The Local asked Joschka Selinger, a lawyer and head of the "Democracy and Fundamental Rights" department at The Society for Civil Rights (Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte - GFF), about the legal limits to the AfD's immigration policies, and how the judicial system could be involved in, and affected by, far-right governance.
The Local: The AfD openly talks about big plans for "remigration" and its manifesto for Saxony-Anhalt called for a "deportation offensive" backed by more state funding and new state authorities. To what extent would they be able to implement these proposals?
Joschka Selinger: A "comprehensive remigration" could hardly be implemented by a state government: asylum, immigration and citizenship rules are a matter of federal law.
However, a state government can influence residency law through individual measures, for example through administrative practice, the exhaustion of discretionary powers and the allocation of resources.
This is exactly what can be found in the AfD's "government program," such as the demand for a "task force for deportations" as well as ankle shackles or house arrest for refugees.
The Local: Could these efforts be blocked by German courts? If so, how long would that process take?
Selinger: Such individual measures can be challenged before the administrative courts. An administrative court can react very quickly in urgent legal protection, sometimes within days to weeks.
In this way, successes can be achieved against concrete individual administrative acts – such as a specific deportation order – but this doesn’t work to stop an entire policy programme.
The greater danger lies beneath openly unlawful administrative acts: a state government could undermine constitutional and fundamental rights guarantees in the long term through its administrative practice and the allocation of resources.
READ ALSO: 'Why is the AfD so popular?' - Your questions answered on the far right threat in Germany
The Local: Because many of its policies would be unconstitutional, the AfD is clearly in conflict with Germany's courts. How could the AfD undermine the courts if it were in power at the state level?
Selinger: A state government would have some levers to influence the composition of courts. These include blocking the election of state constitutional judges, and influencing judge election committees and personnel decisions in the Ministry of Justice.
Exactly this pattern is already evident in Thuringia. The AfD parliamentary group has been blocking the Judicial Election Committee since 2025 in order to force a seat on the Parliamentary Control Commission in return.
In doing so, the AfD parliamentary group is preventing the appointment of new judges for life.
The Local: Speaking of Thuringia, there we have seen the AfD undermine parliamentary processes even without a place in the governing coalition. What could we expect if the AfD fails to join a ruling state government in Saxony-Anhalt, and instead effectively becomes a blocking minority?
Selinger: With more than a third of the seats, the AfD can block all decisions that require a two-thirds majority: e.g. constitutional amendments and the election of state constitutional judges.
The current state parliament has defused this problem and introduced an emergency mechanism that will allow the state constitutional court in the future to propose candidates who can be elected by a simple majority in the event of a blocked election of judges.

items.title: Why Stuttgart has been named Germany's most digital city
items.summary: Germany lags behind when it comes to digitalisation. But a new study says Stuttgart is the most digital city in the country. Here's a look at the digital resources available to people living in the capital of Baden-Württemberg.
items.body_text:
Whether it's the painfully slow process of gaining citizenship or having to correspond with authorities by letter, foreign residents in Germany are well aware of the country's struggles to go digital.
But you could say that things have been improving in the last few years.
In some cities, including Berlin and Hamburg, people can now apply for citizenship online. Meanwhile, federal, state and local authorities have vowed to improve online services, and the German coalition government continually declares it a top priority.
Now the digital industry association Bitkom says it has found Germany's most forward-thinking city when it comes to digital matters – and it's Stuttgart.
Once a year, Bitkom compares 83 major German cities across various digitalisation categories such as administration, mobility, education and society.
Over the past three years, Munich has swiped the top spot, with Hamburg a close second. But now Stuttgart is the new digital king in Germany, ahead of both cities.
Stuttgart received a score of 92.8 points. Nuremberg and Düsseldorf round off the top five. (And if you're curious, Berlin is in 33rd place with 77.5 points.)
READ ALSO: The German states offering the most online services
"For a long time, it was said that these two cities (Munich and Hamburg) were in a league of their own when it came to digitalisation," said Sven Wagner, Head of the Smart City Division at Bitkom. "But Stuttgart has proven that you can also rise to the top through consistent digitalisation."
How is Stuttgart embracing digitalisation?
Like other German cities, Stuttgart is struggling with outdated systems and a shortage of skilled workers. It means that long queues often form outside government offices.
In 2023, The Local reported on foreign workers having to camp overnight outside the immigration offices to get an appointment due to delays.
In the years since then, the city has sought to move more services online. Certain administrative procedures, such as registering a business, can be carried out via video appointment.
"Customers are more relaxed because they can connect directly from home," local government employee Marzena Dolata-Kosiol, who uses a headset and webcam to liaise with members of the public from her desk, told Tagesschau.
"They don’t need to get into a car, so they don’t get stuck in traffic or have to queue at the office afterwards."
International residents in the area will be glad to know that you can register your address online (also known as applying for Anmeldung), while the city says that "many applications relating to immigration matters can be submitted online". These pages are also available in different languages.
People can search here to find the full range of services that are available digitally.
However, applying for citizenship is not an online process in Stuttgart – at least yet.
READ ALSO: Where in Germany wait times for citizenship are the longest
New technologies – such as AI chatbots – are also being trialled in selected areas for initial contact with residents in a bid to ease the burden on staff.
Sandra Baumholz, head of the Strategic Planning, Digital Transformation and Innovation unit at the City of Stuttgart said the changes have had a major effect on everyone.
"I think it’s a win-win situation for both sides," she said.
The move to embrace digital life is going further. Stuttgart now measures water quality in lakes using digital sensors.
Digital signposts guide people through the pedestrian zone and display events.
A ‘digital twin’ of the city takes data from departments and can, for example, map traffic trends in real time and simulate various scenarios.
"The key factor behind Stuttgart’s top ranking is that digitalisation is being tackled on a truly broad scale there," said Sven Wagner from Bitkom.
Stuttgart ranks among the top 10 in all five categories – a feat no other city has achieved.
The city ranks seventh in digitalisation of "society and education" and is hoping to improve this

“This measure is intended to maintain order and security in relation to foreigners’ activities in Bali,” Head of the Ngurah Rai Immigration Office Novyandri said in Badung District, Bali, on Wednesday.

He expressed hope that universities with well-established UPZ management systems would share their knowledge and provide guidance to other universities that are still in the early stages of establishing such philanthropic units.
Additionally, National Board of Zakat (BAZNAS) Leader for Distribution, Utilization, and Empowerment Idy Muzayyad said the potential for managing zakat funds within the higher education ecosystem was substantial.
According to BAZNAS projections, the higher education ecosystem has significant potential for zakat collection, estimated at Rp220 billion annually.
In the education sector, BAZNAS had distributed Rp 1.56 trillion in zakat, infaq, and sadaqah funds nationwide through 2025, benefiting 2,870,976 people.
Muzayyad, therefore, encouraged universities across the country to establish UPZ so that the projected zakat collection could be realized and more students facing financial difficulties could receive assistance.
He said the UPZ establishment became a requirement for universities seeking to partner with BAZNAS in distributing funds for scholarships.
"We require every university seeking access to scholarships funded by zakat to establish a UPZ. The UPZ collects zakat, which is then primarily used for activities benefiting the university's academic community, most commonly for scholarships and payment of the Single Tuition Fee (UKT)," Muzayyad said, adding that BAZNAS continually encourages universities to establish active UPZs.

items.body_text:
College students can get a year of Google AI Plus for free
MANILA, Philippines – Google is offering college students in the Philippines a one-year free subscription to Google’s AI Plus Plan.
Google AI Plus includes Study Notebooks, direct access to Gemini Omni, a personalized Daily Brief, Gemini Live, and 400 GB of cloud storage across Google Drive, Gmail, and Google Photos.
With Study Notebooks, students can upload their class materials to have Gemini create a step-by-step study plan. Guides and practice tests can be generated while important dates like exams and deadlines will directly be integrated into Google Calendar.
Meanwhile, Gemini’s interactive visualizations can help students generate 3d simulations to further understand topics. This can range from visual understanding of tables or grids for various math problems, science topics, and more.
RELATED STORY: Smart Device Link allows one number for phone and Apple Watch
How to avail the plan
Eligible students of college and universities in the country can claim the offer by visiting Google’s student hub.
Click on the student plan, then fill in your details for verification.
Students can only avail the offer until December 31, 2026.
RELATED STORY: How the service industry sees AI as a double-edged sword

NEW YORK — At the end, when five riveting sets and one agonizingly tight tiebreak were over — and when the latest-finishing match in U.S. Open history had concluded — Ben Shelton was not the only player smiling.
Carlos Alcaraz, the player Shelton had just defeated in an entertaining, spine-tingling marathon, was smiling too.
READ: Ben Shelton ends Carlos Alcaraz’s US Open title reign
The dethroned defending champ grinned as he walked to the net to hug Shelton. And he did so again a few minutes later when he stood in a hallway surrounded by reporters, reflecting on a night that seemed to have taken every ounce of his strength to endure.
“I leave the court happy,” Alcaraz said. “I leave the court with a smile. I am proud of myself, how I fought.”
There was probably not a single person in Arthur Ashe Stadium who would have disagreed.
Though many of the thousands of fans who remained until the 3:33 a.m. conclusion – yes, you read that time right – cheered for Shelton, the top-ranked American who now meets compatriot Frances Tiafoe in the semis, there were plenty who cheered for Alcaraz, one of the most charismatic players of his or any generation, and one of the most naturally gifted players ever born.
“Ole, Ole Ole Ole,” Alcaraz’s fans chanted, and “Vamos Carlos!” — competing with shouts of “USA, USA” or just “Let’s Go Ben!”
Most importantly, Alcaraz said he was leaving healthy. That had been a real concern going into this U.S. Open after a four-month break due to a wrist injury.
“As I said before the tournament began, my expectation was to go there, compete, play these kind of matches, be healthy,” he said after his 6-7 (5), 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 7-6 (10-7) defeat.
“I mean it was close, it really was close, so I was disappointed I didn’t get the win in the end, but I’m just happy … physically I was really tired, but I found a way to push myself.”
READ: Returning Carlos Alcaraz vows to take more breaks
The Spaniard also had nothing but praise for Shelton, who played the match of his young career to defeat the seven-time Grand Slam champion.
“Shelton played a very complete, very mature match,” Alcaraz said in Spanish. “He knew exactly what to do at every moment. And, physically, he’s a beast. It seemed like he had no weaknesses whatsoever. “
“It was a war,” Shelton said. “Carlos is one of the greatest champions of our sport. It was the most enjoyable match I’ve had in my career, for sure.”
Alcaraz had arrived at the U.S. Open with much uncertainty as to how much of a liability his wrist injury remained.
READ: Returning Carlos Alcaraz expects to be himself at US Open
But he seemed healthy from the start, and said he felt better than expected. In his first four rounds he lost only one set.
“It feels like I’ve been competing the whole time,” he said of his extended break. “I surprise myself the way that I’m feeling, and the way that I’m recovering after every match. I’m just really happy about it,” he had said after advancing to the fourth round, “that I’m able to perform at my best after every match.”
Alcaraz also said he’d be taking more long breaks in the future, since he didn’t need to depend on a rhythm or to play a lot of tournaments. And he was so relaxed, he didn’t even know, after handily defeating Tommy Paul in his fourth-round match, who he’d be facing next. Former U.S. Open champ Andy Roddick, a commentator for ESPN, let him know.
Then came Tuesday’s (and Wednesday’s) quarterfinals, and Shelton. After Alcaraz won the first, tight set, Shelton started playing out of his mind. He took the next two sets. Alcaraz rallied for the fourth, and then the two traded games in a nerve-wracking fifth.
Among those in the crowd cheering for Alcaraz were Anushka Sancheti and Prajakti Kapde. The two friends, both 28, had traveled to attend together — Sancheti from Atlanta, and Kapde from Raleigh, North Carolina.

items.body_text:
Antique seeks to preserve legacy of local heroes
SAN JOSE DE BUENAVISTA, Antique — The provincial government of Antique seeks to preserve the legacy of its local heroes by dedicating a hall at its old capitol building and publishing reading materials about their lives.
The Provincial Development Council, during its third quarter meeting on Wednesday, approved the inclusion of P3 million budget in the Supplemental Annual Investment Program No. 4 for the initiatives.
“We will be putting up a heroes hall and publication of reading materials to recognize and perpetuate the heroism of Antique’s local heroes,” said Board Member Vincent Piccio in an interview.
The reading materials will be distributed in schools, municipal and provincial libraries, he added.
The Heroes Hall will be placed beside the space reserved for the National Museum of the Philippines to house the memorabilia and artifacts of the local heroes.
“The Old Antique Capitol will then become a one-stop shop where the National Museum of the Philippines-Antique and the Heroes Hall would be located,” Piccio said.
Piccio said they are now coordinating with the National Historical Commission of the Philippines for the list of local heroes.
Meanwhile, he said the 127-year-old Philippine Revolutionary Flag will be installed at the heroes hall on Oct. 27, 2026, during the “Pagtugyan” (entrusting) ceremony.
The installation also marked the first year since it was turned over to the provincial government last year.
National Defense Secretary Gilbert Teodoro and Armed Forces of the Philippines chief of staff Gen. Antonio Nafarrete are among the dignitaries invited to grace the occasion. /apl

items.title: The problem with replatforming Alfred ‘Krip’ Yuson
items.summary: Publishing house Exploding Galaxies announces that it will no longer republish and circulate Yuson's novel 'Great Philippine Jungle Energy Café'
items.body_text:
AT A GLANCE
- Filipino author Alfred 'Krip' Yuson has faced multiple allegations of sexual misconduct and a plagiarism case, raising concerns about the ethics of republishing his work, particularly his novel 'Great Philippine Jungle Energy Café.'
- Despite initial support for the republication from Exploding Galaxies, backlash from the literary community led to a reconsideration of its decision, highlighting the complexities of promoting literature by controversial figures.
- The situation has sparked broader discussions within the literary community about the moral implications of supporting works by authors with problematic histories and the responsibilities of publishers in such cases.
MANILA, Philippines – Filipino literature and the classics that have come out of it always deserve to be known, and it’s often made possible by efforts like republishing and circulating physical copies to make them accessible to even more readers. But when the author behind one of these books has caused more harm than good, it becomes an entirely different story.
Case in point: Alfred “Krip” Yuson and his 1988 novel Great Philippine Jungle Energy Café.
The book was supposed to have been given new life by Exploding Galaxies — with the publishing house even standing by its initial decision to republish the book despite drawing backlash from members of the literary community. Here’s what went down.
Yuson’s web of controversies
Yuson, a Carlos Palanca Memorial Awards for Literature Hall of Fame inductee, has been accused of sexual misconduct on several instances by different individuals. His latest published work was the 2022 book The Mountain That Grew.
“Why re-platform a man who’s responsible for the harassment and suicide of women? I do not care how brilliant you think his book is. I DO NOT CARE. And I will NEVER understand,” writer Katrina Stuart Santiago said in a Threads post on August 26.
Santiago further attested that she knows of young female writers who have had their own share of “horrid” experiences at the hands of Yuson.
“I remember when writers were being ‘cancelled’ left and right for everything from minor indiscretions to horrible mistakes to bad decisions, my question then was: when do we talk about the dirty old men of the literary establishment? Because THAT is a list. And it also has a list of victims. Re-platforming one of them by reprinting his book seems like [a] signal, doesn’t it. Of many things, including that people think we forget who these men are. We do not. We cannot. WE SHOULD NOT,” she said in another post on August 27.
Santiago added that literary workshops fuel Yuson’s predatory behavior, given the power dynamics that exist in these spaces between mentors and their mentees.
In response, Exploding Galaxies had initially attempted to discredit Santiago’s commentary, stating that while sexual harassment isn’t something they take lightly, the allegations that have been thrown at Yuson “have not been proven or independently corroborated.”
“We republished Great Philippine Jungle Energy Café for its well-established literary merit, and we stand by our decision to publish the book,” Exploding Galaxies wrote in its first public statement on September 5.
“We also stand firm against dishonest and unfair attempts to discredit this republication, especially as it is coming from a person who has expressed a longstanding personal grudge against the author, and who has, over the years, leveled serious public accusations against others,” it added.
Public response
Other figures in the literary community were quick to weigh in on the matter, with award-winning writer Jose “Butch” Dalisay Jr. pondering on the topic of art being created by questionable individuals.
“Does moral or political purity translate to some kind of elevated prose, or more honest and insightful poetry?” he wrote in a Facebook post. “Can someone please put together a library of vetted literature (or otherwise a new Index Librorum Prohibitorium) to spare us the

items.title: Supreme Court acquits Imelda Marcos in 7 counts of graft
items.summary: (1st UPDATE) The SC says the prosecution failed to prove Marcos' guilt beyond reasonable doubt
items.body_text:
AT A GLANCE
- The Supreme Court of the Philippines acquitted Imelda Marcos of graft charges related to Swiss foundations, overturning a previous conviction by the Sandiganbayan.
- The Court ruled that the prosecution failed to prove her guilt beyond reasonable doubt, particularly regarding the authenticity of evidence presented against her.
- The 2018 Sandiganbayan decision had sentenced Marcos to prison and disqualified her from holding public office, citing her involvement in the management of the foundations.
MANILA, Philippines – The Supreme Court (SC) 1st Division acquitted Imelda Marcos, the mother of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., in her graft cases related to Swiss foundations.
In a decision made public on Wednesday, September 9, the SC division overturned the Sandiganbayan’s November 2018 decision that convicted the 97-year-old former first lady of seven counts of graft.
“Accordingly, the Appeal is granted. The November 9, 2018 Decision of the Sandiganbayan in Criminal Case Nos. 17287, 17288, 17289, 17290, 22867, 22868, and 22869 is reversed and set aside. Accused-appellant Imelda R. Marcos is acquitted for the prosecution’s failure to prove her guilt beyond reasonable doubt for violation of Section 3(h) of Republic Act No. 3019, in relation to Article IX, Section 8 of the 1973 Constitution,” said the 50-page ruling penned by Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda.
Associate justices Ramon Paul Hernando, Henri Jean Paul Inting, Ricardo Rosario, and Jose Midas Marquez all concurred in the ruling.
The Marcos matriarch is acquitted four years into the presidential term of her son, who won the presidency in 2022.
The ruling
In its decision, the SC division said the prosecution failed to prove Marcos’ guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Beyond reasonable doubt is the threshold needed to convict an accused in criminal cases.
Marcos was charged with alleged violation of Section 3(h), which has the following elements:
- the accused is a public officer
- they have direct or indirect financial or pecuniary interest in any business, contract, or transaction
- they either intervened or took part in their official capacity or connection with such interest, or they are prohibited from having such interest by the Constitution or by any law
The SC said it’s undisputed that the first element is present, but the second and third elements are contested. The Office of the Ombudsman presented documentary and testimonial evidence that sought to prove Marcos’ financial interest, but the SC said they were “inadmissible and lack probative weight.”
In Marcos’ case, the Sandiganbayan found that she had a financial and pecuniary interest in the foundations based on the Swiss documents. The documents were retrieved from Swiss banks and had been authenticated in accordance with Swiss legal procedure.
However, the SC said the Sandiganbayan erred when it considered the Swiss documents duly authenticated.
“The Court has emphasized that the rule on authentication, more particularly as to private documents, is in place to prevent the inclusion of spurious documents in the body of evidence. Thus, it is settled that private documents are generally inadmissible in evidence unless they are properly authenticated,” said the ruling, adding that the prosecution was not able to present a credible witness who could have testified to the documents’ authenticity.
In addition, even if the SC would ignore the probative weight of the prosecution’s evidence, Marcos must still be acquitted, said the Court. The prosecution, according to the SC, failed to prove that the alleged pecuniary interest was “covered by Section 3(h) of Republic Act No. 3019 and Article IX, Section 7 (then Section 8) of the 1973 Constitution.”
“All told, the prosecution failed to establish that the subject foundations are businesses as the term is ordinarily understood. Any financial or pecuniary interest in the subject foundations is not covered by Section 3(h) of Republic Act No. 3019 and Article IX, Se

items.title: 3 Degamo slay suspects convicted in firearms, explosives cases
items.summary: The three suspects were previously identified as former soldiers who are all “highly skilled” in military operations.
items.body_text:
3 Degamo slay suspects convicted in firearms, explosives cases
MANILA, Philippines — Three suspects linked to the 2023 killing of Negros Oriental Gov. Roel Degamo were convicted in separate cases involving illegal possession of firearms, ammunition and explosives, the Department of Justice said Wednesday, September 9.
In a statement, the DOJ said the Manila Regional Trial Court Branch 40 found Joric Garrido Labrador guilty beyond reasonable doubt of violating Section 28 of Republic Act 10591, or the Comprehensive Firearms and Ammunition Regulation Act.
The court also convicted Joven Calibjo Javier and Benjie Rodriguez of unlawful possession of explosives under Section 3 of Presidential Decree 1866, as amended by Republic Act 9516.
Labrador was sentenced to eight years, eight months and one day to 10 years, eight months and one day in prison, while Javier and Rodriguez were each sentenced to reclusion perpetua.
The three suspects were previously identified as former soldiers whom then-Army chief Romeo Brawner Jr. described as "highly skilled military operators."
The DOJ said a .45-caliber pistol, two magazines, 14 rounds of live ammunition and two hand grenades were recovered from the suspects.
In a social media post, Rep. Janice Degamo (Negros Oriental, 3rd District), wife of the slain governor, welcomed the court's decision.
"Every conviction is a step forward. Every person held accountable brings us closer to the truth and to the justice that Roel and every victim of the Pamplona Massacre deserve," the lawmaker said.
On March 4, 2023, Degamo and nine others were shot dead when armed men attacked his residence in Pamplona, Negros Oriental, during the distribution of government aid. Dozens of others were wounded.
Ten suspects in the killing eventually recanted earlier statements linking former lawmaker Arnolfo Teves Jr. to the attack.
Labrador, Javier and Rodriguez were among those who withdrew their previous statements. The suspects alleged they had been tortured and coerced into making the statements, allegations authorities denied.
Teves, whom prosecutors accuse of being among the masterminds of the attack, has denied involvement in the killings.
He remains detained at the Metro Manila District Jail in Camp Bagong Diwa, Taguig City, as he faces separate murder, frustrated murder and attempted murder charges in connection with the Degamo attack.

items.title: Marcos to join BRICS Summit in India
items.summary: President Marcos Jr. is taking ASEAN's agenda to BRICS as emerging powers meet in India.
items.body_text:
Marcos to join BRICS Summit in India
MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. will attend the 18th BRICS Summit in India on September 12 and 13, where he plans to take the Philippines' priorities as this year's ASEAN chair to a bloc of the world's biggest emerging economies.
Marcos and First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos are going at the invitation of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the Department of Foreign Affairs said Wednesday, September 9.
"Through this visit, the president seeks to ensure that our modern partnerships remain open, resilient, and capable of delivering prosperity to our people," DFA spokesperson Analyn Ratonel said at a Palace press briefing.
Marcos will use the summit to lay out the priorities set by the Philippines for ASEAN, such as peace and security and development.
The trip also opens the door for the Philippines and ASEAN to talk trade, investment, regional security and climate resilience with the larger emerging economies, she added.
Modi meeting, business pledges
On the sidelines, Marcos is expected to meet Modi to go over the Philippines-India Strategic Partnership and review how the two countries are carrying out their five-year plan for 2025 to 2029.

items.title: Chinese, Singaporean students lead the world in math, science
items.summary: Students in China have emerged as the world's top performers in mathematics and science in an international assessment measuring how well education systems prepare 15-year-olds for the challenges of the future as Singapore ranked second in both subjects.
items.body_text:
The newly released Program for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2025, conducted by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), shows students in China's Beijing-Shanghai-Jiangsu-Zhejiang (B-S-J-Z) group and Singapore outperforming their peers globally.
The 2025 ranking was the largest assessment to date. It evaluated 760,000 15-year-old students across 91 countries and economies in science, reading, mathematics, and computational problem-solving.
The PISA results showed B-S-J-Z students scored an average of 612 points in mathematics, the highest among all participating education systems.
Singapore followed with 563 points, while the OECD average sat at just 463 points. Macau, Taiwan, Japan, South Korea, and Hong Kong closely trailed the top two.
B-S-J-Z students also topped the global science ranking with an average score of 597 points.
Singapore again ranked second with 560 points, followed by Macau, Taiwan, Japan, Estonia, and South Korea. These results underline the consistently strong performance of East Asian education systems across core academic subjects.
The OECD noted that most participating Chinese jurisdictions, along with Estonia, Japan, South Korea, Singapore, and the U.K., ranked among the top 10 education systems in all three PISA domains: science, mathematics, and reading. Singapore took the top spot for reading.
In science, the gap between the leading systems and the OECD average was particularly striking.
B-S-J-Z students scored 115 points above the OECD average, while Singaporean students were 78 points higher. The OECD stated that students in B-S-J-Z and Singapore demonstrated stronger abilities to engage with broader, more demanding scientific ideas, complex investigations, and diverse sources.
At these top levels, students are expected not only to interpret or select evidence but also to evaluate claims, identify errors, and describe flaws. The results also highlighted that the leading systems had relatively few students struggling with basic science proficiency.
Fewer than 15% of students performed below Level 2 in science in B-S-J-Z, Macao, Singapore, Estonia, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. Level 2 represents the baseline at which students begin using science to reason in familiar, real-world situations.
In computational problem-solving, students in Macao (China), Singapore, B-S-J-Z (China), and Japan achieved the highest scores (572, 563, 560, and 557 points, respectively).
Students in Hong Kong (China), Malaysia, Brunei, the Philippines, Macao (China), and Iceland performed over 30 points above expectations based on their science performance.
Global declines and the future of learning
The strong performance from Asian education systems comes as overall results have deteriorated in many parts of the world. The OECD average mathematics score fell from 485 points in 2015 to 463 points in 2025, a significant decline of 22 points. Science performance declined more modestly, dropping from 489 to 482 points over the same period.
Between 2018 and 2025, reading performance fell in three quarters of the education systems with comparable data. Across the OECD, scores dropped by 25 points, which equates to more than a year of lost learning.
The biggest surprise was who fell furthest behind: it was not the most disadvantaged students, but rather those from wealthy families. This finding points to a much broader challenge than educational inequality alone.
Most troubling is the decline in the very skills that matter most in the AI age: evaluating information, making connections across multiple sources, and thinking critically about what we read. Consequently, the share of "hasty readers"– students who rush through texts and give quick but incorrect answers – almost doubled between 2018 and 2025.
"In a world increasingly flooded with information, our students are less likely to think deeply and separate signal from noise," the OECD said in its statement.

items.title: In Southeast Asia's third richest country, data centers are guzzling more power as temperatures soar
items.summary: Malaysia's data centers are consuming more power as temperatures rise, leaving a ​9 gigawatt gas-fired capacity gap for the government to fill by 2032, ‌officials said on Tuesday.
items.body_text:
The share of data centers in overall power consumption surged to a record 9.3% in the second week of August, compared with an average of 7% this year, Energy Commission CEO Siti Safinah Salleh said.
"With the hotter weather, the cooling system requires a lot more energy," she said.
Data centers could account for as much as 31% of peninsular Malaysia's power demand by 2035, said Zaharin Zulkifli, deputy director for economic statistics and research at the Energy Commission.
As Malaysia, the region's fastest-growing data center hub, gradually phases out coal-fired power, the nation of about 35 million people will have to augment its gas-fired capacity by 9 GW by 2032, economy minister Akmal Nasir said.
Malaysia, Southeast Asia's third richest country by GDP per capita after Singapore and Brunei, plans to retire the last of its coal-fired power plants by 2044, Akmal told reporters at an Energy Commission conference.
Malaysia is attracting billions of dollars in investments from major global tech firms including Amazon and Microsoft, leveraging its domestic gas reserves to address rising power demand this year and buck aregional decline in gas-fired generationas the Iran war chokes liquefied natural gas imports.
But with no additional gas-fired power expected to come online this year and next, Malaysia will "optimize" its current fleet to address rising demand until the end of 2027, Siti said, without providing further details.
The energy commission did not anticipate hot weather persisting longer than early September, which she said resulted in higher power use, she said.
"Because of the hot weather, our hydro dams are also at very low levels."
Still, Malaysia does not face power shortages in the near future due to rising data centre deployments, said Gary Goh, senior manager for business development at Sprint DC Consulting.
"The demand surge is entirely within grid planning parameters and will continue to ramp predictably," Goh said.

items.title: Travel chaos at UK airports as over 1,000 flights canceled due to air traffic control issue
items.summary: An air traffic control problem disrupted travel across Britain on Tuesday, canceling more than 1,000 flights and leaving passengers stranded for hours on airport runways and in terminals, according to flight-tracking website Flightradar24.
items.body_text:
Britain's National Air Traffic Services said it had resolved a problem in its flight processing system in the evening but delays rippled across 15 U.K. airports and beyond as airlines and airports worked to clear a huge backlog of delayed flights.
Josie Donoghue spent three hours stuck on a plane at Gatwick before her Ryanair flight to Ireland was canceled.
"Getting through that airport was like trying to get out of Alcatraz," she said, referring to the notorious former island prison in San Francisco Bay. "It's just an absolute nightmare down there. It's the only word I can use to describe it."
Departures at London Heathrow resumed but the busy airport suspended arrivals for the rest of the night because of the disruption and warned of further delays.
Passengers on a British Airways flight that had been due to fly to Baltimore disembarked after four hours on the ground at Heathrow. During the long delay, flight attendants served pasta and chicken curry while patient passengers watched movies or strolled up and down the aisles.
But passengers then learned their problems were far from over. There was mayhem at the baggage claim area and they were told no one could help them and to file claims for their bags.
British Airways said it was forced to cancel or divert more than 100 flights. Ryanair said more than 65,000 of its passengers had been disrupted and it had canceled more than 50 scheduled flights.
"The severity of the issue means there will be a significant knock-on impact," a British Airways spokesperson said. "This incident was entirely out of our control and incredibly frustrating for our customers and colleagues, with aircraft and crews ending up out of place."
Some passengers took to social media to complain about being stuck on planes for hours and expressed frustration about a lack of communication from airlines.
Affected airports included Stansted and City in London, as well as those in Manchester, Birmingham, Gatwick and Scotland. They warned passengers to check the status of their flight with their airline.
Budget airline EasyJet said some of its flights were "unable to operate" and that the system failure caused "delays to flights across Europe."
