items.title: SA government backed a risky horse in LIV Golf — lucky it hedged its bets
items.summary: The catalyst for the Malinauskas government's $45 million upgrade of the North Adelaide Golf Course has filed for bankruptcy. But the story could have been far worse.
items.body_text:
analysis
Australian Open saves SA government from a LIV Golf bunker
Spending at least $45 million to upgrade a golf course so it can host a tour that's filed for bankruptcy is a hard sell.
But that's the position the Malinauskas government would have been lumped with had it not secured hosting rights to the Australian Open golf tournament from 2028.
The announcement in May that the prestigious, traditionalist golf event would be coming to the redeveloped North Adelaide Golf Course has taken some of the sting out of what would otherwise have been a nasty political headache surrounding LIV Golf's financial demise.
The breakaway tour filed for bankruptcy in the US overnight, four months after Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund announced it would be pulling its billions in funding.
LIV Golf chief executive Scott O'Neil said the move was intended to keep the league in business while transitioning to a player-first ownership model. It hopes to exit bankruptcy in early 2027.
But the optimism of the press release doesn't quash the uncertainty about what LIV Golf will look like next year and whether it can hold onto the top talent — and party-like atmosphere — that made it such a success in Adelaide.
The tour owes huge sums to creditors, including its star players. Jon Rahm is owed more than $10 million, Bryson DeChambeau nearly $8 million, and Australian Cameron Smith about $6.5 million.
They could all walk away if not convinced by LIV's new model.
Premier Peter Malinauskas went all in on the LIV Golf vision back in February 2025, announcing a six-year contract extension until 2031 and that it would be moving to a new Greg Norman-designed championship course at North Adelaide in 2028.
The government has been consistent that there was more to the course upgrade than just LIV Golf, pointing out it will be used by the public outside of events.
But it's also hard to imagine a world where the $45 million upgrade gets green-lighted without LIV Golf in the picture; indeed, the premier indicated as much at the time, saying the 2031 extension "justifies the investment".
"We didn't want to invest heavily in North Adelaide and face the prospect of it [LIV Golf] being lost from South Australia," he said in February 2025.
"This gives us the security that it requires to be able to justify that investment."
As the negative headlines about LIV Golf's finances piled up, so too did the questions about the justification for the course upgrade.
The development and its loss of 585 trees was always going to spark opposition from parklands advocates, the Greens and elements of Adelaide City Council.
But the prospect of spending $45 million on an upgraded course without a major event connected to it risked a much broader backlash.
If you wanted a sense of the political importance of securing the Australian Open, you only have to look at how prominently it featured in the government's talking points about LIV Golf's bankruptcy today.
"We've been focused on not just LIV Golf but other opportunities," Labor minister Clare Scriven said, "which is why we've been so keen to secure the Australian Open."
Cabinet colleague Nick Champion — who in April said the prospect of LIV Golf ceasing to exist was "just speculation" and "not a question we would ask ourselves" — said today that the state government was not "over-reliant" on one event.
"I appreciate that we're going to have endless media speculation about LIV Golf, but we're upgrading the golf course so that we can have a world class golf course next to a world class [Adelaide] Oval in a world class city," he said.
"And we've got the Australian men's and women's open."
The debate moves on
The fight over the North Adelaide course upgrade appears to have largely moved on.
That's partly due to the Australian Open announcement, but also because attention has shifted to the government's controversial MotoGP circuit in the eastern parklands, which will require the felling of at least 377 trees.
Opposition leader Ashton

items.title: Lynagh makes timely return after Wallabies fly half Gordon breaks leg
items.summary: Tom Lynagh's timely return at number 10 for the Queensland Reds and Zac Lomax's move to the centres for the Western Force will have Wallabies ramifications in a pre-season Ballymore hit-out.
items.body_text:
Tom Lynagh makes Queensland Reds return after Wallabies fly half Carter Gordon breaks leg
In short:
Tom Lynagh will make his return to the rugby field this weekend after a horror run of injuries have kept him sidelined.
Lynagh was the Wallabies starting fly half for all three Tests against the British and Irish Lions in 2025, but managed just 18 minutes with the Queensland Reds this year.
What's next?
The four-week Super Rugby AUS competition begins this weekend with Reds vs Force, and Brumbies vs Waratahs.
Tom Lynagh's timely return at number 10 for the Queensland Reds and Zac Lomax's move to the centres for the Western Force will have Wallabies ramifications in a pre-season Ballymore hit-out.
Super Rugby AUS starts on Saturday in Brisbane and there will be immense interest in how both fare ahead of next year's World Cup on home soil.
Lynagh, the starting fly half in all three British and Irish Lions Tests last year, managed just 18 minutes for the Reds because of a series of injuries last season.
All going to script, he will get at least 40 minutes against the Force at Ballymore in new Reds coach Vern Cotter's first game in charge since his historic move from Auckland's Blues to replace Les Kiss.
Lynagh's return comes as Reds teammate and fly half Carter Gordon enters two months of rehabilitation after fracturing his fibula in last weekend's Test draw against Argentina in Mendoza.
Gordon had established himself as the Wallabies' first-choice fly half, leaving Kiss with some big calls ahead of a clash with South Africa and a two-Test Bledisloe Cup in the next six weeks.
"I'm really enjoying Tom in a playmaker role," Cotter said of the son of former Wallabies great Michael.
"He's got a great head on his shoulders, he sees the game well, he's calm and decisive.
"With the niggles he has had, we will probably be a bit careful with him, so it probably won't be 80 minutes, but certainly a good 40 minutes to start with.
"He's a great player in organised play but brilliant at unstructured (play).
"It's a good opportunity for Tom to get out there and boss the team around … pull a few strings and get some combinations."
Harry McLaughlin-Phillips, released by the Reds to join the Force this season, will oppose Lynagh and consider himself in the thick of Wallabies discussions after being part of their training camp earlier this year.
Kurtley Beale has been named on the bench for the Force, but new signing James O'Connor, another sure to be in Kiss's considerations, will not play.
Lomax, an Australian and NSW State of Origin rugby league winger, revealed this week he would be deployed in the number 13 jersey against the Reds.
A dominant showing there would add intrigue to Kiss's midfield selection headache after fellow code-hopper Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii's struggles to nail down the jersey in 24 Tests.
Japan-bound fullback Jock Campbell, replaced in the number 15 by Tom Wright after one Test in July despite a good showing against Ireland, will also get a chance to show something when he comes off the bench for the Reds.
Fellow Wallabies Matt Faessler, Zane Nonggorr and Josh Flook have been named, while Australian under-20s captain Tom Robinson will wear the number 6, and exciting fullback Will McCulloch will start.
NSW Waratahs lock Miles Amatosero, red-carded in his second Test appearance in Osaka, will mount his comeback against the ACT Brumbies on Sunday in Bungendore, east of Canberra.
Teddy Wilson and Max Burey, after earning an early release from the Force, will partner in the halves, while Sid Harvey will start at fullback.
Triston Reilly will wear the Brumbies' number 15 against his former club a week after piloting the First Nations and Pasifika XV to victory in Tonga, while Wallabies wing aspirant Corey Toole will add pace on the flank.
AAP

items.body_text:
Man shot dead outside community centre in Sydney’s south-west
Updated ,first published
A boxing coach has been shot dead in an ambush in Sydney’s south-west, in what police believe is another targeted attack linked to organised crime.
Louis Meehan, 32, was killed behind his boxing gym in the carpark of the Punchbowl Community Centre on Wednesday evening.
Witnesses reported a black ute speeding away from the carpark as multiple gunshots rang out. Police rushed to the carpark, administering urgent CPR to Meehan while two onlookers knelt to pray for the man before he was pronounced dead.
Meehan was shot beside a white sedan at the entry of the carpark, which was full at the time of the attack.
Onlookers, including multiple school students, watched on from the edge of the carpark as paramedics worked to save him.
Meehan has posed online wearing merchandise linked to the Alameddine crime gang. This includes clothing from Proper 60, a Merrylands-based group associated with the family, and Ready 4 War, the name of the Alameddine network’s drug-trafficking operation.
The Punchbowl Community Centre carpark sits one block behind The Boulevarde, a busy high street adjacent to Punchbowl train station.
It is on the same road as St Jerome’s Catholic Primary School and St Jerome’s Catholic Church.
Officers were combing the paths outside the community centre at 7.30pm, shining torches over the ground and gutters.
People at the scene were desperately trying to get the name of the victim, fearing they may have known him. Others were attempting to get their cars out of the open air crime scene.
The street is roped off and blocked by marked and unmarked cars. Police have expanded the crime scene as they work to gather evidence.
The Punchbowl shooting comes two days after the Minns government announced a suite of measures targeting an outbreak of gangland violence on Sydney’s streets.
The measures were flagged in response to last week’s mistaken identity murders of university student Marco Tapia, 23, and business owner Joshua Macdonald, 40, in the city’s west.
The reforms promised tighter targeting of offshore kingpins and local middle men orchestrating violent attacks and tougher penalties for teenagers carrying out gang-related shootings and firebombings.
It marked the NSW government’s third significant crackdown on organised crime in two years and came days after denying police had lost control of escalating violence.
Conflict between the Alameddine crime family and Coconut Cartel has sparked an escalation in underworld violence in recent years, as the warring organised crime syndicates jostle for control of Sydney’s lucrative drug trade.
Powerbrokers for both of the groups are living overseas, where they’re believed to be orchestrating criminal activities in Sydney while out of reach of Australian police.
Asked on Monday if community fears were justified following last week’s shootings, Premier Chris Minns said: “We do think there’s a problem.”
“There [is] a disregard for human life I haven’t really seen before,” he said. “It’s been a regrettable and horrible part of life in Sydney.”
It followed Police Minister Yasmin Catley’s insistence last week that the violence was not “out of control”.
Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane referenced Catley’s comments following the Punchbowl shooting on Wednesday, writing on X: “Another deadly shooting in Sydney – the 3rd in a week. This time in front of a community centre. Do you still have things under control police minister Catley?”
Tapia was killed last Tuesday morning after a group of home invaders stormed his family’s Glen Alpine home before executing him in his bed.
He was in his third year of a biomedical engineering degree at the University of Technology Sydney, and his only brush with the law was through a minor traffic offence.

items.summary: NSW police say a vehicle was seen driving away from the scene in Punchbowl in the city’s south-westGet our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcastA man has been shot dead in the car park of a Sydney community centre in the city’s south-west.Emergency services were called to the community centre on Rossmore Avenue in Punchbowl on Wednesday evening after reports of a shooting. items.body_text:
A man has been shot dead in the car park of a Sydney community centre in the city’s south-west.
Emergency services were called to the community centre on Rossmore Avenue in Punchbowl on Wednesday evening after reports of a shooting.
A vehicle was seen driving away from the location after the fatal shooting, NSW police said in a statement.
Paramedics treated the man but he died at the scene. He is yet to be identified, police said.
The fatal shooting comes two days after the New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, announced measures to curb gangland violence in Sydney.
New laws being introduced in the state include new aggravated offences for conspiracy to commit gang-related murder. The maximum penalty will be increased to life imprisonment.
The government has repeatedly denied criminal gangs are “out of control” in the city after the mistaken identity shootings of electrician Joshua Macdonald and Marco Tapia, a 23-year-old biomedical engineering student last week.
Police said neither man had any link to organised crime.
The new laws being introduced in NSW aim to tackle organised crime by giving police more power, including using new interim serious crime prevention orders to restrict people suspected of serious and organised crime. Those would be applied while the state’s supreme court considers the full order.
Children’s indictable offences would include activities linked to organised crime, and public shootings and firebombings would be added to the scheme.
In a statement on Monday, Minns said people who conspire to arrange a gangland murder should face the prospect of “spending the rest of your life behind bars”.
“We want to hit these criminal networks at every point – the people who organise the violence, the people who facilitate it online and the people who ultimately carry it out,” he said.
Police are urging anyone with information about the Punchbowl incident to contact Campsie police station or Crime Stoppers.

items.title: White Australia party is ‘modern manifestation’ of Nazi movement and should be banned, commonwealth tells high court
items.summary: The former National Socialist Network is challenging ban in high court, arguing law breaches implied freedom of political communicationGet our new political email, free app or daily news podcastThe White Australia party is a “modern manifestation” of Adolf Hitler’s Nazi movement and would motivate hate crimes against sections of the country, the high court has heard.The White Australia party, formerly known as the National Socialist Network (NSN), was designated as an illegal hate group in May a
items.body_text:
The White Australia party is a “modern manifestation” of Adolf Hitler’s Nazi movement and would motivate hate crimes against sections of the country, the high court has heard.
The White Australia party, formerly known as the National Socialist Network (NSN), was designated as an illegal hate group in May after the Australian Security and Intelligence Organisation (Asio) passed on its recommendation to the home affairs minister, Tony Burke.
It is challenging the ban at the high court over two days this week, with its lawyers arguing the law breaches the implied freedom of political communication and that handing the decision to Burke breaches the separation of powers.
It also argues the commonwealth does not have the power to ban political parties, citing a major cold war-era high court ruling in 1951, which overturned a ban on the Communist party of Australia.
The commonwealth’s lawyer, Brendan Lim, told the court on Wednesday that the group sought to create a political party after anti-hate laws passed in the wake of the Bondi terror attack threatened to disband it.
The hate group listing means that supporting, funding, training, recruiting and joining the group constitutes a criminal offence with a maximum penalty of 15 years in prison.
Lim said the group sought “protection” under the guise of creating a political party but remained the same group with the same goals.
The barrister cited a series of examples, including inflammatory rhetoric to encourage communal violence, an alleged physically violent attack by some of its members on Camp Sovereignty in 2025, and past criminal convictions of its leader, Thomas Sewell.
Justice Robert Beech-Jones asked whether the commonwealth believed the group were the “modern manifestation” of Hitler’s Nazi movement. Lim responded: “Yes.”
“There are few legitimate reasons, outside of history books and museum, that warrant the use of Nazi symbols,” Lim said.
Citing a briefing from Asio and public speeches by its director general, Mike Burgess, Lim said the prohibited hate group listing was necessary because the group were security conscious and its operations savvy enough to work within the limits of the law.
“The existence of the group itself is the source of harm,” Lim said.
Lim said stochastic terrorism – the use of media and public discourse to demonise sections of the community – could lead lone wolves or fringe members to commit racially motivated hate crimes.
Lim said the anti-hate laws go “no further than necessary” to remove that harm.
Beech-Jones asked whether the party represented a greater threat to Australia’s nationhood than that of the Communist party in 1950 when prime minister Robert Menzies first banned the party. The ban was overturned the following year as constitutionally invalid.
Lim said the current context was different but both parties represented “great threats” to the country.
Lawyers for the party argued on Tuesday that a total ban on the party was akin to using a “sledgehammer on a nut”.
Barrister Shahed Sharify argued the law’s breach of implied freedom of political communication was “authoritarian in nature” and suggested it could be used to outlaw any political party where its members had threatened or engaged in a hate crime with the assistance of the organisation.
Sharify said the banning of hate groups was determined by a politician, based on an opinion with no judicial fairness to appeal that decision.
Sharify said the law’s purposes would be better served by handing that decision to a judge rather than a “busy minister who flicks through a brief and decides in two hours”.

items.title: Ukraine has been trying to bring the war to Russia. More Russians are beginning to feel it
items.body_text:
Ukraine has been trying to bring the war to Russia. More Russians are beginning to feel it
Summer was marked by fuel shortages and drone attacks on warehouses
As Kyiv reeled Tuesday from another night of deadly strikes by ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, Russia's state-controlled media didn't report on the damaged highrise buildings or the cars that were set ablaze.
Instead, Russian broadcasters reported that several military facilities in Ukraine had been successfully targeted, while at home, the country's air defences had intercepted more than 380 Ukrainian drones.
But Russia's own vulnerability has become harder to conceal.
Local officials reported that two civilians were killed in Russia during the overnight strikes. And there are reports in the country's media that Moscow plans to allow postal workers to arm themselves with anti-drone weapons.
The measures are another sign of how Ukraine's expanding drone campaign is bringing the war deeper into Russian territory — and increasingly into the lives of ordinary Russians.
A summer of strikes
For nearly five years, the Kremlin has tried to shield much of the population from the realities of its full-scale war against Ukraine, as well as its economic consequences.
But Ukrainian drone strikes on refineries, energy facilities and e-commerce warehouses this summer have been a blunt reminder that Russia is not impenetrable.
"After the active drone raids on Russia — on Moscow and the Moscow region in particular — anxiety has increased greatly," said Tatiana, 66, who wanted to be identified only by her first name. "We were driving to the dacha with the children and saw a huge column of smoke. Naturally, that also causes fear."

Tatiana, like others CBC News spoke with for this story, communicated through voice memos sent on a messaging app. No one wanted to give their last names for fear of being punished for speaking to foreign media about the war.
She said she sometimes lies to her grandchildren when they wake up at night because of the noise, telling them it is construction work because she does not want them to be afraid.
At her dacha, a country home, she said people talk about the fear caused by the buzzing of drones overhead.
Ukrainian attacks on refineries and energy facilities have contributed to a fuel shortage in Russia, leading to long lines at gas stations, fuel rationing and public frustration. Videos posted on social media showed fights and arguments breaking out at some stations.
The government has taken steps to stabilize supplies, including importing fuel from countries such as India. It's a significant move given that Russia is one of the world's largest oil exporters.
The shortage has also helped fuel the popularity of GdeBENZ (Where is the Benzine), an app that directs motorists to gas stations with available fuel.
Measuring the mood
Denis Volkov, director of the Moscow-based research and polling organization Levada Center, said as the fuel crisis intensified earlier in the summer, surveys showed rising anxiety and a decline in approval of the Russian government.
But he said the mood has softened somewhat as fuel supplies have improved.
Levada’s August survey, published on Thursday, was conducted through video calls with 1,600 people across Russia. About one-quarter said they were experiencing tension and fear, while nearly 60 per cent described themselves as being in a normal mood.

items.title: Canada was prepared to send ships to Iraq in 2003 if UN approved action, records show
items.summary: Canada, a notable objector to the 2003 Iraq war, was preparing to back the U.S.-led invasion by sending naval ships into combat if the UN Security Council gave the go-ahead, according to cabinet records.
items.body_text:
Canada was prepared to send ships to Iraq in 2003 if UN approved action, records show
Documents suggest ground troops were off the table due to war in Afghanistan
Canada, a notable objector to the 2003 Iraq war, was preparing to back the U.S.-led invasion by sending naval ships into combat if the UN Security Council gave the go-ahead, according to cabinet records.
The minutes from the final cabinet meetings leading up to the invasion show the government was still planning for the possibility that the UN would sanction military action, and shows how that possibility weighed on ministers as they engaged in philosophical discussions around life and death.
The U.S. launched the invasion, purportedly to disarm Saddam Hussein of weapons of mass destruction that were never found. U.S. President George W. Bush's administration billed the conflict as part of the wider war on terror, launched in the wake of the Sept. 11 attacks just under two years prior.
Prime Minister Jean Chrétien officially announced in the House of Commons that Canada wouldn't join the U.S.-led "coalition of the willing" in Iraq on March 17, 2003 — just days before the invasion began.
"If military action proceeds without a new resolution of the Security Council, Canada will not participate," Chrétien declared during question period, eliciting a standing ovation from his side of the aisle.
That same day, the U.S. had withdrawn a resolution from the Security Council that would have explicitly authorized military action after it seemed likely to face defeat.
CBC News obtained a copy of the minutes from the final cabinet meeting — dated Feb. 25, 2003 — prior to Chrétien's declaration through an access to information request.
While the U.S.'s resolution faced opposition before it was even introduced, the documents suggest the Canadian government was preparing possible military options.
Then minister of national defence John McCallum said in the meeting that if the resolution passed, Canada wouldn't be able to offer any ground support at that time due to commitments in Afghanistan. But he indicated that Ottawa could send ships.
"[McCallum] reiterated that the recent commitment to provide a peacekeeping contingent in Afghanistan would prevent Canada from committing ground troops, but that other military assets, such as warships, could be redeployed from their current duties in the area should Canada choose to participate," the minutes read.
Retired general Raymond Henault, who was chief of the defence staff in 2003, says the documents correspond with what he told the government the Canadian Armed Forces could contribute to the Iraq war if Ottawa decided to join.
"We were working under the assumption that we should be ready to do whatever government decided, whether it was going to get involved or not get involved," Henault told CBC News in an interview.
Canada had ships in the Persian Gulf at that time that were conducting counterterrorism and counter-smuggling operations.
CBC News reported in 2011 that, according to a U.S. diplomatic memo published by WikiLeaks, there were discussions between U.S. and Canadian officials about how those ships could be used on the sidelines as the invasion began.
But the cabinet minutes suggest that the role those ships were playing in the wider war on terror could have expanded or have been "redeployed" if the UN sanctioned military action.
Henault said that redeployment meant the ships "would have been involved in any combat operations that were done from a naval perspective in support of the invasion of Iraq" and would have included ships carrying patrol aircraft such as helicopters. He also suggested Canadian special forces would have been involved.
CBC News didn't receive a response from a Chrétien representative when asked if the former prime minister would be available to participate in an interview for this story.

items.title: Ben Shelton beats defending champ Carlos Alcaraz in U.S. Open match that ends after 3:30 a.m.
items.summary: Ben Shelton had gone toe-to-toe with Carlos Alcaraz for five exhausting sets and finally, at 3:33 a.m. Wednesday, came the chance to end the U.S. Open champion's title reign.
items.body_text:
Ben Shelton beats defending champ Carlos Alcaraz in U.S. Open match that ends after 3:30 a.m.
Shelton will play Francis Tiafoe in the semifinals — a matchup that guarantees an American man in the final
Ben Shelton had gone toe-to-toe with Carlos Alcaraz for five exhausting sets and finally, at 3:33 a.m. ET Wednesday, came the chance to end the U.S. Open champion's title reign.
Shelton fired an ace at 146 m.p.h. — a ball that Alcaraz couldn't have gotten back even with fresh legs.
That gave Shelton a 6-7 (5), 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 7-6 (10-7) victory in a marathon tussle that was the latest-finishing match in U.S. Open history.
"I'm tired. It was a war," Shelton said. "Carlos is one of the greatest champions of our sport. It was the most enjoyable match I've had in my career, for sure."
Alcaraz had his 18-match winning streak in Grand Slam tournaments end in a match that lasted 4 hours, 28 minutes. He fought deep into the night and early into the next morning in a bid to get his hands on the trophy again, battling back even as he vomited before the start of the final set.
Alcaraz started the year winning the Australian Open, but was playing his first tournament since April after returning from a right wrist injury.
"I'm leaving happy and my head held high," Alcaraz said. "The truth is, I wanted to win … but also our goal was to leave the tournament having played matches and staying healthy."
The U.S. Open craves its night matches and players love the energy the fans provide — even when a number of matches have already gone past 2 a.m. this year.
Thousands stayed to the end, with Arthur Ashe Stadium perhaps still one-third full for the finish. Shelton benefited from a home-crowd boost even against the popular Alcaraz, with fans chanting his name along with "USA! USA!"
"It's incredible," Shelton said. "I always say that this is the greatest sports city in the world; I say that this is the greatest stadium in the world. I'm just hoping that my best friend and my sister over there don't have to be at work at 6 a.m. in three hours."
Three of the four singles quarterfinals went to match tiebreakers on a marathon day, which started with Aryna Sabalenka edging Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova to keep her hopes alive of a third straight U.S. Open title.
Alcaraz had played in the previous latest finish at the U.S. Open when he outlasted Jannik Sinner in a match that finished at 2:50 a.m. in the 2022 quarterfinals, en route to his first Grand Slam title at 19.
Tiafoe storms back
Shelton, who won his second consecutive Canadian Open title last month, will next play No. 11 seed Frances Tiafoe, who kept coming back until he had reached his third U.S. Open semifinal, beating Alex Michelsen 5-7, 3-6, 7-5, 6-3, 7-6 (10-6).
Shelton seized control by winning nine straight games from early in the second set until he had a 3-0 lead in the third.
Alcaraz ran off four straight points in the tiebreaker to go ahead 5-3, but Shelton came back behind some of his powerful serves that can exceed 140 m.p.h., along with some mistakes from Alcaraz.
The Shelton-Tiafoe matchup guarantees a U.S. player will reach the men's final. The last Grand Slam title for an American man occurred in 2003, when Andy Roddick won the U.S. Open.
Tiafoe reached the U.S. Open semifinals in 2022 and it didn't initially appear he would be going back, as Michelsen continued his dominant run through his breakout tournament.
Michelsen won the first two sets and served with a 5-4 lead in the third, but couldn't finish it off. He hadn't lost a set in the tournament until Tiafoe stormed back.
Tiafoe said his performance to start the match was slow and flat.
"It wasn't good, let's put it that way. It wasn't good," he said. "Three out of five is a blessing, because you have time to get it together. I definitely waited for the last minute."
Michelsen, ranked No. 46, fell to 0-6 in matches that went to a fifth set.

items.title: After 9/11, Canada’s military stepped into the global fight on terror as it headed for war in Afghanistan
items.summary: Canada went to war with its allies to support U.S. and overthrow the Taliban regime which was harbouring the terror group led by Osama bin Laden
items.body_text:
A quarter of a century ago, the terror attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, forced Canadians to quickly wake up to a world that had changed overnight – and to confront a new war which would change everything for Canada’s military.
The Afghanistan war, Canada’s longest armed conflict, taught harsh lessons – some that Canada learned, others it did not.
Soon after the attacks on the Twin Towers and the Pentagon, Canada stepped out of the quiet decade after the Cold War into the global fight on terror, and soon found itself at war with a Taliban insurgency halfway around the world.
“Who would have dreamt the day before that, Canadian troops in their thousands would be serving in Afghanistan – Afghanistan, for God’s sake, of all places. It was a dramatic change,” said retired general Rick Hillier, who led a multinational force of NATO nations in Kabul and would become Canada’s best-known chief of defence staff.
“It was a shift in our understanding of how the world functioned. We no longer operated, if you will, as a country isolated from all that upheaval and turmoil and hatred and violence.”
Canada’s ambassador to NATO moved for the alliance to, for the first time ever, invoke Article Five – the clause in the NATO treaty that says an attack on one member country constitutes an attack on all.
Canada went to war with its allies to support the United States and overthrow the Taliban regime which was harbouring the terror group led by Osama bin Laden that was behind the 9/11 attacks.
That alliance spirit is harder to detect today, with Canada’s relationship with the U.S. tanking over a trade war and President Donald Trump threatening to tear up the NATO alliance and pull more troops out of Europe.
In the immediate aftermath of the terror attacks, no one knew that more than 40,000 Canadians would serve in the 12-year Afghanistan war and 159 Canadian military members would lose their lives there.
Eugene Lang, a former chief of staff to two defence ministers, said Ottawa thought at the time it was entering a short-term conflict.
“Nobody was really anticipating what we got into, and we weren’t really prepared for it, in terms of the severity of the situation, the complexity of the situation and the duration,” he said.
Military doctrine had to change on the fly as Canadians learned to fight an insurgency and the Canadian Forces scrambled to find Pashto speakers to help soldiers talk to locals.
The operational tempo was fast and the military entered the war short of necessary equipment and personnel after its budget had been slashed over the 1990s.
Opinion: I rushed to help Americans on 9/11. Now I’m one of the wounded
“We had a Canadian Forces that was under-strength, under-budget, under-equipped and not ready for operations quite literally anywhere in the world,” Hillier said. “While we were trying to rebuild the basis for an armed forces, we were also getting ready to go to war, and those two things were demanding in a way that was quite incredible.”
Hillier said while Canadians rose to the challenge, the lesson of Afghanistan is that countries can’t afford to take a decade to prepare their armed forces for the next war.
When Canadian troops arrived in Afghanistan, they were the only ones to show up in green uniforms. The military also had wound down its tank fleets and would need to acquire new ones to deal with the proliferation of roadside bombs.
While Canada went into Afghanistan believing NATO allies would cover any equipment shortfalls, Canadian troops often ended up last in line to use any equipment that could be spared – and often did without.
Canada didn’t have helicopters suitable to deploy at the outset, making operations more risky. That’s when Ottawa bought the air force’s Chinook transport helicopters.
Another key lesson from Afghanistan, Hillier said, is that fighting a modern war takes an enormous number of people. The size of the regular force contracted by tens of thousands after the end of the Cold War, and numbered around 60,00

items.title: Iran hits ships near Hormuz in retaliation for U.S. attacks on tankers
items.summary: It’s the biggest declared wave of tit-for-tat attacks on shipping by both sides since the start of the six-month-old war
items.body_text:
Iran said on Wednesday it had attacked 10 ships near the Strait of Hormuz after the U.S. sank five Iranian oil tankers, in the biggest declared wave of tit-for-tat attacks on shipping by both sides since the start of the six-month-old war.
The attacks in and around the vital waterway sent the price of oil surging, with the international Brent crude benchmark breaching US$100 a barrel for the first time since July. The politically sensitive average retail price of diesel fuel in the United States hit a fresh all-time high above US$5.94 a gallon.
Iran also said it had fired ballistic missiles at a base used by U.S. forces in Jordan. Attacks by both sides since the end of August have shattered a month of relative calm, with the U.S. and Iran hitting military, shipping and energy assets.
Recent days have also seen an escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen, a second theatre of war that threatens global energy supplies from the Middle East.
The Americans said they destroyed five Iranian oil tankers overnight, releasing video of ships ablaze before they sank. The U.S. military’s Central Command called its attacks a response to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targeting a U.S. Navy warship twice with ballistic missiles over the previous two days. No Americans were harmed, the U.S. said.
Washington has announced a new policy of attacking Iranian tankers in retaliation for fire that threatens its warships. Iran says it is imposing a wider off-limits zone around the strait and using new, more capable missiles to attack U.S. ships.
“Iran continues to try to hit U.S. naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers,” U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters during a visit to Colombia.
Benchmark Brent crude oil futures rose past US$100 a barrel on Wednesday, breaching the symbolic barrier for the first time since July 24.
Reuters
The IRGC said on Wednesday it had responded with a ballistic missile attack on a base used by U.S. forces near Al Azraq in eastern Jordan, and had fired on two U.S. vessels and eight oil tankers attempting to cross an area of the Strait of Hormuz that it has declared off limits.
The British maritime security agency UKMTO said it had received reports of several merchant ships struck by disabling fire in the northern Gulf and Gulf of Oman, on either side of the strait. It was not immediately able to confirm casualties or environmental impact.
The agency also said a vessel was reported listing, possibly indicating it had taken on water after being struck by a projectile off Port Rashid, in the United Arab Emirates.
Iran has also threatened oil tankers in Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports, according to a statement carried by state media. A maritime security source reported a liquefied natural gas tanker was damaged in the Emirati port of Khor Fakkan.
Brent crude rises above $100 a barrel as Middle East conflict intensifies
Iran has largely choked off transit through the strait that carried a fifth of global oil before the war.
Washington has responded with a blockade of Iranian ports, and says it has been able to guide many tankers through the strait, although independent monitors say the extent to which oil is escaping has become increasingly difficult to assess. Preliminary data showed just six ships crossing with transponders on over the last 24 hours.
Iran said that its missiles fired at Jordan inflicted heavy damage. Jordan said its air defences had intercepted 18 of the 20 Iranian missiles, with two falling in unpopulated areas and no casualties. A U.S. official said Iran’s strikes in Jordan were ineffective and all American troops were accounted for.
Video filmed in Ash-Shajarah, in northern Jordan, and verified by Reuters showed flashes lighting up the night sky. Iran has targeted U.S. bases in the region throughout the war and killed at least two U.S. military personnel in a strike on Jordan in July.

items.title: Drones to be used in search for missing Canadian skyrunner Kalie McCrystal
items.summary: Sunday’s helicopter missions on the Matterhorn found no trace of her
items.body_text:
Drones will be used in the Italian alpine search for missing Canadian skyrunner Kalie McCrystal after helicopter flights over the weekend found no trace of her.
Ms. McCrystal, 38, a lawyer from Squamish, B.C., has not been seen since the afternoon of Sept. 1, when she was spotted by Polish climbers high on the Italian side of the Matterhorn mountain, which straddles the Swiss border. She was alone and was training to set a new record time for ascending and descending the 4,478-metre mountain, one of the highest peaks in the Alps.
In an interview Monday, Valerio Segor, director of civil protection for the Aosta Valley region in Italy’s northwest, near the French-Swiss border, said that drones have proven to be capable search devices in the past.
“You can get much closer to the mountain face with drones than with helicopters,” he said. “Drones can see more details and software can be used to analyze the images, so that things that are not rock, like a jacket or other gear, can be spotted and identified.”
He said it was unlikely that the drones would fly on Tuesday, because of the forecast for high winds and cloud cover, but could be deployed on Wednesday.
Canadian skyrunner still missing on Italian side of Matterhorn
Mr. Segor said a mountain rescue team of Italy’s quasi-military Guardia di Finanza, which operates under the economy ministry, learned that the last signal from the electronic SIM on Ms. McCrystal’s phone came on Sept. 1.
Two Polish climbers saw Ms. McCrystal ascending and descending from Pic Tyndall, a “sub-summit” about 200 metres below the Matterhorn’s peak on the Italian side of the mountain, last Tuesday afternoon. The two women shot a video, which the rescue teams have seen, of Ms. McCrystal ascending the mountain. “They said she was going up the mountain very fast,” Mr. Segor said.
The initial searches concentrated on that area of the Matterhorn.
He said the Guardia di Finanza found her hotel room in the alpine village of Cervinia, also known as Breuil-Cervinia, at the foot of the Matterhorn. Her luggage, including clothing, was in the room.
The most recent helicopter search flight was on Sunday. Ms. McCrystal’s parents were on the flight. Italian search and rescue teams have not released their names.
Mountaineer missing while climbing near Switzerland-Italy border, Athletics Canada says
The Matterhorn is considered a treacherous mountain for even well-trained hikers and climbers, including skyrunners. Skyrunning is a relatively new sport that requires athletes to run up high-elevation mountain trails and slopes with inclines as much as 30 per cent. Sometimes they rely on chains fastened to the rock faces to assist their climbs.
Various Matterhorn records say that 500 to 600 climbers have lost their lives on the mountain since the first recorded ascent in 1864. A male Finnish climber went missing on the Matterhorn in late July. His body has yet to be located.
Parts of the upper Matterhorn are particularly dangerous. “If you fall, you could fall several hundred metres,” Mr. Segor said.
Ms. McCrystal is a seasoned, trophy-winning skyrunner who has trained and competed in mountain races in South America and in Europe.
Athletics Canada said in a statement last week that “Kalie is an experienced skyrunner and mountaineer, with many years of experience on technical and high-altitude mountain environments. She has extensive knowledge and experience of alpine terrain and previously climbed the Matterhorn.”
As a lawyer, Ms. McCrystal specializes in international arbitration. She is an instructor in the school of legal studies at Capilano University, which has a campus in Squamish, where she lives. She is a graduate in law from the University of British Columbia.

items.title: Interior design: The new crown jewel of the room
items.summary: No longer relegated to a builder's white or popcorn finish, the ceiling is taking centre stage
items.body_text:
Interior design: The new crown jewel of the room
No longer relegated to a builder's white or popcorn finish, the ceiling is taking centre stage
We independently select everything we recommend. Buying through us may earn us a commission, which supports our work.
When Lori Lievonen and her husband moved into their new condo in Stouffville, Ont., they wanted to make it their own. Yes, they could personalize the furniture, the cabinetry, the wall colour, the decor, but what about… the ceiling? The condo had a large open-concept kitchen, dining and living space that was mostly black and white. Lievonen began browsing the work of muralists online, when she was struck by a photo of a bathroom with elaborate painted flowers flowing from the ceiling down the walls.
The artist was Toronto muralist Jasmin Pannu, and soon Pannu was up a ladder in Lievonen’s home, covering the ceiling in oversized, hand-painted flowers in blues and pinks that spilled down onto the mouldings below. Today, the ceiling is the centrepiece of Lievonen’s home.
“I tell everyone that they just have to come and see my ceiling,” says Lievonen. “It’s a real piece of art that brings joy to me and my husband. I could never move — I couldn’t take it with me.”
Lievonen’s ceiling is just one whimsical example of a growing trend. No longer relegated to a builder’s white or popcorn finish, the ceiling is taking centre stage.
“The ceiling is the crown,” says Toronto designer Lori Morris, whose maximalist, “no rules” approach saw her named to the Interior Design Review’s list of the world’s top 100 designers. “It’s the crown jewel of the room. I don’t view any part of a room — the walls, the coverings, the decorations — as more important than any other. We design the floor, the walls, the archways and the ceiling all with the same intensity and purpose.”
For Morris, giving the ceiling the royal treatment can mean deep coffered mouldings, hand-leafed gold detailing, or a richly patterned wallpaper applied overhead. The one rule she won’t break is proportion.
“For example, a ceiling medallion that’s too small for the chandelier — once you understand scale and proportion, there are no rules for design,” she says. “But the math has to be right first.”
Houzz’s Fall 2025 design report named statement ceilings as a trend to watch, grouping them with jewel-toned paint and bold wallpaper as part of a broader move away from safe, resale-driven decorating and toward homes that feel unmistakably personal. In 2026, Houzz found searches for wooden ceilings up 275 per cent in the first three quarters, while Pinterest clocked a 40 per cent jump in searches for striped ceilings heading into 2026, part of a maximalist circus-inspired wave the platform is calling “FunHaus.”
That appetite for drama overhead has a distinctly local flavour, according to Arnie Popov, a Toronto finish carpenter who has been building custom crown mouldings and waffle ceilings since the mid-2000s.
“Go to Halifax or Vancouver and search for waffle ceilings — you won’t find much,” Popov says. “In Toronto, you’ll find fifty people doing it. It’s a Toronto thing.” As an early ceiling specialist, Popov has watched the trend take off: “Neighbours see it, real estate agents see it, and it spreads.”
Though some designs can be pricey – custom medallions and chandeliers don’t come cheap – not every ceiling has to break the bank. For the budget-conscious, Popov suggests starting with crown moulding or a flat-stock version of the waffle look, which creates the same graphic effect, but is far simpler and cheaper to construct.
“There are a lot of options, depending on the room,” he says. “A coffered box built above a kitchen island can become the centrepiece for the whole space.”
And for those ready to really make a splash, there’s always paint. Toronto muralist Jasmin Pannu has painted close to a dozen ceilings since she saw demand begin to increase in 2020.

items.title: Scott Stinson: Dylan Marando tells Ontario Liberals some things they want to hear, and some they don’t
items.summary: The former policy adviser says he wants Liberals to get back to what they're good at: governing
items.body_text:
Scott Stinson: Dylan Marando tells Ontario Liberals some things they want to hear, and some they don't
The former policy adviser says he wants Liberals to get back to what they're good at: governing
Dylan Marando has some of the trappings of a long shot entrant in the Ontario Liberal leadership race.
When he went on a tour of the province’s northern ridings, he slept in tents alongside his campaign manager to save money. (Conveniently, she is also his wife, Elise Maiolino.) He’s trailing the fundraising race, in fifth spot among the five candidates trying to ultimately unseat Doug Ford. And, having never run for elected office before, he’s lower on name recognition than some of his rivals.
Recommended Videos
But the 39-year-old introduced himself with something of a bang at last month’s leadership debate, delivering the line of the night in a sleepy affair. “The milk has soured on Doug Ford,” Marando said. “And soon, it’s going to get chunky.”
A memorable, if somewhat gnarly, metaphor.
Somewhat surprisingly for a guy who has never done this before, Marando appeared confident and assured on the Brampton stage that night. He comes across the same way in a recent conversation at a Toronto coffee shop, acknowledging that he’s a relative outsider in the race but pleased with the momentum of his campaign.
“I say this with all the humility I can muster, I’m a winner,” he says. “I worked for (Dalton) McGuinty in his premier’s office, I worked for (Kathleen) Wynne in her premier’s office, I worked for (Justin) Trudeau in his PMO, all my experience comes on the winning side of politics, so I know how to win. I know how to govern, and, ultimately, I think that’s the skill set a voter in a general election is looking for.”
But first, the former policy adviser has to convince the voters in a Liberal race that lost a bit of momentum last week when the party was shut out in three provincial byelections. The party has polled near the governing PCs on province-wide surveys for months, but the three losses, all in greater Toronto, suggest there is much work to be done to rebuild the brand. And on that front, Marando has a message that would appeal to a lot of party supporters: Liberals, he argues, are good at being in government.
“I describe myself as a meat-and-potatoes Liberal,” he says. “The meat and potatoes part is publicly funded education, publicly funded health care and empowering local governments to make investments in local infrastructure. I don’t think the assignment is much more complicated than that.”
Marando says that Ford, for all of his grand visions like an expanded Toronto airport and a tunnel under the 401, had been unable to deliver on the basics.
“So in some ways, my bid is pretty boring,” he says “Get back to doing all the things that I’d argue Premier McGuinty and Premier Wynne were pretty good at, and recognize that government isn’t very good at picking winners and losers in the economy.”
But if Liberals might like hearing about the good old days when they were in charge, Marando does have a few opinions that are not widely shared among them.
Asked if the Liberals can take any lessons from Ford, who has won three elections without ever being particularly popular, Marando says, “I do think stylistically he’s instructive as a politician. I do think he has an ability to read the room, and he has an ability to speak the language that that folks are speaking.”
But he also says the premier hasn’t delivered on many of his promises.
“He says all the right things, but health care isn’t any better than it was years ago. Schools aren’t any better. But I think — and many of my Liberal colleagues might not might not share this perspective — he probably gets up in the morning and wants to do the right thing. I don’t think he’s being insincere when he when he’s talking to Ontarians, but for whatever reason, he and his team have demonstrated incapacity to follow through on the things that they’re talking about.”

items.title: Chris Selley: There are American eggs in our midst!
items.summary: Scandal: 5.6 per cent of the eggs that showed up in Canada in 2024 were imported from the U.S.
items.body_text:
Chris Selley: There are American eggs in our midst!
Scandal: 5.6 per cent of the eggs that showed up in Canada in 2024 were imported from the U.S.
A classic set-piece political controversy is playing out yet again in Quebec. There are eggs from Donald Trump’s United States! Dozens and dozens of them! On Canadian supermarket shelves!
But here we are in 2026, “in the middle of a full-blown trade war,” TVA Nouvelles reported the other day, and “American eggs are flooding Quebec supermarkets.”
Recommended Videos
“Several Quebecers who were happy to have paid $2.99 for their dozen (large) eggs at Maxi last week were disappointed once they got home when they found that the eggs came from the United States,” we read. (Maxi is a discount supermarket chain under the Loblaw umbrella — essentially Quebec’s version of No Frills.)
TVA did not name or interview anyone who was thusly disappointed, though it did say the network had received several emails.
It all seems unbelievable, I know, especially in this day and age. But it’s true. Again. Just like it was true in 2025, and just like it was true in 2024 when similar stories about American egg imports surfaced in Quebec. Canadian egg colossus Burnbrae Farms explains on its website: “On rare occasions, the available supply of eggs cannot meet the demand from our customers and on these occasions we will import eggs from the United States … This (usually occurs) in high-demand times such as Easter, Thanksgiving and Christmas.” Maybe Labour Day is one of those times.
Eggs are protected by Canada’s supply-management system. And if you thought supply management was supposed to be “a system that balances supply and demand … through production setting (quota), price setting and import control as a means of avoiding overproduction and underproduction” (my italics), well, I can’t really blame you. That’s precisely what it says on the Farm Products Council of Canada’s website, after all. But as a well-to-do hip-replacement candidate might say, the U.S. is always there in a pinch.
No doubt there are at least a few hundred Canadians who care very deeply about the provenance of their eggs. I would expect such people to be quite knowledgeable egg shoppers. And I would have thought the first thing that would tip off a knowledgeable egg shopper that something was a bit special about these eggs — if it not the “USDA A Grade” stamp on the carton — would be the fact they only cost $2.99.

Alas, that’s not a Canadian price for a dozen eggs. Walmart in Montreal wants a minimum of $4.08 for a dozen large Canadian eggs. Only if you buy 30 at a time you can match the Yankees’ per-egg cost. No, $2.99 is more like an American price for a dozen eggs, though you can find them considerably cheaper in the U.S., even once you convert to Canadian dollars. (For the record, you can buy a pack of large Canadian eggs at Maxi for $3 — but you only get six of them.)
Obviously eggs that cross the border, like all other agricultural products, must be certified safe according to Canadian standards. None of this angst makes any sense in any context except for the trade war with Washington. And a trade war with Washington necessarily makes less sense if you’re struggling to feed yourself or a family. Food inflation in Quebec from 2019 to 2025, total, was 31 per cent. Food bank usage has soared, as it has in many provinces.

items.title: Pour émuler Vivaldi au rythme des saisons
items.summary: «Les quatre saisons du Québec», de François Dompierre, est la seconde collaboration entre le compositeur et Francis Choinière
items.body_text:
Le vendredi 11 septembre, Francis Choinière, son Orchestre FILMharmonique et la violoniste Isabella d’Éloize Perron présenteront aux Montréalais en grande première Les quatre saisons du Québec de François Dompierre. Entretien avec le chef avant cette création.
Présenté comme une « première mondiale », le concert du 11 septembre à la Maison symphonique sera en fait une « quatrième », puisque les artistes ont déjà proposé ce même programme — associant Les quatre saisons de Vivaldi, Les quatre saisons de Buenos Aires d’Astor Piazzolla et Les quatre saisons du Québec de François Dompierre — au Palais Montcalm de Québec vendredi et samedi derniers et à la salle Les-frères-Lemaire de Victoriaville dimanche.
Encouragement
Le disque et les fichiers permettant de découvrir l’œuvre en téléchargement ou en écoute à la demande sont même accessibles depuis le 28 août. « C’est ce que l’on veut faire désormais. Pour l’enregistrement en général, mais tout particulièrement pour de nouvelles créations. Je crois que c’est encore plus important que les gens puissent découvrir une œuvre avant d’entrer en salle. Ça permet une meilleure appréciation, une meilleure capacité d’écoute et de compréhension de l’œuvre », dit au Devoir le chef Francis Choinière, désormais partie prenante dans les décisions artistiques de l’étiquette Atma, qui a publié l’enregistrement.
« Même dans l’industrie du film, très souvent la trame sonore va être disponible avant le film. Idem pour une nouvelle création de Broadway : les promoteurs veulent exposer quelque peu les gens à la musique avant qu’ils l’entendent en spectacle. »
Le projet des Quatre saisons du Québec est né dans la foulée de la création du Requiem. « Avant tout ça, François Dompierre avait plutôt déclaré que ça ne lui tentait plus vraiment de composer. Mais après le Requiem, je me souviens, en coulisses, juste avant de monter sur scène, il m’avait dit : “Si jamais tu as d’autres trips comme ça, moi je suis partant.” Donc, deux ou trois mois plus tard, je lui ai fait une proposition : “Nous avons notre tournée des Quatre saisons. Ça fait trois ou quatre fois qu’on fait cette tournée-là et on aimerait la renouveler avec une nouvelle œuvre. Est-ce que ça te tenterait de composer Les quatre saisons du Québec ?” Il y a réfléchi une ou deux semaines et a dit oui. Il a composé l’œuvre en trois ou quatre mois et on l’a enregistrée deux mois plus tard, en mars 2026, pour une sortie avant la tournée. »
Avec l’ancienne mouture à huit saisons (Vivaldi et Piazzolla), Francis Choinière, l’Orchestre FILMharmonique et Isabella d’Éloize Perron s’étaient rendus aux États-Unis, notamment à Carnegie Hall. Avec la création et les douze saisons, ce sera bientôt l’Europe : Paris, Bordeaux, Vienne, Berlin et Prague.
Profondément québécois
Dans sa très habile et attachante composition, qui s’articule comme un « concerto symphonique en quatre mouvements » (allegro/rigaudon ; mouvement lent/complainte ; scherzo/valse, contredanse ; Finale/quadrille), François Dompierre procède un peu comme Astor Piazzolla. items.title: Les tout-petits rapportent beaucoup à l’économie
items.summary: Chaque dollar investi dans la petite enfance générerait de deux à quatre fois plus de gains économiques.
items.body_text:
Le dynamisme économique, la santé des finances publiques et la prospérité individuelle et collective vous tiennent à cœur ? Investissez dans la petite enfance.
On peut difficilement demander un meilleur rapport coûts-bénéfices, dit un rapport sur le sujet dévoilé ce mercredi par l’Observatoire des tout-petits. De manière générale, chaque dollar investi dans les programmes qui visent spécifiquement les premières années de la vie d’un individu, allant de la grossesse à l’âge de 5 ans, génère de deux à quatre fois plus de gains économiques.
Dans le cas de l’accès précoce aux traitements de trois maladies chroniques pédiatriques au Canada, les retombées d’un dollar supplémentaire vont de 1,39 $ à 4,89 $ en réduction des coûts de santé à long terme, en amélioration du parcours scolaire et en participation économique plus forte à l’âge adulte, selon une étude canadienne.
Chaque dollar additionnel investi dans l’éducation pendant la petite enfance peut rapporter jusqu’à 5,83 $, selon une autre étude. Des experts ont estimé que la mise en place d’un réseau de services de garde éducatif au Québec est rapidement venue grossir son produit intérieur brut de 1,7 %. Le soutien financier direct aux familles constitue aussi un levier d’intervention efficace pour réduire l’impact de la pauvreté.
« C’est non seulement profitable pour les tout-petits et les adultes qu’ils deviendront, mais c’est économiquement rentable pour le Québec », résume la présidente du conseil d’administration de l’Observatoire des tout-petits, Julie Meloche. À l’inverse, l’inaction a un lourd prix.
« Effet domino »
Cet effet des mesures qui visent la petite enfance, dit le rapport, « s’explique en grande partie par la nature même du développement humain ». « Durant cette phase, le cerveau se développe à un rythme très rapide et les bases sur lesquelles reposeront les apprentissages ultérieurs se forment. Les divers milieux de vie et conditions dans lesquels grandissent les tout-petits jouent un rôle déterminant dans ce développement et peuvent influencer durablement le parcours de vie de l’enfant et de l’adulte qu’il deviendra. »
À certains égards, le Québec fait figure de chef de file dans le domaine, notamment en raison de son réseau public de service de garde à prix modique et son régime de congé parental plus généreux. Mais même là, tout est loin d’être parfait, le manque de places en garderie se faisant encore sentir, par exemple, dans les quartiers défavorisés où leur effet serait particulièrement important.
Quant au reste, plus d’un enfant de 0 à 5 ans sur dix vit dans une famille sous le seuil de faible revenu, plus d’un sur six est exposé à au moins une forme de violence dans la famille, et plus d’un sur quatre vit dans un logement considéré comme non acceptable en raison de son coût, de sa taille ou de son piètre état.
« Jusqu’à présent, on n’a pas beaucoup entendu parler d’investissement dans la petite enfance dans le cadre des élections », a déploré Julie Meloche en entrevue au Devoir la semaine dernière. « Ce serait pourtant une bonne façon de s’attaquer à nos problèmes en éducation, en santé, en logement, en protection de la jeunesse ou en itinérance en raison de leur effet domino. »
Près de 9 Québécois sur 10 considèrent d’ailleurs que les partis politiques devraient faire de la petite enfance une priorité, selon un sondage Léger réalisé pour le compte de l’Observatoire.
Plus que de l’argent, évidemment
La recherche et l’expérience ont montré qu’il ne suffit pas d’y ajouter de l’argent pour améliorer les résultats obtenus, explique-t-elle. La qualité des services offerts, leur accessibilité ainsi que leur capacité à s’adapter aux besoins des différents milieux se sont révélées des facteurs déterminants.
Pour ce faire, il est important que les différents ministères, organismes et acteurs impliqués apprennent à coordonner leurs efforts plutôt que de travailler en silos, explique Julie Meloche. Il faudrait aussi, dit-elle, qu’on apprenne à évaluer sa perform

items.title: Le baril de Brent dépasse les 100 dollars après de nouvelles frappes dans le Golfe
items.summary: Plusieurs navires sont actuellement en feu dans la région du Golfe, selon l’agence maritime britannique UKMTO.
items.body_text:
Des navires sont en feu dans le Golfe après l’annonce par l’Iran de frappes contre une vingtaine de bateaux, dont deux américains, faisant flamber les cours du pétrole, qui repasse la barre symbolique des 100 dollars pour la première fois depuis juillet.
Téhéran a justifié ces attaques par les frappes américaines contre des pétroliers iraniens, et de nouveau mis en garde son ennemi.
« Les actions agressives des États-Unis contre des navires commerciaux iraniens ne font pas qu’accroître les dangers liés aux tensions dans la région, elles constituent également une menace manifeste pour la paix et la sécurité régionales et internationales », a déclaré le ministère des Affaires étrangères, invoquant la « légitime défense ».
Dans le détail, les Gardiens de la Révolution ont affirmé avoir visé deux bateaux américains, huit pétroliers et dix autres navires dans le Golfe.
L’agence maritime britannique UKMTO a fait état de plusieurs navires en feu à différents endroits, sans préciser dans l’immédiat si des victimes étaient à déplorer.
Pour le marché de l’or noir, c’est « une nouvelle escalade », explique Arne Lohmann Rasmussen, analyste chez Global Risk Management. « Si l’Iran commence à viser des pétroliers dans les ports et les zones de mouillage d’autres États du Golfe, une part bien plus importante des infrastructures pétrolières de la région et de la flotte de pétroliers pourrait potentiellement être impliquée ».
Alors que les frappes se concentrent dernièrement sur l’eau et autour du stratégique détroit d’Ormuz, l’Iran avait annoncé dimanche la création d’ici « quelques jours » d’une zone interdite près de cette voie maritime stratégique verrouillée par Téhéran depuis le début de la guerre avec les États-Unis fin février.
Elle couvrira une partie du Golfe d’Oman « et au-delà », ont précisé mercredi les Gardiens, affirmant que ses coordonnées exactes seraient annoncées ultérieurement.
Tout navire entrant dans cette zone sans autorisation s’exposera à des sanctions, ont-ils ajouté.
La Jordanie visée
Cette puissante force armée iranienne a également revendiqué mercredi des attaques contre une base militaire américaine en Jordanie, destinées à « punir l’agresseur ».
Vingt missiles ont été tirés sur le pays, selon l’armée jordanienne, dont 18 interceptés et deux tombés dans des zones désertes.
Mardi, l’armée américaine — qui impose un blocus sur les ports iraniens en réponse au verrouillage d’Ormuz — avait annoncé avoir détruit cinq pétroliers, en représailles à des attaques des Gardiens contre un navire de l’armée américaine.
« L’Iran continue d’essayer de frapper des navires de guerre américains, et à chaque fois qu’ils le font ou tentent de le faire, ils vont perdre des pétroliers, et je pense que vous verrez cela à nouveau aujourd’hui », avait souligné le secrétaire d’État américain Marco Rubio.
Dans leur communiqué mercredi, les Gardiens confirment donc que cinq pétroliers iraniens au total ont bien été attaqués.
Ils ont par ailleurs affirmé la veille avoir « capturé l’un des drones sous-marins les plus modernes de l’armée américaine à l’entrée du détroit d’Ormuz ».
Sans dire s’il s’agissait du même, l’armée américaine a parlé d’un « modèle ancien » tombé en panne près du détroit.
Depuis le début de la guerre, le trafic y est quasiment paralysé, perturbant les marchés mondiaux de l’énergie et faisant régulièrement flamber les cours du brut.
L’Iran exige désormais des navires qu’ils obtiennent une autorisation pour franchir le détroit, une mesure fermement rejetée par Washington et plusieurs pays de la région.
Les négociations diplomatiques, quant à elles, restent au point mort.

items.title: New 11-tower hotel and apartment complex proposed for Bahía de Banderas
items.summary: The latest proposal for a beachside tourist development on the Nayarit coast comes as Sheinbaum works with the governor on a Master Plan for responsible construction and tourism. The post New 11-tower hotel and apartment complex proposed for Bahía de Banderas appeared first on Mexico News Daily
items.body_text:
A major new 11-tower housing and hotel development in Bahía de Banderas, Nayarit, has been proposed at a projected cost of 515 million pesos (US $30.5 million).
The proposal from BM/5096 Business Trust was published in the Environment Ministry’s Ecological Gazette on Aug. 20 for review, and the start of construction is contingent upon the development obtaining the necessary Environmental Impact Assessment (MIA).
The project, known as Ocean II, will cover 65,453 square meters of land, including private land, land reclaimed from the sea and a portion of the Federal Maritime-Terrestrial Zone. It is expected to consist of a hotel zone and a residential zone, accessible from Paseo de los Cocoteros Avenue.
A 187-room hotel will occupy the Palapar Lot within the Los Flamingos Master Condominium across five towers, ranging from five to 10 stories high, while six residential towers will contain 275 apartments. There are plans for basement parking for 784 vehicles.
Planned amenities include restaurants, a spa, a gym, a beach club, an event hall, retail spaces, swimming pools and over 25,000 square meters of green space.
The developers noted in their submission to the Environment Ministry that they expect the project to take around seven years to complete, with the first phase of construction slated to begin in March 2027 and completion expected in 2033.
The announcement is for a general area where beachside development has been controversial, as it is a nesting habitat for the olive ridley sea turtle.
In July, the Environment Ministry revoked a federal concession for a luxury development in Punta de Mita after finding unauthorized construction and environmental violations by developer Cantiles de Mita.
President Sheinbaum visited Nayarit over the weekend to deliver her second annual report, announcing the creation of a Master Plan to conserve beaches, guarantee free access and protect the entire state coastline’s biodiversity.
“I want to tell you that we’ve been working with the [state] governor for over a year on a master plan for tourism in Nayarit, because we don’t want the mangroves destroyed or all the beaches privatized,” said Sheinbaum in a speech.
With reports from El Sol de México and Tribuna de la Bahía

items.title: Mexico fails the 2025 PISA evaluation: A perspective from our CEO
items.summary: Globally, the 2025 PISA testing results are concerning, but Mexico's results are a significant red flag. Here's why, according to MND CEO Travis Bembenek. The post Mexico fails the 2025 PISA evaluation: A perspective from our CEO appeared first on Mexico News Daily
items.body_text:
Just this morning, the 2025 PISA 2025 results were released and as feared, they are very concerning both on a global scale and for Mexico specifically.
As a reminder, PISA assessments test 760,000 15-year-old students in 91 countries in science, mathematics and reading. The results show a continued decline globally in all three areas with reading being the largest long-term weakness. Singapore students scored highest, followed closely by China, Japan and South Korea.
Mexico, which historically has done poorly, did even worse than in previous years. Some of the lowlights of Mexico’s performance:
- Mexico performed below the OECD average in every 2025 PISA domain and placed 64th out of 91 participating countries/economies globally.
- The last time the testing was done, in 2022, Mexico placed 51st out of 81 participating countries/economies.
- Mexico declined in country rankings in math and reading, as well as compared to its previous performance.
- Mexico ranks significantly below the OECD mean in math, science and reading.
- This was Mexico’s fifth consecutive decline in reading since 2009. (The test is taken every 3 years.)
- Half of Mexican 15-year-olds read below the minimum proficiency threshold. This is the threshold that one needs to be able to read in order to learn.
Other than the slight gain in science, the results are a disaster. Not only is Mexico getting worse in math and reading scores, but actually getting relatively much worse than other countries.
I often write about the potential of the Mexican economy, but these testing results are a significant red flag. I have written before about two concerns regarding the Mexican workforce:
1. The education barrier means companies have to make significant investments in workforce development and training to prepare workers. This is both a financial cost and a time loss, and puts Mexican operations at a disadvantage versus other countries.
Could education be a barrier to Mexico’s nearshoring success?
2. The strengthening peso increases the cost of the Mexican workforce. A relatively lower-skilled, relatively expensive workforce means that many companies will instead invest in automation and robotics versus investing in workers.
Solving this problem will not happen overnight, and it will take a massive effort to change the very concerning trend. It will take a combination of parents, entire families, teachers, administrators, politicians and just about everyone else to slow the troubling declines. We as a society need to get back to prioritizing the simple benefits and joy that come from reading and writing. Of course, it is increasingly difficult in the age of AI, but what is more important than making sure the next generation of kids can read and write? We need to get our priorities straight before it is too late.
The MND team will continue to do our part, and we invite kids, parents and grandparents to all enjoy reading via our MND and MND KIDS platforms. If you haven’t invited your child or grandchild to check out MND KIDS yet, what are you waiting for?
Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

items.title: Goods from Mexico now make up almost one-fifth of the US import market
items.summary: Mexico's share of the $332.92 billion U.S. import market in July was 18.2%, ahead of Canada (10.1%) and more than double that of China (8.1%). The post Goods from Mexico now make up almost one-fifth of the US import market appeared first on Mexico News Daily
items.body_text:
Mexico captured almost one-fifth of the U.S. import market in July, well ahead of second-placed Canada, shipping a record US $60.55 billion worth of goods to its northern neighbor, according to official U.S. data.
Mexico’s share of the $332.92 billion U.S. import market in July was 18.2%, ahead of Canada (10.1%); China (8.1%); Vietnam (7.9%); and Taiwan (7.7%), according to data published last Thursday by the U.S. Census Bureau and the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis.
In other words, nearly one in every five dollars the United States spent on imports in July was spent on products from Mexico.
Compared to a year earlier, Mexico’s share of the U.S. import market increased 2.7 percentage points in July.
The difference between Mexico and Canada’s shares of the U.S. import market in July 2025 was 4.5 percentage points. In July of this year, the difference was 8.1 points. Similarly, the difference between Mexico and China’s shares of the U.S. import market increased significantly, rising to 10.1 points in July from 6.5 points in the same month of last year.
The increase in Mexico’s share of the U.S. import market coincides with a boom in Mexican exports. The boom is largely driven by a sharp increase in the export of computer equipment, including AI servers, and other electronics to the U.S.
Mexico in Numbers: How Taiwanese imports are fueling Mexico’s record tech exports
While such products are helping to boost Mexico’s overall export revenue and share of the U.S. import market, their Mexican content is generally very low. That means that a significant share of the revenue Mexico receives from the export of tech products has already been spent on imported inputs, especially from Taiwan.
Mexico’s export revenue increased 33% annually in July
In July — for the first time in any month on record — Mexico’s revenue from selling goods to the United States exceeded $60 billion.
The year-over-year increase in revenue was 33.6% in July. The month-over-month increase was 9.6%.
Canada’s revenue from exports to the United States also increased on an annual basis in July, but only by 4%. Canada’s income declined on a month-over-month basis in July, falling 10%. Canada’s revenue from products shipped to the United States in July was $33.49 billion, equivalent to 55.3% of Mexico’s income in the same month.
China’s revenue from goods shipped to the United States in July was $27.07 billion, up 2.6% from the same month of last year.
Mexico’s exports to the United States reached a record level in July at a time when there was significant uncertainty in the bilateral trade relationship. On July 1, the U.S. government announced that it had declined to renew the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA), the free trade pact that superseded NAFTA in 2020.
Despite that decision, the USMCA remains in effect, allowing most Mexican goods to enter the United States tariff-free and giving Mexico a significant comparative advantage over most of its competitors.
Mexico’s exports to the US increased 16% between January and July
The U.S. data also shows that the United States imported goods from Mexico worth $358.7 billion in the first seven months of 2026. That figure represents an increase of 16% compared to the same period of 2025.
Mexico’s share of the $2.08 trillion U.S. import market between January and July was 17.3%, up from 15% in the same period of last year.
Canada’s share of the U.S. import market remained virtually the same on a year-over-year basis, while China’s share fell almost two percentage points.
Canada’s income from goods shipped to the United States between January and July increased 1.8% to $233.66 billion. Its share of the U.S. import market was 11.24% in the first seven months of the year, an increase of just 0.08 percentage points compared to the same period of last year. Canada and the United States are currently engaged in a significant trade dispute.

items.title: Editorial: Sanciones a Israel: insuficientes pero necesarias
