items.title: Sweden heads to the polls in close election race
items.summary: Sweden votes Sunday in a tight general election that could see the left-wing opposition oust the government after a campaign dominated by concerns over healthcare and the welfare state.
items.body_text:
Audio By Vocalize
Sweden votes Sunday in a tight general election that could see the left-wing opposition oust the government after a campaign dominated by concerns over healthcare and the welfare state amid fears over Europe's security.
Opinion polls have pointed to a victory for the centre-left opposition headed by the Social Democrats.
But Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's centre-right coalition and its parliamentary ally, the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats, have narrowed the gap in the final weeks of campaigning and the election could go down to the wire, experts say.
"There's still a bit of suspense. But all the polls have for a long time shown a very large lead and it's usually difficult to make up that much ground," Stockholm University political scientist Jan Teorell told AFP.
Three polls in the past week credited the four parties on the left with around 50 percent, and the four on the right with around 47 percent.
The right-wing bloc has vowed to pursue its crackdown on crime and immigration, after years of shootings and bombings linked to organised crime networks.
But the bloc has failed to muster the momentum that swept it to power four years ago.
"It came to power very much on a programme to bring down crime and energy prices. And crime and petrol prices have come down, so those issues no longer top voters' agendas," Teorell said.
Filip Lundin, a 35-year-old businessman, told AFP the government had done "a really good job", with "less shootings, better control of where society is going (and) our economy is growing."
The left has vowed to raise taxes on banks and high incomes to invest in healthcare and schools, and help struggling households face rising costs amid growing economic inequality.
That appeals to 46-year-old Hanna Justine Hallbo who works in fashion.
"Healthcare and the social security system must be improved. That has gone down in the last couple of years."
Opposition leader Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats, Sweden's biggest party, told AFP the election was "about what country Sweden should be."
Voters were faced with the choice of "a Sweden that is more like Sweden, where people have a job and where we can improve our welfare", or "a completely different country with a government dominated by Sweden Democrats, a far-right party founded by neo-Nazis."
Stay informed. Subscribe to our newsletter
The far right, the second-biggest party with around 20 percent of votes, is hoping to enter government for the first time.
The populist party has promised Swedes the lowest gas prices and migration in Europe, and dental care reform.
Kristersson became prime minister in 2022 after his minority coalition reached an unprecedented agreement with the Sweden Democrats, giving the former political pariahs significant influence over government policy, especially crime and immigration, in exchange for its support.
Kristersson has promised the far right cabinet posts, including the migration portfolio, if re-elected.
Sweden Democrats leader Jimmie Akesson insists his party should hold several key portfolios, but he is not vying for Kristersson's job -- yet.
"There will be more elections to come, so I'd like to aim for the post of prime minister in 2030 or later," he told AFP in August.
Just over a week before the election, extremism watchdog Expo revealed that a Sweden Democrat civil servant in parliament had shared pro-Russian propaganda for years.
Kristersson, dogged by scandals during his term, reacted sharply.
"We are in the middle of a European war," he told daily Aftonbladet.
"You can't have people who spread pro-Russian narratives working in parliament."
Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Sweden has joined NATO and is massively rearming and boosting civil preparedness.
It has blamed Moscow for cyberattacks, disinformation and intelligence operations, as well as drone and jet incidents over the Baltic.

items.body_text:
President Adama Barrow has declared the country's prolonged electricity crisis a national emergency and promised to increase power generation as protests over rolling blackouts intensify ahead of the December presidential election.
Barrow urged citizens to remain calm over prolonged power cuts. He said that the country is not alone in facing an electricity crisis that has affected several parts of West Africa.
Demonstrators in Banjul and surrounding areas burned tyres, erected roadblocks and called for Barrow to resign after some communities experienced outages lasting up to 48 hours during the hot season.
Police used tear gas to disperse protesters gathering near Barrow's residence and the headquarters of the National Water and Electricity Corporation.
Barrow has promised a 24-megawatt generation machine by the end of October. He announced plans for a further 50-megawatt solar power plant. The electricity provider has blamed soaring temperatures, climate change and wider geopolitical disruptions for the crisis.

Kenya Launches Crackdown on Foreign Informal Traders
Kenyan officials have started to crack down on foreign nationals running small businesses in the informal economy. This comes after President William Ruto backed measures reserving activities such as hawking and petty retail primarily for Kenyan citizens. Ruto said that foreign investors should focus on bringing capital, creating jobs and supporting local production rather than competing with citizens in businesses requiring little capital. Kenyans have reacted with mixed feelings to the move, with some welcoming it as a way of protecting jobs amid high unemployment. Others fear it could fuel xenophobia and discourage foreign investment. Political economist Sheila Owigo Olang questioned whether removing foreign traders would create more opportunities for Kenyans, describing the policy as potentially populist ahead of elections. The government has insisted that foreign nationals who comply with immigration, work permit and licensing requirements remain legally protected. Questions remain over who will ultimately be affected and how the policy will be enforced.

Funding Cuts Push Sudan's Health System to the Brink
Sudan's already fragile health system is nearing collapse as international funding cuts force healthcare facilities to close amid the country's devastating civil war, said Médecins Sans Frontières. More than 33 million people now require medical assistance following the conflict between the Sudanese army and the Rapid Support Forces. The loss of USAID funding and reductions in European aid have left many humanitarian organisations unable to sustain their operations. MSF reported a sharp increase in patient admissions at facilities it supports and said the closure of dozens of healthcare centres is placing enormous pressure on the hospitals that remain open. In some displacement camps, maternity and surgical services have shut down, forcing patients to travel long distances for treatment. The crisis is compounded by attacks on healthcare facilities, widespread hunger and continuing violence, prompting MSF to urge world leaders gathering at the UN General Assembly to increase support.
WFP Says Food Aid Key to Fighting DR Congo Ebola Outbreak

items.title: South Africa: Fake Toys Raise Safety and Job Concerns - South African News Briefs - September 9, 2026
items.summary: [allAfrica]
items.body_text:
Fake Toys Raise Safety and Job Concerns
Concerns are mounting over counterfeit toys flooding the South African market, reports EWN. Fake products are now estimated to account for 25% of sales. Farrel Frank, managing director of the South African Toys and Games Association, warned that counterfeit toys can pose serious health and safety risks and cost jobs. He said the growth of online sales platforms has contributed to the problem. Some major platforms are working with the industry to remove suspicious listings. Consumers are also being urged to remain vigilant after a recent complaint involving a toy with a strong chemical smell that allegedly caused burning and tingling when it touched a consumer’s face.
More Witnesses to Testify in Anele Tembe Inquest
Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn
More witnesses are set to testify in the inquest into the death of Anele Tembe, who fell from the 10th floor of a Cape Town hotel in April 2021, reports SABC News. Lawyers representing Tembe's family questioned witnesses about whether her fiancé, the late rapper Kiernan "AKA" Forbes, had asked for her family to be informed of her death. Two police officers told the court they had no knowledge of whether the family had been contacted. One officer said Forbes did not ask police to contact them. The inquest has also heard from a nearby resident who reported hearing an argument between a man and a woman shortly before Tembe’s death.
Tshuma Extradition Hinges on Plea Deal
Extradition proceedings against UK fugitive Ndodana Tshuma could depend on whether the Johannesburg Magistrates Court accepts a plea agreement between him and the State, reports EWN. Tshuma, who is accused of murdering his wife and two young daughters in the UK before fleeing to South Africa, pleaded guilty to firearm and immigration-related charges following his arrest in Johannesburg. Details of the proposed plea deal and sentence have not been disclosed. The magistrate must still decide whether the agreement is just and appropriate. A custodial sentence could further complicate his extradition to the UK, where he is expected to face the murder allegations.

items.title: Nigeria condemns Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia
items.summary: Nigeria urged the warring parties to “uphold international law, exercise maximum restraint, and refrain from further actions that could escalate the situation, endanger civilian lives.” The post Nigeria condemns Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia appeared first on Premium Times Nigeria.
items.body_text:
The Nigerian government has condemned the recent attack on Saudi Arabia by the Yemeni rebel group, the Houthis, which injured 73 people and destroyed an oil installation.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs, in a statement issued on Tuesday night, warned of the impact of the escalating crisis on regional stability and global energy supplies.
It also said the escalation threatens the kingdom’s sovereignty.
Nigeria said it regarded the “fresh hostilities” as a “serious threat”. It urged the warring parties to “uphold international law, exercise maximum restraint, and refrain from further actions that could escalate the situation, endanger civilian lives.”
The Houthis targeted five cities in Riyadh and have been targeting its tankers in the Red Sea. When confirming the Monday attack, the group said it targeted Saudi Arabia’s state oil company in Abha, Najran, on the Yemeni border, and the Aramco facility in Jizan.
The group said they launched a broad operation deep into Saudi territory using drones and missiles to strike an airbase in the southern city of Khamis Mushait, according to Al Jazeera.
The impact on civilians suggests that this is likely one of the largest attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent years, especially since the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran on 28 February, leading to reprisal attacks on US interests in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries. Saudi authorities said women and children were among the 73 people hurt.
The Houthis and Saudi Arabia have been in a long-running conflict, but have maintained a ceasefire in recent years. The conflict escalated following the US-Israel war on Iran. PREMIUM TIMES reports that a strike exchange between the two parties in July opened a new front in the US-Iran war. The Houthis broke the truce after accusing Saudi Arabia of maintaining a blockade that has worsened the economic situation in the Yemeni capital Sanaa and other parts of the country controlled by the Houthis.
READ ALSO: Britain, France, others to impose sanctions on Israel over West Bank settlements; Israel reacts
Oil prices rose past $100 (£74) a barrel on Wednesday for the first time since July.
Saudi Arabia launched retaliatory strikes against the group a day after the Monday attack. On Wednesday, the Houthis reported more than 30 Saudi strikes on several regions in Yemen.
“Saudi enemy aircraft launched 32 airstrikes on various areas across the governorates of Marib, Al-Jawf, Taiz and Hodeidah over the past few hours,” the rebel group declared.

items.title: Police launch manhunt after mob kills alleged motorcycle thief
items.summary: “Anyone found culpable will be brought to justice in accordance with the law,” the police said. The post Police launch manhunt after mob kills alleged motorcycle thief appeared first on Premium Times Nigeria.
items.body_text:
The police in Akwa Ibom State have launched a manhunt for members of a mob who allegedly beat and set ablaze an unidentified man accused of attempting to steal a motorcycle in Uyo.
The incident occurred at about 7:05 a.m. on Wednesday, at Ikpe Ikot Akpan Village, along the Ikot Ekpene-Uyo Road, Timfon John, the police spokesperson in the state, said in a statement.
Ms John, a deputy superintendent of police, said the slain man was “accused of attempting to steal a motorcycle belonging to Idoroenyin Udo.”
According to the police, Mr Udo resisted the alleged theft and raised an alarm, prompting some people in the area to pursue and apprehend the suspect.
Rather than hand him over to the police, the mob assaulted him and later set him ablaze, killing him.
Police begin investigation
The police said operatives were immediately deployed to the scene after receiving a distress report and that an investigation had commenced.
Ms John said efforts had been intensified to identify, track down and arrest everyone involved in the mob action.
“Anyone found culpable will be brought to justice in accordance with the law,” the police said.
The identity of the deceased had not been established as of the time the police issued the statement.
Police warn against jungle justice
The incident has again raised concerns over mob justice in Akwa Ibom, coming after the police recently announced the arrest of four suspects over the alleged mob killing of a 21-year-old man, Emmanuel Effiong, in Uyo.
READ ALSO: Police foil planned kidnap operation, recover arms in Akwa Ibom
Mr Effiong was allegedly accused of stealing chickens and eggs from a poultry farm in Mbak 4 Community, Uyo Local Government Area, on 19 April.
This newspaper reported that the police said a group of people brutally assaulted Mr Effiong and later died from his injuries. His body was allegedly buried in a shallow grave.
The police subsequently arrested four principal suspects and recovered a Mitsubishi pick-up van allegedly linked to the incident.
The latest killing has prompted another warning from the police against residents taking the law into their own hands.
Investigation into Wednesday’s killing is ongoing, while police efforts to apprehend those connected with the incident continue.

items.title: ‘Regina Daniels didn’t reconcile with Ned Nwoko’ — Mother clarifies
items.summary: The actress’s appearance at the senator’s residence triggered reconciliation and pregnancy speculation months after their acrimonious separation. The post ‘Regina Daniels didn’t reconcile with Ned Nwoko’ — Mother clarifies appeared first on Premium Times Nigeria.
items.body_text:
Rita Daniels, mother of Nollywood actress Regina Daniels, has dismissed speculation that her daughter reconciled with her estranged husband, Delta North senator Ned Nwoko, following her recent visit to his residence.
Rita said the actress was invited to the residence to see her children, adding that the visit did not indicate that the estranged couple had reunited.
Rumours about Regina and Mr Nwoko resurfaced on social media over the weekend after the actress was spotted at his residence, months after their widely publicised marital crisis and separation.
PREMIUM TIMES earlier reported that the estranged couple traded allegations during their separation, with both sides making several claims against each other publicly.
Mr Nwoko accused Regina of drug addiction and alleged that she damaged his property, among other claims. Regina, however, accused the lawmaker of creating a false narrative to tarnish her reputation and portraying her family as enablers while concealing his own actions.
She also accused Mr Nwoko of employing a calculated pattern of control and isolating her from her loved ones. The actress further claimed that their union was never legally formalised, among other allegations.
Visit sparks reactions
Speculation about a possible reconciliation began after a video showing Regina at Mr Nwoko’s residence circulated online.
The actress’s appearance there generated reactions from Nigerians, including some celebrities who had publicly supported her during the couple’s acrimonious separation.
Some social media users alleged that Regina had secretly reconciled with the senator, while others speculated that she was pregnant with his child.
The development also prompted some of her supporters to say they would no longer intervene in disputes involving the estranged couple.
Actor Stanley “Stanley Ontop” Ajemba, one of Regina’s prominent supporters during the marital crisis, criticised the actress in an Instagram post and questioned why she had returned to Mr Nwoko’s residence.
Mr Ajemba said he had publicly defended Regina during the dispute and claimed that his involvement almost landed him in prison.
He also expressed frustration that Regina had not informed him about the visit and vowed not to intervene in another marital dispute.
Mother clarifies
Amid the backlash and speculation about reconciliation, Rita said her daughter’s presence at Mr Nwoko’s residence was solely to see her children.
She clarified during an Instagram conversation with actor Uche Maduagwu, who later shared their exchange on his page.
READ ALSO: Why Ogogo entrusted me with ₦25 million before his death — Ilaro Chief Imam
“It is well, my dear. She was invited to see her children; that was what happened. Thanks a lot for your support and concern,” Rita said.
Her explanation echoed an earlier clarification by Regina’s sister, Destiny Daniels, who said the actress had been granted a visit to see her children and remained single.
Destiny also dismissed speculation that Regina was pregnant, attributing the change in her appearance to weight gain.
Regina and Mr Nwoko held a traditional marriage ceremony in Aniocha Local Government Area of Delta State on 26 May 2019.
They have two sons together: Munir, born in 2020, and Khalifa, born in 2022.

items.title: 'You're not alone in the darkness': Gambia president urges calm after violent blackout protests
items.summary: The country has faced persistent blackouts since June, with some lasting up to 48 hours, residents say.
items.body_text:
'You're not alone in the darkness': Gambia president urges calm after violent blackout protests
- Published
The Gambia's President Adama Barrow has urged citizens to remain calm over prolonged power cuts, saying the country is not alone in facing an electricity crisis that has affected several parts of West Africa.
His comments follow protests on Monday night in the capital Banjul and surrounding areas over blackouts that residents say have sometimes lasted up to 48 hours.
"When you lie down in the heat and the dark, believe that you are not alone in that darkness," Barrow said, pledging to boost power supplies by next month.
The Gambia supplements its own generation with imported electricity, including supplies from Guinea and neighbouring Senegal.
The tiny West African country has endured persistent blackouts since June, with outages becoming longer and more frequent during the current hot season as soaring temperatures drive up electricity demand.
Frustration boiled over on Monday night, when protesters took to the streets in Banjul and surrounding areas, burning tyres and blocking roads over the prolonged power cuts.
Police used tear gas to disperse crowds in Westfield area as they moved towards the headquarters of the national electricity company, Nawec, with some chanting. "Barrow must go".
Protesters also gathered outside the vice-president's residence in Farato, where banners at an office of Barrow's ruling National People's Party were damaged.
The unrest comes just months before a presidential election expected in December, in which Barrow is seeking a controversial third term.
In a televised address on Tuesday night, Barrow acknowledged the hardship caused by the blackouts but warned protesters against damaging public infrastructure, saying it would only worsen the disruption and divert money towards repairs.
"Let us not destroy in a moment of anger what we suffered so long to gain," he said.
The president admitted there had been shortcomings in the government's planning, power generation and maintenance systems, calling the resulting outages "a national security issue" and an "emergency".
"I know that the fans have stopped turning, children work in the dark, mothers throw away stale food, and the heat is unbearable by day and by night," the president, promising that supplies would improve by the end of October.
He said a new 24-megawatt generating unit was being installed at the Brikama power station and would be commissioned by the end of next month.
A contract has also been awarded for a 50MW solar power plant in Soma, although no completion date was given.
"For a system of our size, this is considerable power, enough to make a big difference in your homes," Barrow added.
The president visited facilities for the national energy utility on Tuesday morning and promised that The Gambia would receive new generators this week.
Gallo Saidy, the Nawec chief, also appealed for patience, saying reduced electricity imports from the regional grid had contributed to the shortages.
He said lower rainfall this year had reduced the electricity available through the regional network.
"We are aware of the frustration and constraints that the Gambian people have," he said. "We are just asking The Gambian people to give us a little bit of time and patience."
Nawec had warned in August that unusually high temperatures had driven a surge in electricity demand, while a technical problem had also affected a major generating unit supplying imported power.

items.title: Kenya moves to register frightened Burundians as tension over foreign traders rises
items.summary: All foreigners without proper documents in Kenya are urged to register through their embassies.
items.body_text:
Kenya moves to register frightened Burundians as tension over foreign traders rises
- Published
Kenya says it will register undocumented Burundians and other East Africans living in the country, following days of anxiety over President William Ruto's directive targeting foreigners in small-scale businesses.
On Monday, hundreds of Burundians scrambled to process travel documents amid uncertainty over whether they could remain in Kenya.
Charles Owino, the Kenyan government spokesperson, has now said those without proper documents should register through their embassies or high commissions as the authorities work with diplomatic missions to regularise their status.
Those undergoing registration would be presumed legally in Kenya during the process, Owino said.
Ruto had set Monday as the deadline for foreigners operating small-scale businesses to cease work. The directive came after the trade ministry said some foreigners exploit visa rules to work without the required permits.
Long queues were seen outside Burundi's embassy in the capital, Nairobi, after it said it would offer free emergency travel documents to citizens who wanted to go back home.
Others were seen racing to buy bus tickets.
Some Burundians have reportedly faced hostility after President Ruto ordered action against foreign street vendors and those operating small shops, saying such jobs should be protected for Kenyans.
Kenyan officials have since sought to reassure neighbouring countries that there is no blanket ban on foreign traders.
Addressing a news conference on Monday, Owino said the government had opened registration and documentation of all foreign nationals residing in Kenya without valid documents.
He acknowledged that because of historical circumstances and regional dynamics, a number of East African nationals, including several Burundians, resided and operated in Kenya without full documentation.
"To address this constructively, the government of Kenya is establishing a formal documentation and registration window," Owino said.
"We call upon all undocumented East African community nationals, and specifically Burundian citizens currently residing in Kenya, to immediately present themselves to their respective high commissions or embassies for formal identity registration."
In a statement on Tuesday, the Kenyan government said foreign nationals running businesses had 90 days to regularise their immigration status, work permits, business registrations and licences.
After that the requirements would be "enforced firmly and strictly", it said.
"During this period, the responsible government agencies will provide the necessary guidance and administer the applicable requirements fairly, consistently and without discrimination," Kenya State House's statement added.
It also warned that no individual or group had "the authority to harass, intimidate, threaten or interfere with foreign nationals or their businesses".
Senior Kenyan foreign affairs official Korir Sing'oei has apologised to Burundians over the harassment some have faced, saying the president's directive had been misunderstood.
"I want to say sorry to all the Burundi nationals here," Sing'oei said during a visit to the Burundian embassy in Nairobi on Monday.
He said the government would tighten security in areas where Burundians live.
Kenya hosts hundreds of thousands of migrants from across East Africa seeking work and business opportunities.
According to the United Nations refugee agency, there are around 16,000 Burundian refugees and asylum seekers in Kenya.
It is unclear how many are involved in small-scale trading.
On Monday, some of them were seen carrying all their belongings - from suitcases to mattresses - as they tried to leave Kenya. However, some of them said they could not afford the cost of travel and urged the Kenyan government to extend the deadline.
Ruto's directive follows a similar crackdown in Tanzania last year and rising antiâmigrant sentiment in South Africa.

items.title: Sudan's healthcare system on brink of collapse after cuts, medical charity warns
items.summary: Médecins Sans Frontières is urging world leaders to increase funding to help the millions who need aid.
items.body_text:
Sudan's healthcare system on brink of collapse after cuts, medical charity warns
- Published
Sudan's fragile health system is on the brink of collapse as global funding cuts have led to the closure of healthcare facilities across the country, MÃ©decins Sans FrontiÃ¨res (MSF) has warned.
Dozens of organisations were unable to find alternative funding after the US - the largest donor to Sudan - closed USAID, its body for delivering foreign aid, last year, the medical charity said.
MSF urged world leaders gathering at the UN General Assembly in New York to take action.
The war that erupted in April 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, with more than 33 million people needing medical assistance.
MSF said while the US was still the largest donor to Sudan, existing grants to many USAID-funded organisations ran out in June - as European governments were also reducing international assistance.
According to the Paris-based Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), international aid fell globally by 21.3% in 2025 compared to the previous year.
- A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan 
  - Published13 November 2025
- Sudan's invisible children - born in war with no legal identity 
  - Published7 August
"War is driving Sudan's needs; funding cuts are shrinking the response," said Muhammad Ibrahim, the head of charity in Sudan.
"MSF's work in Sudan is privately funded. But when funding disappears from other health services, clinics close, patients have fewer places to go, and pressure shifts to the facilities that remain, including ours."
This has meant that patients often have to make dangerous and long trips to get treatment.
"After a longer and more expensive journey, patients often arrive in a much more serious condition, and the hospital may already be full," explained SebastiÃ¡n Traficante, MSF's emergency co-ordinator in the western region of Darfur, which has experienced much of the fighting over the last three years.
Between January and April 2026, MSF saw admissions jump by 22.5% in facilities it supports in central Darfur, when compared to the same time last year.
In May alone, 45 healthcare centres in the area had stopped receiving funding, it said.
According to MSF, the closure of frontline services was putting other hospitals under severe strain - as they were losing their capacity to function and medicines were disappearing.
It gave Gedaref state's Tanedba camp, where 18,400 people who have fled their homes live, as an example. Its maternity and surgical wards have closed down after a humanitarian organisation left in June.
As a result, MSF is now running an emergency room there, but pregnant women who need surgery to deliver a baby, have to travel three hours to the nearest city.
In the Um Rakuba camp - also in Gedaref - the number of aid agencies working there has dropped from 35 in 2021, to less than 10.
According to the charity, the camp currently hosts around 17,000 people, most of whom are women and children.
"If support does not increase, more patients will face longer journeys, fewer treatment options and greater risk of arriving too late for care," MSF's UK humanitarian representative Liz Harding said.
At the same time as the health system was struggling with funding, attacks on healthcare workers were continuing, MSF said.
In 2025, Sudan saw 1,620 people killed in attacks on medical facilities - which the charity said accounted for 82% of all global deaths from attacks on healthcare worldwide.
According to the UN, more than 19.5 million people are also experiencing "crisis levels" of food insecurity and more than five million are facing "emergency levels of hunger".
The fighting shows no sign of easing - despite the expected arrival of international diplomats in the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, for consultations aimed at ending the civil war.

items.title: German Democracy, as We Knew It, Is Over
items.summary: A far-right state election victory is ushering in the end of the country’s postwar political system.
items.body_text:
German Democracy, as We Knew It, Is Over
A far-right state election victory is ushering in the end of the country’s postwar political system.
Has a small, largely elderly, left-behind pocket of Germany struck a fatal blow against its postwar liberal democracy? That is the question many are asking after Sunday’s election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, which saw the Alternative for Germany (AfD) trounce the mainstream parties to stand on the verge of power—the first time a far-right party would do so in Germany since the fall of the Nazi regime.
As has been the case when other tsunamis have struck—Donald Trump’s presidential election victories in the United States, Brexit in the United Kingdom, to name but two of many around the world—the response of those in the political center has ranged from fury to consternation to despair. But most of all, a sense of dumbstruck paralysis. They could see it coming; they took some action, but they were swept away. And now, as they face the consequences, so the recriminations begin.

That is the question many are asking after Sunday’s election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, which saw the Alternative for Germany (AfD) trounce the mainstream parties to stand on the verge of power—the first time a far-right party would do so in Germany since the fall of the Nazi regime.
As has been the case when other tsunamis have struck—Donald Trump’s presidential election victories in the United States, Brexit in the United Kingdom, to name but two of many around the world—the response of those in the political center has ranged from fury to consternation to despair. But most of all, a sense of dumbstruck paralysis. They could see it coming; they took some action, but they were swept away. And now, as they face the consequences, so the recriminations begin.
In Washington, the targets of opprobrium ranged from presidential nominees Kamala Harris and Hillary Clinton to Democrats in Congress to the entire party establishment. In the United Kingdom, they were many and varied, from then-Prime Minister David Cameron, who called the 2016 referendum, to then-London mayor Boris Johnson, who changed his mind at the last moment to lead the calls to quit the European Union, to the ever-present right-winger Nigel Farage, to Jeremy Corbyn, the left-wing Labour leader who campaigned half-heartedly to stay while purportedly preferring to leave.
In Germany, it’s simpler. All the guns are trained on Friedrich Merz, the chancellor of the past 16 months with the ignominious distinction of historic low opinion poll ratings. He is the man who boasted when first challenging for the leadership of his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party in 2018 that he would halve the popular support for the AfD, only to see it double. He is the man who promised voters an “autumn of reforms”—he meant 2025, and yet they are still spluttering their way through parliament.
Merz spent years trying to become CDU leader, criticizing former Chancellor Angela Merkel, openly and behind her back, for taking the party too much to the center, for being too generous to welfare claimants and too welcoming to migrants. What Germans wanted, he insisted, was more genuine conservatism.
They’ve now got that, but they’ve decided they would rather eat their meat rare. items.summary: An erratic United States and a rising China have the region recalibrating.
items.body_text:
Southeast Asia’s Subtle Shift on Taiwan
An erratic United States and a rising China have the region recalibrating.
Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Southeast Asia Brief.
The highlights this week: China is making ground on Taiwan in the region, Prabowo swings by Russia again, and Thailand sends mixed messages about AI.
Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Southeast Asia Brief.
The highlights this week: China is making ground on Taiwan in the region, Prabowo swings by Russia again, and Thailand sends mixed messages about AI.
A Shift in Stance on Taiwan
China is making ground on Taiwan in Southeast Asia.
The issue swam into view last month. First, the Indonesian navy performed a joint exercise with the Chinese navy off the east coast of Taiwan—which it then hastily downplayed.
A few days later, on Aug. 16, Al Jazeera aired an interview with Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, in which he made comments suggesting sympathy with China taking military action against Taiwan.
“I always take Malaysia as an example. If one province decides to break away, do we use force? I think I will protect the sanctity and unity of the nation,” Anwar said when asked if he would condemn China using force against Taiwan.
Anwar subsequently walked back these comments, emphasizing that a peaceful approach was best.
However, while his comments were unusually strong, they reflect a slow drift from Malaysia toward Beijing’s line on the matter.
Just compare Malaysia and China’s joint statements past and present. One in 2014 affirmed that “Taiwan is an inseparable part of China” but also pointedly mentioned support for “peaceful reunification.” But in 2024 and again in 2025, there was no specific mention of peace.
Other countries have also dropped mentions of peace. Joint statements with Cambodia included it last in 2019 but not since 2022.
Thailand has also subtly shifted its position. In 2023, statements simply recognized “Taiwan as an inalienable part of China.” In 2025, new language appeared declaring that Thailand would not “support any call for the independence of Taiwan,” and in 2026, it “firmly supported peaceful reunification.”
The Philippines, while keeping to the “one China” policy, has usually taken a stiffer line on potential force against Taiwan. This reflects its closeness to the United States and its own strong stance against China in the South China Sea. However, this year has seen President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. soften somewhat.
Taiwan has attempted to bolster its position. In 2016, it launched the New Southbound policy, aimed at deepening diplomatic ties with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and India.
The ideological resonance of democracy can also cultivate sympathies in the region. From 2020 to 2021, citizens of Thailand, Myanmar, Taiwan, and Hong Kong expressed solidarity with one another in the face of authoritarian pressure from China and domestic governments.
Taiwan also sometimes pushes back. In July, Cambodia was removed from Taiwan’s visa-privilege programs, which all other ASEAN members are part of, because of its repeated “inappropriate statements denigrating Taiwan’s sovereignty.”
Still, overall, the various diplomatic moves toward China’s position in the region show Taiwan has lost ground.
Do these shifts in wording, stray comments, and ill-judged exercises add up to anything substantive though?
Some might argue no. Whatever Anwar says, all Southeast Asian nations are acutely aware that an invasion of Taiwan would be, at best, an economic catastrophe for the region. At worst, it could suck in the United States, turning the area into a charnel house—and that’s before we even consider nuclear risk.
Furthermore, most Southeast Asian countries continue to maintain strong relations with Taiwan, covering trade, investment, and migration of Southeast Asian workers. items.body_text:
Introducing the Fall 2026 Print Issue
How to survive in a world without rules.
The liberal international order, flawed and unequal as it was, is gone. Personally, I’ve grown tired of wringing my hands at what is no more. I’m focused on what might come next—and how we can shape it to be peaceful and fair.
“It’s time to throw some spaghetti against the wall,” one former diplomat suggested to me recently. Consider this issue to be exactly that: an assortment of new, perhaps even radical, ideas. Some of them won’t be quite al dente, but all good dishes are born of trial and error. And the current moment, ahead of the U.S. midterms, is exactly the time to experiment.

“It’s time to throw some spaghetti against the wall,” one former diplomat suggested to me recently. Consider this issue to be exactly that: an assortment of new, perhaps even radical, ideas. Some of them won’t be quite al dente, but all good dishes are born of trial and error. And the current moment, ahead of the U.S. midterms, is exactly the time to experiment.
The question we wanted to grapple with is how countries and companies can survive in a world without rules. And as they do that, what kind of order should come next?
Hal Brands takes a stab at a survival guide for the here and now. Don’t be nostalgic, get ready to pay higher risk premiums, and start investing in your own defense and manufacturing, he advises. That might get countries through the next few years, but what then?
Charles A. Kupchan has a plan. The world’s only real hope of maintaining order, he argues, is a system that has both a bottom-up and a top-down component. The former is necessary because that is the direction in which the world is already headed—a diffusion of power and a bigger role for regional groupings. The latter, however, is where we’ll have to get creative, especially since the United Nations won’t magically start working again. Kupchan proposes a flexible and informal steering group resembling the 19th-century Concert of Europe, sitting above the U.N. and directing a symphony of tiered groups. I found the idea compelling and thought-provoking, and I hope you engage with it. Now there’s just the small matter of getting Beijing and Washington on board.
We had to explore how the flow of money fits into our rewiring of power, of course. Countries in the global south have struggled of late with the trend toward nationalism and protectionism and without the tailwinds of unfettered free trade and globalization. Michael Beckley makes the case that there’s a useful synergy right in front of our eyes. The developed world is cash-rich and labor-poor, while the developing world is cash-poor and labor-rich; each side needs the other for its future growth, so why not embrace their respective opportunities for arbitrage? Beckley explains how to get there.
Mariana Mazzucato injects a dose of fairness. The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank were created as global organizations but in reality concentrate power in a handful of countries. Mazzucato argues that a world without rules is the crisis we needed to rewrite some of those rules with the common good at the center.
The final essay in our cover package is by me, and it’s a deliberate provocation. U.S. President Donald Trump started his second term with a bang, as we all know. He has been incredibly disruptive for global order. But Trump has peaked, I argue. His coercive powers are now in decline, in large part because of his own policies. The key example is this year’s Iran war and how it has drained the U.S. military of munitions. Countries and companies are already realizing this and adapting how they navigate Trump—and how they will approach discussions about a future world order.

items.title: How al-Qaeda Ended
items.summary: Terrorists sometimes defeat themselves.
items.body_text:
Al-Qaeda has ended. The organization that Osama bin Laden founded and led, that attacked the United States 25 years ago and killed 2,977 innocent Americans in the World Trade Center, the Pentagon, and rural Pennsylvania, no longer survives—and U.S. officials should say so, instead of burnishing the group’s legacy by acting and speaking as if it still exists. Terrorism has not ceased, jihadism has not gone away, and the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran may ignite more anti-American sentiment and violence. But the group that attacked the United States on 9/11 is finished.
In the years following that assault, thousands of Americans dedicated their lives to avenging the victims. The nationwide horror of watching planes go into towers—innocent people crushed, burned, or jumping to their deaths—catalyzed a passionate response. And the cost to those who responded was high: in the post-9/11 wars, more than 15,000 U.S. military members and contractors died in combat, and some 1.8 million became disabled. And from 2012 to 2021, four times as many active-duty or veteran military members died by suicide as died in combat. Service members from loyal U.S. allies, especially Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, and the United Kingdom, joined the United States in combat; hundreds of them died fighting alongside Americans. They and their families deserve to know their efforts were not in vain. Washington and its allies lost the war in Afghanistan but succeeded against al-Qaeda.
Jihadist terrorism persists as a threat, and not every group using the name “al-Qaeda” has been neutralized. Dangerous organizations operate in the Arabian Peninsula, the Horn of Africa, North Africa, the Sahel, and South Asia. They carry out attacks and hold territory, and some have come close to taking down governments, especially in Mali, Somalia, and Yemen. Jihadists of various stripes train in Taliban-governed Afghanistan—a development that must be closely monitored. But none of what are sometimes called “al-Qaeda affiliates” is centrally directed or led by bin Laden’s organization, and officials should cease suggesting they are, since doing so inflates the threat they pose without making it any easier to combat them. Indeed, it would be best to cease using the term “al-Qaeda affiliate” altogether.
Studying the pattern of attacks tied directly to al-Qaeda shows how the central organization ran out of steam. Before 9/11, the core al-Qaeda organization kept up a steady pace of global operations against U.S. targets, with a track record that included the 1993 bombing of the World Trade Center (six dead, more than 1,000 injured), the 1996 bombing of Khobar Towers (19 killed, hundreds injured), the 1998 bombing of the U.S. embassies in Kenya and Tanzania (224 killed, thousands injured), and the 2000 attack on the USS Cole (17 killed). After 2001, core al-Qaeda’s efforts against the U.S. homeland included a fumbled 2001 attempt to ignite a bomb placed in a shoe on an airliner bound for Miami and a failed 2009 suicide bombing plot targeting the New York City subway. The group caused more pain for U.S. friends and allies than for the United States itself, with deadly attacks in Bali in 2002, Riyadh in 2003, and London in 2005. But following that spike in the first decade of the twenty-first century, the momentum shifted to other jihadist groups, and after 2009, core al-Qaeda’s global operations essentially ceased.
For decades, I have studied how terrorist groups end, based on a dataset of 457 terrorist campaigns and organizations going back a century. By analyzing their makeup, targets, and intended audiences, one can identify common trajectories. Although not mutually exclusive, there are six major pathways such groups ultimately take: decapitation, negotiation, success, failure, repression, and reorientation to another mode of operation (such as ordinary criminality or insurgency). items.title: The Right Way to Sanction Russia
items.summary: How Europe can disrupt Moscow’s oil windfall.
items.body_text:
When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, Western countries responded with aggressive economic restrictions, freezing Russia’s official foreign exchange reserves, placing export controls on critical technology, and sanctioning scores of its political, military and business leaders. Yet more than four years later, the war is still going on, and Western sanctions have inflicted only limited pain on the Russian economy. Russia continues to trade oil and other commodities, recently receiving a massive windfall as the closing of the Strait of Hormuz caused global oil prices to soar. These profits are raising the government’s tax revenue at a critical time, helping it fund the war in Ukraine and stabilize the country’s financial markets. If sanctions were looking ineffective before, Russia’s economic rebound since the start of the United States’ and Israel’s war with Iran have only strengthened that perception.
But it is wrong to write off sanctions as a policy tool. When Western policymakers portray them as a wasted effort or counterproductive, their governments are playing right into Moscow’s hands. And they are discounting the enormous strain that sanctions could still place on the Russian system if properly enforced. By reducing the flow of hard currency into Russia, sanctions have the potential to send the ruble into a spiral of depreciation, which in turn would send inflation soaring and destabilize the country’s broader economy.
It is not too late to make sanctions effective. One-fifth of Russia’s GDP is directly linked to oil and gas extraction, and exports account for nearly one-third of government revenues. Russia evades Western oil sanctions primarily by using a shadow fleet of oil tankers, and that fleet is vulnerable to European pressure. It passes through European-controlled waterways, replenishes its numbers with European-owned ships, and can be forced to engage with a Western-dominated insurance industry. All of this gives Europe the power to restrict the fleet’s operations, and thereby drastically reduce Moscow’s ability to finance its ruinous war.
THE RISE OF THE SHADOW FLEET
The sanctions that the United States, the European Union, the United Kingdom, and Canada placed on Russia in early 2022 ran the gamut. They included export controls on sensitive goods such as semiconductors, computers, and lasers as well as the freezing of Russian foreign exchange reserves held by Western central banks. Yet efforts to curtail Russia’s oil exports back then were limited. The world economy was still rebounding from the COVID-19 pandemic, oil demand was strong and rising, and Russian oil accounted for roughly one-tenth of global supply. Western countries did not want to drive up prices by embargoing Russian oil, but the mere fear that they might do so caused oil prices to surge anyway, delivering enormous profits to Moscow. Russia’s current account surplus, or the amount by which its export receipts exceeded its import payments, soared to an all-time high of $235 billion in 2022. Within one year, Russia had nearly recouped the foreign exchange reserves that were frozen by Western countries.
Western countries needed to figure out a way to prevent Moscow from generating large amounts of cash from oil exports without causing global prices to spike. Many oil and commodity analysts worried that any attempt to take Russian oil off global markets could lift crude prices from their prewar baseline of around $75 per barrel to $200 or higher, allowing Russia to make enormous profits from its remaining exports even if the volume of exports were lower. Such a substantial price increase would almost certainly drive the world into recession.
The solution the G-7 came up with in December 2022 was an oil price cap. Around 70 percent of the vessels shipping Russian oil were Western-owned and close to 90 percent used Western insurance, financing, and brokering services. items.title: Why America Can’t Strangle Iran
items.summary: The sources of Tehran’s economic resilience.
items.body_text:
For Iran and the United States, August 24 was Groundhog Day. “We are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe,” declared U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. “Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime.” It was the same promise he made in April, when he said that the United States was “imposing a financial stranglehold on the Iranian regime” under what the White House called Operation Economic Fury. It was also akin to the May 2018 rollout of the first Trump administration’s “maximum pressure” campaign, in which Secretary of State Mike Pompeo announced that Iran would be targeted by the “strongest sanctions in history.” And it sounded like U.S. President Barack Obama’s promise, made in 2012, that the Iranian government was to face “even more crippling sanctions.”
The Iranian economy has certainly felt the effects of all the successive restrictions. Ever since U.S. President Donald Trump’s first term in office, the country has experienced little growth and high inflation. As a result, Iranian firms have built less infrastructure and adopted fewer new technologies compared with peers in other developing economies. Iranian households, once increasingly affluent, are now at risk of falling below the state’s poverty line.
Yet for the better part of a decade, Iran has been able to resist U.S. economic coercion. Until the recent blockade, it used sanctions-evasion techniques to continue oil exports to its key customer, China. Its non-oil industries also adapted to the sanctions, as currency devaluation reduced competition from imports and made Iranian products more competitive in regional markets, boosting exports. Iran thereby avoided the kind of runaway economic collapse seen in other sanctioned countries, such as Syria and Venezuela.
Today, war is testing the resilience of the Iranian economy in ways that sanctions alone could not. Numerous U.S. and Israeli airstrikes have targeted critical industrial facilities, including some of Iran’s most important steel and petrochemical plants. The damage sustained during these attacks has led to major production outages for key industrial goods. The general decline in maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz and the specific disruptions caused by the U.S. naval blockade have not only reduced Iran’s exports; they have also throttled imports of much-needed capital and consumer goods. According to a July estimate by the International Monetary Fund, Iran’s GDP is set to contract 5.4 percent this year after shrinking by less than half that over the previous 12 months. Year-on-year inflation climbed from 52.6 percent in December 2025 to 88.6 percent by the start of the summer. The value of the country’s currency has hit a record low of over two million rials to the dollar.
But even as the country’s economic situation is getting worse, Iran’s leadership remains better able to resist the coercive effects of sanctions than it might appear. The state of the economy is not yet impinging on Iran’s ability to wage war. Stockpiles of various goods remain deep, thanks to years of sanctions experience. And the Iranian state, with its powerful repressive tools, has figured out how to offload much of the economic pain onto ordinary Iranians while making sure its own needs are met. Trump’s approach, in other words, can certainly immiserate most of the country’s people. But it cannot successfully strangle the Islamic Republic itself.
ANATOMY OF A CRISIS

items.summary: Francis Fukuyama has long been considered a naive triumphalist. He now wants to set the record straight.
items.body_text:
Why the End of History Is So Miserable
Francis Fukuyama has long been considered a naive triumphalist. He now wants to set the record straight.
Francis Fukuyama never promised us we’d be happy.
To be fair to the many readers who thought otherwise, The End of History and the Last Man, his famous 1992 book, did give off a whiff of utopia, trumpeting a post–Cold War world in which liberal democracy had vanquished competing political systems and everyone could lie back on their affordable chaise longues and raise a glass to the expiration of all strife and struggle. “Several” people each week still ask the poor man whether he would like to unwrite that book, he says. Yet Fukuyama insists today that if you had read to the last page—in fact, the last five chapters—you would not have expected serenity. His more sober forecast is right there in the original essay that led to the book: “The end of history will be a very sad time.”
Fukuyama has published a new memoir, In the Realm of the Last Man, in which he hopes to shake off a reputation that he clearly can’t stand. He is not a naive Pollyanna, and he never was. By the “end of history,” he did mean that we had arrived at the best of all possible worlds—and he still does. But being the “Last Man,” inhabiting this ending, was always presented as an unstable condition. Fukuyama borrowed the concept from the dark mind of Friedrich Nietzsche, who used it to refer to a person bored out of their senses, someone who lives in a society where there is nothing left to risk their life for.
What appeared in his earlier book as an alarming afterthought is now front and center for Fukuyama. He wrote The End of History during a time of American triumphalism, as the Berlin Wall was turned into rubble, but the events of the past three decades—9/11, the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, Donald Trump—have offered up a different story. Fukuyama knows this. His defensiveness keeps him from fully acknowledging how far he’s had to step back from his own previously boosterish views, but he speaks about liberal democracy, this supposedly happy end state, in much gloomier tones. It now sounds like a scary cul-de-sac at night, where the streetlight is busted, an eerie tension fills the air, and there seems to be no way forward.
Purely as a memoir, I should say, this one is disappointing. Fukuyama loses interest in telling his own life story around page 60. The fun and revealing anecdotes are front-loaded. For example, as a young foreign-policy analyst, he kept failing a CIA polygraph test because a question about whether he had ever had sex with a man got him completely flustered (he hadn’t, he hastens to tell us). He writes about his father, a sociologist and committed liberal, who never stopped giving Fukuyama a hard time for his once-conservative political opinions (he did work for Ronald Reagan and the RAND Corporation, after all), telling him he was “brainwashed” by other people. When these more intimate insights taper off, so does any causal connection between Fukuyama’s personal background and his evolving thinking. His grandparents were Japanese immigrants who spent World War II in an internment camp. But this is only briefly mentioned, which left me wondering whether the stories they told him made him more attuned to the vulnerabilities of a pluralistic society.
We do get a few chapters about what an unapologetic gearhead he is, a lover of woodworking who can also assemble a computer from scratch. Yet Fukuyama spends most of his time and energy on summarizing the ideas that have animated his work, producing a greatest-hits album of insights. This succession of shifting concepts helps clarify how much the bravado that marked The End of History has seeped out of his work. The invasion of Iraq and the long chaos that followed were a turning point. Fukuyama broke with the neocon friends and mentors who had shaped his career until then. items.title: This Was a Good Sculpture
items.summary: Washington, D.C., is full of cords of connection. By removing a Joel Shapiro work, the Kennedy Center severed one.
items.body_text:
This Was a Good Sculpture
Washington, D.C., is full of cords of connection. By removing a Joel Shapiro work, the Kennedy Center severed one.
Until last week, a big electric-blue sculpture by Joel Shapiro sat next to the Kennedy Center. Boxy and rigid but seemingly weightless, Blue looked like a clumsy person who’d been swept by a breeze into an accidental pirouette. Shapiro called the metalwork a “celebration of possibility.” Some people thought it looked like Gumby. I loved it. The leaders of the Kennedy Center—and there is really just one leader of the Kennedy Center—did not.
Workers dismantled Blue last Wednesday. No specific reason was given, save that the change had occurred at the center’s request. Internal documents obtained by The New York Times say that the sculpture was targeted for removal soon after Donald Trump took control of the institution.
Shapiro—one of the most important American sculptors of his generation—died last summer. He spent decades coaxing human gesture and emotion from the austere geometry of minimalism. His abstract shapes and forms have strong personalities. They lie in wait for their audience, then suddenly come alive.
I knew Shapiro a little, through his wife, the artist Ellen Phelan. He was owlish, warm, blunt, and inspiring to be around, always searching for what he called a “little moment of rapture.” Blue was one of those. It wasn’t gilded.
Shapiro spent two years in India in the Peace Corps, which President John F. Kennedy established. The antecedent for the Kennedy Center was right there in New Delhi: the architect Edward Durell Stone’s striking new American embassy, which he would channel in his later design for a national arts center—which would be named for Kennedy after his assassination. Decades later, Shapiro made monumental works for American diplomatic missions overseas. Blue, fittingly, stood near the Kennedy Center’s Peace Corps Gallery.
Washington, D.C.’s landscape is full of these cords of connection—some accidental, some carefully arranged. This one was simply cut, leaving a blemish in a city full of symbols.
Those symbols are everywhere. You can walk from the Kennedy Center to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum in a brisk half hour. I’ve taken this route frequently, usually while running. The parks, the monuments, the cherry trees, and the limestone edifices of federal power all prompt questions: about who gets memorialized, what myths and whose money might explain why, and who’s missing.
One reason I repeat this route so often is to keep an inventory. What moved? What vanished? What’s next? Some landmarks—the State Department, in Foggy Bottom, for instance—haven’t changed but were hollowed by the Trump administration’s personnel cuts. The Lincoln Memorial is no longer visible in the botched Reflection Pool, an eyesore that’s been drained again to fix a shoddy renovation.
Keep going, past the memorials to World War II and the Korean War, and, nearby, Maya Lin’s black-granite scar, elegizing U.S. troops in Vietnam. I love odd and nerdy things along this route: statues of 19th-century Latin American liberators, Cold War allegorical bronzes, and, tucked away, Robert Berks’s playful Einstein. (People like to sit on his lap and rub his nose.) Einstein said, “Force always attracts men of low morality.” Another cord of connection: Berks made the giant bronze bust of Kennedy that resides inside the Kennedy Center.
Push farther, past the Jefferson Memorial and the Tidal Basin, until Independence Avenue and the Holocaust Museum—which had its own upheaval last year, when Trump purged its board of trustees—come into view.
Here, less than two miles from the Kennedy Center, stands another big Joel Shapiro—his portentously titled Loss and Regeneration. It’s one of his most painful, deeply moving works. Two black-bronze forms: a windowless house crashed upside down on its roof and, 100 feet away, an unstable but determined tree-like shape. Life after genocide.

items.title: What September 11 Took From Me
items.summary: There are some things time doesn’t heal.
items.body_text:
During a visit in May to the Maritime Museum in Halifax, Nova Scotia, I watched a film about a 1917 cargo-ship explosion that killed more than 1,700 townspeople and injured many more. The grainy black-and-white images of the flattened city catapulted me back to the devastation of Lower Manhattan after terrorists attacked the World Trade Center on September 11, 2001. Halifax suffered a blizzard following the cargo-ship catastrophe, and the sight of the city covered in a deep blanket of snow recalled the dust and debris from the once-glimmering towers that coated the Financial District. When I heard the recorded voices of the Haligonian survivors recounting their memories, I walked out of the small theater to cry.
Twenty-five years on from September 11, 2001, an image or memory can still evoke the very moment I learned that my 36-year-old redheaded husband, Jeffrey R. Smith, would not be coming home from work that day.
I, too, am now a voice in a museum. At the National September 11 Memorial & Museum, any visitor can replay my family’s intensely personal memories of a national horror. Years before the museum had a building, curators teamed up with StoryCorps, an oral-history nonprofit, and tried to make it easy for families to contribute by giving us a special number to call and record from home. Making this call felt like a leap of faith. How would these recordings be used? Where would they be stored? Still, my two daughters—who were then 8 and 10 years old—and I decided we wanted to participate.
I remember sitting on the couch while the girls took turns, cupping their hands over my cellphone in a semblance of privacy. I also recall one of them wandering the house, chatting like a teenager. I remember wanting them to practice what they would say, and I wanted to hear it before they called, but my girls had their own ideas. I found it nerve-racking until I realized that whatever they said would be straight from the hearts of girls who were not yet 3 and not yet 1 when their father was killed.
I haven't heard the recordings. I recently thought that I wanted to, but I couldn't imagine donning headphones and listening to my voice or my daughters’ amid strangers at the museum. I contacted the chief curator, who kindly offered a private place for me to revisit what we had said. I made a date, then canceled it. I doubt I will reschedule. I know that if I listened, the editor in me would wish we could rerecord, and the rest of me would fall apart.
When we were in Nova Scotia, my friends and I took turns reading historical plaques out loud. I always make a point of reading the names on memorials wherever I find them. Years ago, one Presidents’ Day weekend, my daughters and I took the train to Washington, D.C. I remember standing in front of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial and deciding that we would read one young soldier’s name aloud as we traced our fingers over the letters. We looked up a 19-year-old soldier on a sheaf of laminated paper that was hanging on the wall and read the name of his hometown. We said a prayer for him and his family because, as I remember explaining to the girls, “one day Daddy’s name will be on a plaque somewhere, and we want people to read his name out loud.”
The name Jeffrey R. Smith can be found by museumgoers in Lower Manhattan, and is also on two plaques at the University of Rochester, where Jeff earned both his undergraduate and master’s degrees. I went with my daughters to see these tributes when the girls were 18 and 16. We walked in Jeff’s footsteps. We read all of the names out loud.
Unlike the men and women whose names appear on the Vietnam memorial, Jeff and the thousands of other innocent victims that Tuesday morning were not casualties of war. This is an important distinction, a line that I, like most September 11 widows and widowers, believe should not be blurred. items.title: Remembrance of September 11th
items.summary: It became immediately evident that this was terrorism on an unexampled scale. The twentieth century had ended, and the twenty-first had begun.
items.body_text:
The millennial celebration that wrapped around the world as 1999 turned into 2000 will remain, for anyone who witnessed it, a spectacle of amazing amplitude, weighted with a tiny note of anticipatory dread. It was, mostly, a good night. The widely predicted Y2K disaster failed to take place: the creaky antediluvian computer systems, as they seem in retrospect, did not all crash at once. Even recalling the fear now recalls a quainter time, when your chief cyber worry was that your software would stop working, rather than become so much smarter than you that it would take, first, your job, and then your life.
Indeed, that night was a kind of celebration of the (by the hard standard of history) broadly benevolent American empire that just then seemed to engirdle the world. Not even the British Empire at the turn of the twentieth century had seemed so omnipresent, so rich in financial, cultural, and military power. Yet anyone with even a minimal historical sense could hear a whisper of potential disaster. History never lets us off that easy. If history has no laws, it has regular leanings, and the hardiest is that power precedes a fall. Every 1900 has its 1914. Asked to gamble on a competition between hubris and nemesis, bet on nemesis.
And nemesis arrived, with a vengeance and a shock that still unsettles the heart to remember. The morning of Tuesday, September 11, 2001, as those who were in New York will recall, dawned beautifully. August is a muggy month in the city, and October often bites hard, but September has a golden light, a softened weather, unlike that of any other month. That perhaps explains why the first stirrings of disquiet that morning came in a form that wanted to be categorized as bad but accidental: a plane, it seemed, had struck the North Tower of the World Trade Center. It chimed with a still vaguely remembered incident from the nineteen-forties, when a bomber, lost in fog, struck the Empire State Building. But then, as we watched on television—or, perhaps, from a downtown street corner—a second plane struck the South Tower, slicing into it at an angle. With a sudden flowering of flames, it became immediately evident that this was terrorism on an unexampled scale. The twentieth century had ended, and the twenty-first had begun.
The horror of the events seemed to mock the beauty of the day. We learned, in the following days and weeks, that the two planes had been hijacked by ten men belonging to Al Qaeda, the jihadist group founded by Osama bin Laden, a son of an immensely wealthy Saudi family. The plot had been devised by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed; an Egyptian engineer, Mohamed Atta, served as its tactical commander in the United States. Nine other terrorists hijacked two other planes that day, one of which hit the Pentagon, while the other crashed in a Pennsylvania field after the passengers and crew fought back. Four of the nineteen men had trained as pilots in the United States, each preparing to fly one of the hijacked planes. Atta appears to have chosen a date after the first week of September in part because he wanted Congress, a possible target, back in session, and in part simply because, by then, they were ready.
The dislocation and disorientation of those first days in the city, and of the weeks, months, and even years that followed, are hard now to redescribe adequately, even for those who lived through them. Grief rose like wildflowers. No one who walked Manhattan’s streets then will forget the most heartbreaking spontaneous memorial of the time: thousands of small homemade posters plastered on walls, all sharing the same unplanned format and elegiac mode—a picture of someone lost, with the word “Missing,” and often a gentle appended annotation, noting a tattoo, or a religious medal, or simply “Had no beard that day.” Everyone—including, surely, the people who had so delicately made the handbills—came to understand that nearly all those pictured were among the almost three thousand who were gone. items.title: Tom Sachs Channels Chanel
items.summary: At his downtown studio, the perennially provocative artist makes a lo-fi version of the brand’s flagship Parisian store.
items.body_text:
In the winter of 1994, Barneys, the former high-end Manhattan department store known for its daring storefront displays, unveiled its Christmas windows: three hundred and nine original works by both well-established and emerging artists which the store planned to auction off to support local schools. What began as a gesture of holiday charity, however, soon devolved into chaos, after a three-by-two-by-two-foot sculpture, “Hello Kitty Nativity Scene,” drew the ire of Catholic groups. Fashioned out of colored duct tape by a then little-known twenty-eight-year-old sculptor named Tom Sachs, it was a punky act of pop-culture bricolage that starred Madonna as the Virgin Mary, three Bart Simpsons as the wise men, and the titular white cat as the baby Jesus. After weeks of public protest, Barneys removed the work and apologized in a full-page ad in the Times. In the kind of career-making scandal that many young artists dream of, Sachs, who was born in Manhattan, grew up in Connecticut, and studied art at Bennington College, became the city’s newest enfant terrible.
On a recent sweltering morning, Sachs, now sixty, stood outside his sprawling SoHo studio, on Centre Street—where he has been making art for the past forty years—thinking, yet again, about a window display. For his latest work, “31 Rue Cambon,” an immersive installation that opens to the public on September 11th, during New York Fashion Week, Sachs converted part of his studio into an uncanny simulacrum of the luxury fashion house Chanel’s flagship boutique, in Paris. Viewers will enter directly from the street, where Sachs and his team of around twenty people were in the process of re-creating the iconic Chanel storefront, with cream-colored awnings made of cardboard and wrought-iron gates emblazoned with the brand’s interlocking “C”s. Inside, viewers will find a mirrored entrance hall and a showroom stocked with handbags, shoes, sparkly baubles, and Chanel’s signature two-piece suits—all painstakingly handcrafted out of everyday materials such as cardboard, paper, plywood, and broken glass. Sachs, who has the garrulous, jittery mien of a hyperactive teen-ager, explained that he intended to conceal the exterior till the last possible minute. “We’re keeping butcher paper up on the windows until we open,” he said. “I think shock and awe is best.”
This is not the first time Sachs has repurposed Chanel’s enduring iconography in order to shock: in 1998, he made a giant, fully functional guillotine out of stolen police barriers and covered it in Chanel logos—in part, he has said, to make a statement about “cultural fascism.” (The piece now resides in the permanent collection of Paris’s Centre Pompidou.) Over the years, Sachs, whose work is also found in the collections of the Metropolitan Museum, the Museum of Modern Art, and the Guggenheim, has positioned himself as a cultural provocateur who re-creates loaded objects and spaces—he’s made a toilet plunger out of Hermès wrapping, a McDonald’s meal from Tiffany packaging, and a model of a Nazi death camp stamped with Prada insignia—in what he has called a dual exercise in “brand critique and brand affection.” But “31 Rue Cambon” may be his most comprehensive engagement with consumerism yet, and it comes at a moment when Chanel frenzy is at a newfound high, thanks to the brand’s creative director, Matthieu Blazy. (The French label reported a revenue increase of about sixteen per cent in the first half of 2026.) “This store, for me, is real, even though you cannot buy anything in it,” he said. “Maybe, in a way, that inaccessibility makes it feel more real. For me, the lust for consuming things is replaced by making them.” As a maximalist Gesamtkunstwerk, it echoes another of Sachs’s major works, “Space Program,” which débuted at the Gagosian gallery, in 2007. items.title: The Culture Wars Have Come for Lingerie
items.summary: The culture wars have come for lingerie as the right, once the advocates of promise rings and purity culture, embarks on a crusade to “Make America Hot Again.”
items.body_text:
Martin Luther King, Jr., once observed that one of the “most segregated hours” in American life is Sunday at eleven in the morning, referring to church service. Today, the same might be said about the month of April as it unfolds in Indio, California, where throngs of people descend each year to worship at the altars of live music and brand activations. Two weekends are set aside for Coachella, the music festival known for its eclectic mix of headliners, from Björk to Bad Bunny; for its Summer of Love-inspired dress code (e.g., crocheted booty shorts); and for being the preferred setting for celebrity couples to make it desert official on Instagram. (This year, Katy Perry and her boyfriend, the former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, sporting a backward baseball cap, posted from the arid environs.)
But, on the weekend after Coachella, the very same grounds are occupied by Stagecoach, a country-music festival that’s often thought of as the conservative Coachella—or “Trumpchella,” as one Reddit user put it. An event where influencers in cowboy boots and Marlboro Man jackets can take selfies with the Budweiser Clydesdales, it has a reputation as a safe space for uncritical displays of red-blooded American patriotism. Since 2020, though, the festival has been trying to promote a different image by banning displays of the Confederate flag, which some venders used to sell in bikini form. This year, near the main stage, where the rising star Ella Langley was singing her hit “Choosin’ Texas,” I saw a man wearing—in a show of inclusivity, perhaps—a shirt that read “Show me your boobs if you hate racism.”
Funnily enough, I was actually at the festival to investigate the political implications of cleavage. The month before, it had been announced that SYRN, the newly launched underwear line from the actress Sydney Sweeney, would be the “official lingerie partner” of Stagecoach. (The brand would have a pop-up karaoke bar on site—the SYRN Saloon—with daily panties giveaways.) The setting was certainly an interesting choice on the part of the “Euphoria” star, who spent the better part of last year running from the controversy over her ad for American Eagle Outfitters—also a sponsor of this year’s Stagecoach—in which, following a brief explainer on genetic determinism, a voice-over boasted of the blond, blue-eyed actress’s “great jeans.” The inspiration had seemingly been “Genes,” a near-identical ad that Brooke Shields did for Calvin Klein in the nineteen-eighties, but, in 2025, jokes about Sweeney’s supposed physical supremacy appeared to be giving free press to a right-wing talking point. By then, conservatives had concocted a theory that the fifties-pinup physique of Sweeney, a registered Republican, was an affront to progressive sensibilities; a year earlier, the National Post, a right-leaning news site, had raised the question “Are Sydney Sweeney’s breasts double-D harbingers of the death of woke?” While we were pretending not to be looking, breasts had somehow become Republican-coded.
Sweeney remained mostly silent throughout the fracas; “I’m in the arts. I’m not here to speak on politics,” she told Cosmopolitan. But was launching a lingerie brand itself a statement? When Lauren Sanchez showed up alongside her fiancé, Jeff Bezos, to Trump’s second swearing in with a white lace bra peeking out from under her Alexander McQueen pants suit, she inaugurated a surprising new front in America’s culture wars: lingerie. Through the tech venture-capital fund Coatue, Sanchez and Bezos have both provided financial backing for SYRN, as has Michael Dell, the billionaire founder of Dell Technologies and a prolific G.O.P. donor. And Trump himself, according to financial-disclosure documents filed with the U.S. Office of Government Ethics, purchased as much as a million dollars’ worth of Victoria’s Secret corporate bonds in December of 2025.
