items.title: UK plan to sanction Israel’s illegal West Bank settlements is a historic shift in tone and policy
items.summary: The government’s move is a direct cricitism of the Netanyahu government.
items.body_text:
The UK, which in 1917 issued the Balfour Declaration supporting the establishment of a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine, is now initiating a historic and consequential shift in its foreign policy.
In response to the massive expansion of illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and credible reports of increased violence by settler groups towards Palestinian residents, the government has announced it will institute a trade ban targeting goods produced in Israeli settlements within the occupied West Bank.
The UK will also impose a new ban for arms licences and other exports that “materially contribute to the occupation”.
UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, told the House of Commons on September 8 that Jewish “settler terrorists” were guilty of ethnic cleansing in the Occupied Palestinian Territory. This is a dramatic change in tone from the UK government which – while recognising the state of Palestine and voiced support for a two-state solution – has previously moderated its criticism of Israel’s policies towards the Palestinian people.
Writing in The Guardian newspaper, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, said: “For too long, we have been hesitant to act, fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel. Today we are announcing carefully judged, targeted steps that are not aimed at the Israeli people, but at the unacceptable policies of the current Israeli government.”
A key factor behind this decision was the July 2024 advisory opinion issued by the International Court of Justice (ICJ). The court ruled that Israel’s ongoing presence in the West Bank has no legal basis and confirmed that states have a duty not to support or facilitate the continuation of that situation.
The UK is one of 12 countries, including France, Ireland and Canada, to sanction Israeli settlements. Ireland and Spain have already introduced some measures, while France has been lobbying unsuccessfully for the EU to act.
The economy of the West Bank relies heavily on agriculture and resource extraction. According to UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), 16.4% of West Bank households depend on agriculture for their livelihoods.
Primary goods facing the import ban include fresh produce cultivated in the fertile Jordan Valley, which includes Medjool dates, along with grapes, citrus fruits and various greenhouse vegetables. The ban also targets processed foods, wines produced from settlement vineyards and cosmetics manufactured using minerals extracted from the Dead Sea shores.
Israel is the UK’s 43rd-largest trading partner, according to UK government figures for March 2025-2026, with trade amounting to about £6 billion (£3.5 billion exports and £2.5 billion imports). Settlement-related goods make up a relatively small share of that total. But the UK will also restrict certain services that support construction, infrastructure, financing or real estate.
The move appears to be a direct response to Israel’s advancement of the controversial E1 settlement plan. This project, announced in August 2025 by Israel’s far-right finance minister Bezalel Smotrich, would effectively cut the West Bank in half.
Announcing the scheme, Smotrich said it “buries the idea of a Palestinian state, and continues the many steps we are taking on the ground as part of the de facto sovereignty plan”. This was widely interpreted as an intention to annex the territory, something he foreshadowed in 2017 in his “Decisive Plan”.
How a trade ban might work
Passing a law in Westminster is completely different from implementing it at the border. The whole Israeli economy is integrated. So the central dilemma facing UK customs is differentiating between Green Line products (goods produced within Israel’s pre-1967 borders) which are eligible for trade agreement incentives, and goods produced in the occupied West Bank.
In order to solve this implementation puzzle, the UK government does not have to start from scratch. It has a recent precedent to draw upon.

items.title: How ‘egalitarian’ Sweden became more comfortable with wealth
items.summary: After the end of its wealth tax came a newfound ‘wealth porn’.
items.body_text:
Sweden is imagined as the land of equality, modesty and Jantelagen – the unwritten rule that no one should think they are better than anyone else. But there has also been a fascination within Sweden with its billionaires, especially those who abide by these dominant cultural norms.
In the case of Ingvar Kamprad, the founder of furniture giant IKEA, Swedes appreciated that he drove an old car (a Volvo, of course), engaged with employees working on the floor in his stores, and every year personally handed out Christmas gifts. His (some would say strategic) display of ordinariness made people overlook the fact that Kamprad was one of the world’s richest people and had moved to Switzerland to avoid Sweden’s high taxes.
But things have changed. The Wall Street Journal has written about Sweden’s surprising “capitalist makeover” and the Financial Times has reported on the idea the country is “overflowing with billionaires”. And in 2024 The BBC broadcast a documentary podcast called Super-rich Swedes. There are good reasons for their interest.
We think we know Sweden – a peaceful nation grounded in social democracy, natural beauty, IKEA and Abba. But in 2026, is this still the real Sweden? Ahead of the country’s general election on September 13, The Conversation UK has teamed up with its Swedish partner universities for a series of articles examining why this small nation remains so fascinating.
While for a long time Sweden was a country with some of the world’s highest taxes, this no longer applies to capital taxation. For instance, it no longer has a wealth tax, an inheritance tax or a property tax. The ideal of egalitarianism doesn’t seem to align with patterns of wealth accumulation, especially at the very top.
Forbes calculates more than 50 US-dollar billionaires in Sweden. This becomes even more extraordinary in a country of just 10.6 million people.
We used Forbes and UN data and found that in 2025 Sweden ranked fourth globally, with 4.7 dollar billionaires per million people. When excluding micro-states (fewer than one million people), Sweden is outnumbered only by Singapore (9.9), Hong Kong (9.1) and Cyprus (7.3), but before Switzerland (4.6) in fifth place. It ranks much higher than some of the world’s largest economies like the US (2.7), Germany (2.1), Canada (2.0) and the UK (0.8).
It is difficult to say for sure whether changes in regulation and wealth concentration have altered cultural norms, but there are clear indicators. Younger generations are now expressing strong materialistic values. When they rank what matters in life, earning money comes second to being with friends and far more important than being with family or getting an education.
Young Swedes and adults alike dream of building a “money machine” by investing in stocks so they can exit the labour market long before retirement. This might be surprising to some, since Sweden has long been shaped by a strong work ethic, both politically and culturally.
In research for a yet-to-be published paper, we found Swedish tabloids and business magazines show a remarkable rise in reporting about billionaires. This includes a fascination with their personal lives and framing them in positive terms such as “entrepreneurs”, “investors” and “philanthropists” (rather than “capitalists”, for example).
Awe and suspicion
This does not mean that wealth is no longer a sensitive topic in Sweden. When studying articles about billionaires in one of the country’s leading tabloids, we found an ambivalent form of “wealth porn”. In Sweden “wealth porn” tends to oscillate between celebrating it and questioning the luxurious lifestyles of billionaires.
The articles tempt readers with drone images and descriptions of lavish mansions – but they also repeatedly point out how reluctant the billionaires are to display and talk about their wealth. This frames the topic as socially sensitive and sometimes even dangerous to the billionaires’ personal safety. Readers are invited to fantasise about

items.title: Germany: why the AfD won in Saxony-Anhalt – and what happens next
items.summary: The AfD received by far the most amount of votes in Saxony-Anhalt, falling marginally short of an absolute majority.
items.body_text:
The results of Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt state election on September 6 were far worse than feared for the country’s mainstream political parties. The far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) came close to winning a majority of votes, with 43.8%. This was about 4% higher than polls had suggested.
Support for the centre-right Christian Democratic Union of Germany (CDU), on the other hand, imploded. It won 17.2% of the vote, down from 37.1% in 2021, performing substantially worse than predicted.
At nearly 78%, turnout was up substantially compared with 2021 – in a way that helped the AfD. Analysis suggests the growth in its support came mostly from former non-voters, joined by a substantial number of erstwhile CDU supporters.
The polarised nature of the election, with 41% of voters surveyed beforehand wanting an AfD-led government but 46% favouring one led by the CDU, had some surprising effects. One was that it flattered the social democratic SPD and the Greens.
Both the SPD and Greens received tactical support from CDU and Left Party voters to make sure they reached the 5% of votes required to win seats in the state parliament.
The AfD, which had said it would only seek to govern if it had a majority, now has several paths to seeing its candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, elected as Saxony-Anhalt’s minister president. Most likely is a deal with the Bündnis Sahra Wagenknecht (BSW), a party that combines left-wing economic policies with conservative ones on topics such as migration.
On election night, the BSW made clear it had “overlaps” with AfD positions in some areas and that it would be “completely undemocratic” for the AfD to be excluded entirely from government.
If this failed, some support from the CDU would be a further route. The election of minister president is a secret ballot, and several CDU MPs reelected on Sunday have a long history of suggesting there should be more openness to working with the AfD.
Support across society
The AfD did best in Saxony-Anhalt among working-class voters (59%), as well as those with a lower level of education (57%) and those who perceived their economic situation as bad (65%). But even among graduates (30%) and voters who saw themselves in a good economic situation (37%), the AfD performed respectably.
It also secured over 40% of support among all age groups apart from the over 70s (31%). So the AfD can really claim to be a Volkspartei or “people’s party”, with support from across society, across the state.
By no means was this a single-issue election. Exit polls revealed immigration was one motivating factor for AfD voters, with 91% of them agreeing with the statement that they “were very worried too many foreign people live in Germany”. But so too was concern with security and the economy.
There was also real dissatisfaction (66% of all voters) at the state government, which had been led by the CDU since 2002. But the standing of Friedrich Merz’ government in Berlin was worse, with 83% taking the view it was insufficiently concerned with the problems of ordinary people. Just 20% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt trust it to improve the country substantially in the coming years.
Accompanying these sentiments, which can be found across Germany albeit more strongly in Saxony-Anhalt and other eastern states, there is a strand of dissatisfaction particular to the east. Seventy-three percent of all voters in Saxony-Anhalt believed easterners were still second-class citizens in many situations.
This view is taken by 83% of AfD voters. The AfD has been rather successful in mobilising grievances about reunification and some nostalgia about the days of the communist East Germany.
Assuming the AfD does form a government, there will be close scrutiny of the extent to which it can implement its hard-right manifesto – and, indeed, whether it confirms the view of German intelligence that the party is demonstrably “right wing extremist” in the state.

items.body_text:
Elyanna faces backlash over prison visuals in ‘BOSA’ music video
Palestinian singer Elyanna has drawn criticism over her latest music video, with viewers questioning the decision to set the lively and playful clip in a jail while Palestinian women face widespread abuse in Israeli prisons.
Released on 4 September, BOSA opens with Elyanna behind metal bars. The video then moves through a stone prison-like compound, where she and a group of female dancers perform in courtyards and around barred windows. Throughout the song Elyanna is inviting the listener to “give [her] a kiss, kiss".
The women eventually walk out of the compound. Speaking to Complex MENA, Elyanna said: “With BOSA, I invite women to be loud about their femininity, desire, confidence, and freedom.”
But for some viewers, the prison setting was difficult to separate from the reality of Palestinians in Israeli detention.
“Wtf why is this set in a prison?” one commenter wrote under a promotional clip of the video.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Another asked whether “no one on the team” had considered that the concept might be “distasteful”.
Some also critcised the dancing and accused Elyanna of “self-orientalism”, arguing that Palestinian, Arab and South Asian motifs and dancing were purposefully transformed into “exotic” visual aesthetics that cater to the western gaze.
Can someone help explain to the “it’s just a music video crowd” that prison is not an abstract symbol for Palestinians. The prison is an actual institution of colonial violence. Palestinian prisoners have been subjected to torture, sexual abuse, humiliation and other forms of… https://t.co/N3UMmYZekA
— Nerdeen Kiswani (@NerdeenKiswani) September 7, 2026
“Honestly as a Palestinian. this isn’t it,” another viewer wrote.
The reaction has also played out on X, where users have questioned the decision to turn a jail into the backdrop for a stylised music video.
Edward Said rolling in his grave lmfao https://t.co/l3Fz4f9Q8F
— Charbel (@7elo3anepls) September 5, 2026
“This so beyond tone deaf *especially* in this climate,” posted one user. “Our women are burying their kids, getting kidnapped, jailed and sexually abused by the iof [Israeli Occupation Forces, Israeli army] every single day. and "عطيني بوسة" [give me a kiss] at the men who locked her up… the orientalist gaze… yeah this is NOT it.”
The response comes as Palestinian women and girls continue to face abuse in Israeli prisons.
Harsh prison conditions
Nearly 100 female Palestinian prisoners are currently held in Israeli detention, according to Palestinian organisations, including pregnant women and teenage girls.
Israel's far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir boasts of worsening conditions for Palestinian prisoners during a visit to female inmates, after one prisoner tells him they lack basic necessities. pic.twitter.com/OC6WytNUxv
— Middle East Eye (@MiddleEastEye) August 30, 2026
Former detainees and rights groups have described conditions including inadequate food, restrictions on hygiene and medical care, strip searches and other forms of abuse.
And the issue was particularly visible in the days before BOSA was released.
Israel’s far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir filmed himself on 30 August at Damon Prison, where dozens of female Palestinian prisoners are held. 
After a prisoner complains about the harsh conditions, including a lack of proper showers, Ben Gvir says: “I am pleased with these conditions.”
On social media, he described the issues raised by the Palestinian woman as “whining”, saying the days of “summer camp” in Israeli prisons were over, and boasted that he was responsible for reducing conditions to what he called the “bare minimum”.
i cannot get over how awful this is. what are you, as a palestinian woman, doing singing "give me a kiss", while playing the role of a woman

items.body_text:
9/11 at 25: Trump finds new targets for America's endless war on terror
On 11 September 2001, I was driving to work on the freeway in Austin, Texas when I heard the news on the radio that planes had crashed into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon.
As I went about nearly crashing my own car while trying to phone my best friend in New York City, I remember thinking that we were going to be hearing a lot about this particular date for a long time to come.
Sure enough, a quarter of a century has now passed since 9/11, and the events of that day continue to shape daily existence in the US - as trite as it sounds to say it.
Those of us who are old enough may remember the pre-9/11 panorama, when it was still possible to go through airport security with your water bottle and shampoo and Muslims could go to mosque without being pursued by FBI informants.
And while the US was never exactly all it was cracked up to be in terms of democracy and respect for basic rights, 9/11 definitively obliterated the right to privacy and other civil liberties upon which the country was supposedly founded.

Obviously, the fallout of 9/11 was quite a bit more physically and psychologically catastrophic for many people beyond US borders - like the millions of humans from Afghanistan to Iraq and beyond who were killed, mutilated, irradiated and otherwise targeted by the so-called "global war on terror".
Recall, too, the CIA's ritual torture at assorted international "black sites" and a certain infamous illegal US penal colony on occupied Cuban territory.
Terrorism, defined
It has become almost tiresome to have to repeat, time and again, that this alleged war on terror has itself constituted terrorism plain and simple - at least if we go by, say, the Cambridge Dictionary definition of the word: "violent action or threats designed to cause fear among ordinary people, in order to achieve political aims".
It has become almost tiresome to have to repeat, time and again, that this alleged war on terror has itself constituted terrorism plain and simple
Indeed, it goes without saying that the US military's habit of indiscriminate slaughter has done much to instil fear among ordinary people. Drone strikes on wedding parties are but one example of, um, "violent action".
As per the official narrative, of course, the US is always and forever a victim of terrorism rather than its preeminent perpetrator - a line that is perennially propagated by a disgraceful corporate media establishment that declines under any circumstances to speak truth to power.
To be sure, the US has gotten a run for its money on the whole terror-victimhood front from Israel, which refuses to cede its self-appointed position as number one victim of terrorism in the history of the world - and never mind its lengthy history of terrorising Palestinians.
Predictably, Israel wasted no time in jumping on the post-9/11 "war on terror" bandwagon, paving the way for eventual all-out genocide in the Gaza Strip, which now proceeds apace with US backing and in spite of an ostensible ceasefire.
Scared silly
It bears mentioning that, in addition to sowing terror across the globe, the US government has done a bang-up job in causing fear among its own citizens to further political goals.

items.title: Gambian leader vows power boost after violent blackout protests
items.summary: Gambian President Adama Barrow on Tuesday pledged to boost power supplies by next month after violent protests over blackouts that have dogged the west African country since June
items.body_text:
The Gambia
Gambian President Adama Barrow on Tuesday pledged to boost power supplies by next month after violent protests over blackouts that have dogged the west African country since June.
The rolling power outages, which are occurring during the country's hot season, have lasted up to 48 hours in some areas.
Demonstrators in Banjul, and other nearby cities protested overnight Monday to Tuesday, setting fires and blocking traffic while chanting "Barrow must go!"
In the Westfield district on the outskirts of the capital, police used tear gas as crowds headed towards the headquarters of The Gambia's energy provider, the National Water and Electricity Corporation (NAWEC).
Barrow called the outages "a national security issue" and "an emergency" Tuesday, while declaring that it was "time for action", as he visited the NAWEC power station in the city of Brikama, near the capital.
In an address on Tuesday evening, he said: "I know that the fans have stopped turning, children work in the dark, mothers throw away stale food, and the heat is unbearable by day and by night.
"The government is in the final stage of installing an additional 24-megawatt generation machine... This will be commissioned by the end of October 2026. For a system of our size, this is considerable power, enough to make a big difference in your homes," he said.
"The contract for a 50-megawatt solar power plant in Soma has also been awarded, and the contracted company is now mobilising the necessary resources to begin work soon," he said.
"We commit that the electricity supply situation in the country will improve by the end of October".
The demonstrations mark a sharp escalation from earlier power protests and come just months before December elections, in which Barrow is running for a third term.
NAWEC in mid-August said the blackouts were due to surges in demand, mainly because of high temperatures, combined with "constraints on electricity imports".
On Tuesday, Gallo Saidy, NAWEC managing director, said the problems were due in part to climate change and war in the Middle East, while appealing to Gambians for patience.
He cancelled his attendance at a road inauguration Tuesday to visit the NAWEC facility at Brikama and also Kotu, two of the areas hardest hit by both outages and protests.
Information Minister Ismaila Ceesay said in a statement that The Gambia was "treating the situation with the seriousness and utmost urgency it deserves, and we want to assure every Gambian that we are working relentlessly".

items.title: Concerns over wildlife, water supply, as wildfire rages across Mount Kenya
items.summary: A wildfire has burned about 8,700 hectares of vegetation on Mount Kenya since the fire was first reported on Sept 1, Mount Kenya Trust, an environmental conservation group, said.
items.body_text:
Kenya
A wildfire has burned about 8,700 hectares of vegetation on Mount Kenya since the fire was first reported on Sept 1, Mount Kenya Trust, an environmental conservation group, said.
Authorities are yet to announce the cause, but teams from the Mount Kenya Trust, Kenya Forest Service, Kenya Wildlife Service, Kenya Defence Forces, Lewa Wildlife Conservancy and Rhino Ark, assisted by community members and aerial support from Tropic Air, continued efforts Tuesday to contain the remaining flames.
The fire has raised concerns about possible damage to wildlife, water sources and the mountain’s fragile high-altitude habitats.
Mount Kenya National Park and the surrounding natural forest are part of a UNESCO World Heritage site encompassing forests, wetlands and alpine ecosystems.
Rivers originating on the mountain provide water for communities, farms and wildlife across parts of central and eastern Kenya.
The wider Mount Kenya ecosystem is also home to threatened wildlife, including the critically endangered mountain bongo.
Mount Kenya rises to 5,199 metres, making it Kenya’s highest mountain and Africa’s second-highest after Mount Kilimanjaro in neighboring Tanzania, which stands at 5,895 metres.
Mount Kenya is considerably lower than Mount Everest, the world’s highest mountain at 8,849 metres, but its equatorial alpine ecosystem, glaciers and biological diversity give it global environmental importance.

items.title: 'We are tired': Gambians struggle after months of power outages
items.summary: After months of electricity outages which have recently grown more severe, residents of The Gambia are becoming desperate. Thousands took to the streets on Monday in protest over the blackouts, burning tyres and chanting against the president.
items.body_text:
Adama Barrow
Gambia’s president Adama Barrow called for calm on Tuesday after protests over the country’s persistent power outages.
Residents of the capital Banjul and surrounding areas blocked streets and burned tyres overnight on Monday, and called for Barrow to resign.
The blackouts started in June and have become longer and more frequent as high temperatures drive up demand. Authorities have blamed climate change and supply chain disruptions due to the war in Iran.
"Our business is stalling because of the lack of electricity," says fishmonger Nyima Sonko.
"All our fish is getting spoiled, and this is our only source of livelihood. Our business has perished."
Jula Jagne is a market trader:
"We are tired of this problem. We sometimes go a full day without electricity. Sometimes we get power during the day, and sometimes at night. The power can be out for six or seven hours at a time. We don’t have ice to keep our chicken meat cool, which can cost as much as three hundred dalasis. We, the women of The Gambia, are tired.”
Barrow, who is running for re-election in December, called the outages "a national security issue" and "an emergency.”
He’s promised to increase supply by next month and called for people to be patient.

items.title: Samarkand to Host the Largest Chess Olympiad in History
items.summary: The 46th World Chess Olympiad is being held in Samarkand.
items.body_text:
On 15 September this year, the 46th World Chess Olympiad will start at the Silk Road international tourism centre in the city of Samarkand. In the history of the prestigious competition, held since 1927, Central Asia will host the chess world’s largest team tournament for the first time.
The Olympiad is expected to set a new record for the number of participants and teams. A total of 398 teams will take part: 208 teams in the men’s (Open) section and 190 teams in the women’s section will compete for victory. This will break the record of 380 teams set in Budapest in 2024. The Olympiad will bring together 1,974 players, including 240 grandmasters. Together with coaches and delegation members, Samarkand will welcome more than 4,000 guests during the competition. The tournament will consist of 11 rounds and will run until 27 September.
From 10 to 18 September, Samarkand will also host the 3rd Chess Paralympiad. A total of 41 teams will take part — the highest figure in the history of the Chess Paralympiad. By comparison, 26 teams competed in Belgrade in 2023 and 34 in Astana in 2024. This year’s event will bring together 196 players, including 150 men and 46 women. It will be held over seven rounds under the Swiss system. The record scale of the Chess Paralympiad is particularly significant for the development of inclusive sport and for raising the standing of chess as an intellectual sport open to all.
Holding the competition in historic Samarkand, a city inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List and one of the key crossroads of the Great Silk Road, combines a sporting contest with a platform for cultural diplomacy and international dialogue.
According to the teams’ average rating, the United States is seeded first in the men’s (Open) section. Its line-up features Fabiano Caruana, Wesley So, Levon Aronian and Hans Niemann, who is making his Olympiad debut. Reigning champion India is seeded second and Uzbekistan third. Germany will be represented by Vincent Keymer and France by Maxime Vachier-Lagrave.
Credit: Michal Walusza / FIDE
According to the teams’ average rating, India starts as the top seed in the women’s section. The Kazakhstan team includes three-time world blitz champion and Norway Chess Women 2026 winner Bibisara Assaubayeva. Ukraine’s first board will be 16-year-old European champion and woman grandmaster Anastasiya Hnatyshyn.
The line-ups of the Uzbekistan national teams reflect the emergence of a new generation of Uzbek chess. For the first time, the men’s and women’s squads will each enter three teams made up of young players. In particular, Nilufarkhon Imomkuziyeva and Khumoyun Begmurodov, both aged 16, will make their Olympiad debut. Gulrukhbegim Tokhirjonova, who played for the United States at the 2024 Olympiad in Budapest, will defend the colours of Uzbekistan this time.
FIDE World Champion Rustam Kasimdzhanov has been brought into the main men’s line-up, and Uzbekistan’s first woman grandmaster, Nafisa Muminova, has joined the women’s team as captain. In the Uzbekistan men’s team, Javokhir Sindarov (4th), Nodirbek Abdusattorov (7th), Nodirbek Yakubboev (39th) and Shamsiddin Vokhidov (61st) are among the 100 strongest players in the world rankings. The fact that Javokhir Sindarov and Nodirbek Abdusattorov are among the world’s ten strongest players clearly demonstrates the competitiveness of the Uzbek chess school. The women’s team also holds high positions in the world rankings. Afruza Khamdamova is 26th and Gulrukhbegim Tokhirjonova 80th.
The rise of Uzbek chess on the international stage is also reflected in the team rankings. Compared with 2025, the Uzbekistan men’s team has climbed 15 places in the FIDE ranking of 204 countries to take sixth place. The women’s team has climbed 17 places to take 21st.
Credit: Michal Walusza / FIDE

items.title: A Himalayan Flood Brings Economic Collapse to Nepal’s Border Region

On August 26, a massive glacier collapse near Langtang Lirung triggered a chain of flash floods and mudslides along the Trishuli and Bhotekoshi river systems. The event has not only caused damage to what was developed there but also to what was being built in that area, including infrastructure, hydropower projects, and private businesses, primarily small and medium enterprises (SMEs). Losses are estimated at more than $5 billion, which is almost one-third of Nepal’s annual budget.
Settlements, roads, bridges, hydropower plants, trade facilities, farmland, and human lives across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, and downstream districts were swept away or buried beneath mud and boulders. Early estimates of the damage could be made using the household-level data from these locations and the data from the 2018 economic census. But that could be misleading.
The contribution to the GDP from those areas is going to be minimal when looking at the immediate numbers. However, the share could be far more significant if we factor in indirect benefits from the river systems and economic hubs in that corridor. Especially important is the opportunity cost, as Nepal was attempting to build up a vibrant trade link with China in exactly this region.
The human toll alone is immense. More than 1,300 people are confirmed dead in Nepal, while over 4,000 people are missing. For those who survived, the loss is not limited to houses and belongings. Families have lost relatives, farmland, livestock, food stocks, shops, vehicles, savings, identity documents, and the means to earn an income. Entire local economies in the peripheral areas of the flood-hit districts have been disrupted, which has a direct impact on key sectors such as tourism and agri-businesses.
The Trishuli-Bhotekoshi corridor is more than a river valley. It connects mountain communities to Kathmandu, national markets, tourism destinations, hydropower investments, and cross-border trade with China. Its destruction is therefore a local tragedy with national economic consequences.
The complete destruction of the Gyirong Port border complex is especially serious. The port was Nepal’s primary trade and tourism gateway with China. At the moment, Nepal has no fully functional border crossing point with China, which has a high cost for an economy that relies on imports of raw materials and other goods from China.
When the flood hit, more than 300 vehicles waiting at the border were swept away. About 42 kilometers of road and 41 bridges were damaged, with road and bridge repairs alone estimated to cost 15 billion rupees ($99.4 million).
The estimated cost to repair is one thing; it’s much more difficult to calculate the cost that accumulates when the movement of local people is limited due to the absence of infrastructure, especially in a border region. Sections of the Prithvi Highway are still blocked, delaying relief operations and disrupting the transport of goods, fuel, food, and passengers. The loss of the Gyirong-Rasuwagadhi trade route will affect importers, exporters, freight companies, customs agents, drivers, hotels, warehouses, retailers, and consumers throughout Nepal. Most of the freight companies have been damaged, with their containers being completely wiped out.
China has closed the Tatopani customs point following the complete destruction of the Rasuwagadhi border point linking Rasuwa and Gyirong. With no functional border crossing between Nepal and China at the moment, supply chains have been disrupted. This has a direct impact on customs revenue and will raise prices for consumers due to lack of supply.
People already suffering from the price hikes due to the Iran-U.S. war, among other global events, will have to face more severe economic hardships. Local economic centers, including Syabrubesi, Betrawati, Trishuli, and Rasuwagadhi had been developing through tourism, trade, transport, agriculture, construction, and hydropower investment. items.title: Asia’s Migrant Workers Need Protection from Gulf Wars
items.summary: The migrants who build, clean, drive, guard, and operate the Gulf’s economies have become the forgotten civilian casualties in its wars.
items.body_text:
Asian migrant workers are indispensable to the Gulf’s economy. Yet, they remain highly vulnerable and unprotected when regional conflict reaches their homes and workplaces. On February 28, after the Iranian attack on the United Arab Emirates, the first deaths included a Bangladeshi, a Pakistani, and a Nepali worker.
Human Rights Watch reported at least 11 civilian deaths and 268 injuries across the Gulf by March 16, with migrant workers comprising most of the victims. At least 10 of those killed were foreign nationals. Some died in direct strikes; others were killed by falling debris from air defense interceptions.
The known death toll is likely an undercount. There is no public, regionwide casualty registry that consistently records victims’ nationality, occupation, and immigration status. Nor is there a standing regional mechanism that guarantees compensation, evacuation, or income protection for migrants caught in hostilities. The people who build, clean, drive, guard, and operate the Gulf’s economies have become the forgotten civilian casualties in its wars.
Migrants make up an overwhelming share of the population in states such as the UAE and Qatar, and South Asians constitute a large part of that workforce. They work at ports, airports, construction sites, logistics hubs, energy facilities, hotels, and industrial zones – precisely the places most likely to be disrupted or targeted in a regional confrontation. During the Iran war, reporting documented workers’ fears about workplace safety, restricted access to shelter, job losses, and employers’ failure to communicate emergency plans.
For many workers, leaving the region is difficult financially and logistically. Migration to the Gulf is often financed through loans used to pay recruitment fees and travel costs. A worker who returns home abruptly may lose both income and the means to pay back that debt. The decision to remain during a conflict is therefore not always a choice between safety and work; it can be a choice between physical danger and financial collapse for an entire household.
Even for those who wish to leave, it can be difficult to do in practice. Sponsorship-based labor systems, despite reforms in several states, can still leave workers dependent on employers for documents, housing, transport, and information at the very moment mobility matters most. Current labor and compensation systems in the Gulf are designed mainly for routine occupational injuries, not missile attacks, prolonged airspace closures, or emergency evacuation.
Some labor-sending countries attempt to provide some safeguards for their citizens. Bangladesh, for example, repatriates the bodies of deceased workers and provides support to their families. Its official migrant-insurance system can provide up to 1 million taka ($8,140) in death compensation to registered workers, alongside the Wage Earners’ Welfare Board’s grants for bereaved families. But those protections depend on registration, documentation, and successful claims processing. Undocumented workers and workers who fall outside formal recruitment channels often receive much less or nothing beyond repatriation assistance. Even where compensation is paid, a one-time benefit cannot replace the lifetime earnings of a person whose household borrowed heavily to send them abroad.
When workers are injured, stranded, or laid off during hostilities, in practice, the costs fall on the household as a family loses its main earner while retaining the migration debt that financed the journey.
This outcome is not accidental. Origin states measure the success of overseas employment through remittance flows. Recruitment intermediaries’ profit when placement costs are shifted onto workers. Destination-state employers’ benefit from a labor system that supplies workers cheaply and flexibly. items.body_text:
Iran’s threat to target American warships with an enhanced ballistic missile appears to mark a new and potentially more dangerous phase of the Middle East conflict, six months in.
Tehran says its solid-fuel Qassem Basir missile enables it to “take action against any threat, even before it is carried out.” Reports have suggested that the Qassem Basir was the missile used in tests Iran claimed to have carried out against US warships on September 5.
Washington acknowledged an Iranian attack on its nuclear-powered aircraft carrier USS George Washington and a guided-missile destroyer near the Strait of Hormuz. But it said it was unclear whether the new missile had been used and confirmed its vessels had evaded the attack.
But the more assertive rhetoric coming out of the Islamic Republic suggests it is moving beyond the largely retaliatory strategy that characterized much of the war and is increasingly prepared to raise the stakes itself.
Tehran has also announced it is preparing to sign an agreement with Oman which would establish a new corridor through the Strait of Hormuz extending out into the Persian Gulf, although this has yet to be confirmed. Taken together, these developments suggest that Iran is no longer simply responding to escalation – it is increasingly trying to drive it.
This does not mean Iran has the upper hand militarily. Far from it. But Tehran appears to have concluded that prolonging and widening the conflict can improve its bargaining position by making the war increasingly expensive for the US and the rest of the world.
It’s an extraordinary reversal for a conflict intended to force Tehran’s hand and even possibly achieve regime change. Military superiority, while inflicting enormous damage on Iran, has not produced the political outcomes aimed at by the US and Israel.
The regime survives, its missiles continue to operate, the question of its nuclear programme remains unresolved, and its regional network retains offensive capabilities – something seen clearly in the latest attacks by Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia. Meanwhile, the Strait of Hormuz has become a potent instrument of economic leverage for Tehran.
Never-ending cycle of confict
The war seems to have settled into a cycle: escalation, diplomacy, agreement, renewed coercion and then another return to diplomacy. Far from resolving anything, however, the six-month conflict looks to have taught Tehran that resisting US pressure eventually produces better terms.
The latest escalation suggests Iran is now exploiting that lesson. Tehran does not need to defeat the US navy or completely control the Strait of Hormuz. It needs only to make passage sufficiently dangerous that shipping companies hesitate, insurance premiums rise and energy markets price disruption into every barrel of oil.
Recent shipping data show commodity traffic through Hormuz falling to its lowest level since May. Tehran is now threatening wider restrictions on navigation and “economic warfare” if Washington continues trying to strangle the Iranian economy.
This changes the logic of the conflict. Trump sought to make Iranian resistance progressively more expensive. Iran is now making American coercion progressively more expensive too.
It cannot match American firepower, but possesses something Washington cannot eliminate by force militarily: its geography and ability to control one of the world’s most important energy corridors.
The conflict should therefore be measured against its political objectives. The broader ambitions associated with the Trump-Netanyahu campaign were to fundamentally weaken or change Iran’s political system, eliminate its nuclear threat, destroy its long-range missile capability and break its network of regional allies.

items.title: What Iran’s resilience tells China, Russia about US power
items.summary: When the US-Israeli war against Iran began, few in Beijing or Moscow likely expected Tehran to withstand military pressure from two of the world’s most capable powers. In the early days, US and Israeli air, intelligence and technological superiority were striking, and Iran suffered heavy blows. But what could have been a short campaign to […] The post What Iran’s resilience tells China, Russia about US power appeared first on Asia Times.
items.body_text:
When the US-Israeli war against Iran began, few in Beijing or Moscow likely expected Tehran to withstand military pressure from two of the world’s most capable powers.
In the early days, US and Israeli air, intelligence and technological superiority were striking, and Iran suffered heavy blows. But what could have been a short campaign to disable Iran’s military capabilities has turned into a longer, costlier war.
Despite severe losses, Iran has preserved its political structure and much of its military response capability — proof that inflicting extensive damage and forcing surrender are two very different things.
This resilience is more than a battlefield development. For China and Russia, the war has become a real test of the limits of American power. The two countries have different stakes in the conflict, but neither can treat a decisive Iranian defeat as a purely Middle Eastern matter.
Both appear to understand that if the United States can use military superiority to strategically weaken one of West Asia’s most important independent powers, the region’s balance of power will shift, with consequences reaching into the broader geopolitical and geoeconomic contest among Washington, Beijing and Moscow.
China’s dilemma
China may have more economic reason than any other major power to want the war to end. Disruptions to energy flows and insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz hit the Chinese economy directly, since China has been Iran’s largest oil buyer for years.
Reuters reported that China’s seaborne crude imports in August 2026 stood at roughly 7.14 million barrels per day, nearly 40% below the prewar average. The disruption has also cut Chinese refineries off from a key source of crude.
But this is where Beijing’s central contradiction begins. The war’s continuation hurts China, yet it cannot easily welcome Iran’s strategic defeat either. Iran is not merely an oil exporter to Beijing; Tehran is part of the network of relationships China has built across West Asia to expand its economic and political influence without the military alliances the US relies on.
A severe weakening of Iran would mean more than a shift between Tehran and Washington — it would mean greater US influence in the region and less strategic space for China. China’s conduct bears this out. Its support for Iran has never been confined to political statements during years of maximum US pressure.
For one, Beijing has remained a major buyer of Iranian oil, and independent Chinese refineries have remained among the most important markets for that oil even under threat of secondary US sanctions, which is why Washington has made Chinese purchases a centerpiece of its economic pressure campaign.
That relationship has only grown more consequential during the war. As Washington works to cut off Iran’s oil exports and related financial channels, China remains one of the few major economies able to absorb part of the pressure on Tehran.
For Beijing, buying Iranian oil is not simply a commercial transaction — it’s part of a larger contest over how far US sanctions can dictate the behavior of major economies outside Washington’s orbit. That is also why US pressure on Chinese buyers has become a persistent point of friction between the two powers.
China’s support isn’t limited to economics, either. US reports in recent years have pointed to Iranian access to certain dual-use technologies, including some used in its drone and missile programs, through companies and commercial networks linked to China.
A distinction should be drawn between official Chinese government policy and the activities of China-based commercial networks. Still, those networks illustrate how the economic relationship helps preserve part of Iran’s technological and industrial base under sanctions.

items.title: When weddings become battlefields, the laws of war begin to fail
items.summary: On September 1, a US airstrike hit a family compound in Kuhestak, southern Iran, as women and children gathered for a wedding celebration. At least five people were killed and dozens more injured. Associated Press reporters who visited the town documented extensive damage and civilian suffering. items.body_text:
On September 1, a US airstrike hit a family compound in Kuhestak, southern Iran, as women and children gathered for a wedding celebration. At least five people were killed and dozens more injured.
Associated Press reporters who visited the town documented extensive damage and civilian suffering. Reuters later reported that imagery, debris, and weapons assessments were consistent with a direct hit by a US munition, while US officials said the incident was under review. The immediate facts matter. But the larger question is already unavoidable: What happens to the laws of war when civilian spaces repeatedly become part of the battlefield?
The significance of Kuhestak extends beyond the number of casualties or the identity of the weapon. The deeper danger is what incidents like this can do to the norms meant to limit warfare. If homes, schools, hospitals, wedding gatherings, or refugee sites are repeatedly treated as tolerable consequences of military necessity, the distinction between battlefield and civilian life begins to lose practical meaning.
International humanitarian law was designed precisely to prevent that erosion. Its rules do not make war safe, and they do not prohibit every attack that may harm civilians. They do, however, require parties to distinguish between civilians and military objectives, prohibit attacks expected to cause excessive incidental civilian harm in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated, and require feasible precautions to minimize civilian loss.
The principles of distinction, proportionality, and precaution are not political preferences. They are the legal architecture intended to preserve a minimum boundary between military necessity and human life.
That distinction matters when assessing the US position as well. Washington says it does not target civilians and that its operations in southern Iran were aimed at military infrastructure, including air-defense, communications, and maritime assets. The Associated Press reported those stated objectives alongside the civilian toll in Kuhestak. Under the laws of war, the existence of a legitimate military objective can matter greatly.
Civilian casualties, by themselves, do not automatically prove an unlawful attack. But that is precisely why transparent investigation is essential: Was the target properly identified? Were the expected civilian risks assessed? Were feasible precautions taken? And was the anticipated military advantage sufficient to justify those risks?
Kuhestak is especially troubling because it follows another catastrophic episode in the same province. On February 28, a strike hit a school in Minab.
In March, Amnesty International said its investigation found US forces responsible for the attack, which killed 156 people, including 120 children, and concluded that the United States had failed to take all feasible precautions to avoid civilian harm. Amnesty called for a transparent and thorough investigation and accountability for those responsible. Minab therefore cannot simply be treated as an unresolved rumor in the background of the current war.
Seen together, Minab and Kuhestak raise a deeper concern. One catastrophic civilian strike may be explained as a failure of intelligence, targeting, weapon performance, or judgment. A pattern of incidents, however, raises a different question: whether civilian protection is being pushed too far to the margins of operational decision-making. The danger is not only the immediate loss of life. It is the gradual normalization of exceptions.
International law rarely collapses in a single dramatic moment. More often, norms weaken when exceptional conduct is repeated, defended, or left without meaningful scrutiny. Each time a serious civilian-harm incident is absorbed into the routine language of war without transparent findings or accountability, the practical force of the rule diminishes. items.title: Russia trains Ugandan specialists amid Ebola threat
items.summary: Russia’s public-health watchdog says it is training Ugandan health specialists in infection control amid a deadly Ebola outbreak Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
Russia trains Ugandan specialists amid Ebola threat
Russia has begun training Ugandan health specialists in infection-control measures, Russia’s public health watchdog announced on Tuesday. The program comes as the East African nation remains on alert for Ebola, which continues to spread in neighboring DR Congo and has killed more than 3,200 people.
Ten specialists from Uganda’s Health Ministry and leading research institutions are taking part in the two-week course at the Erisman Institute of Disinfectology, according to Rospotrebnadzor.
The training covers Russia’s regulatory framework, methods, and equipment for disinfection, insect, and rodent control, as well as zoological and entomological surveillance. Participants will also conduct practical exercises and fieldwork. The initiative is part of its broader program to help African countries prevent infectious diseases and strengthen epidemiological preparedness.
Uganda was declared free of Ebola on August 27 after recording no new infections for 42 days. The outbreak, which began in May, caused 20 confirmed cases and two deaths in the country. Fifteen infections were imported from DR Congo, while five occurred among contacts and health workers linked to those cases, the authorities said.
Surveillance has continued due to the risk of further cross-border transmission. DR Congo has recorded 6,686 confirmed cases and 3,226 deaths, according to official figures reported on September 7.
The epidemic has reached 61 health zones across six provinces. The World Health Organization (WHO) has assessed the risk within DR Congo as ‘very high’, citing sustained transmission, armed conflict, displacement, and weaknesses in the healthcare system. It has identified Uganda, the Central African Republic, and South Sudan as particularly vulnerable to cross-border cases.
No vaccine or specific treatment has been approved for the Bundibugyo strain driving the outbreak, which the WHO has classified as a public health emergency of international concern.
Russia sent epidemiologists to Uganda in May to assist with outbreak investigations. Rospotrebnadzor said in July that Russia also delivered thousands of Ebola diagnostic test kits to DR Congo, Uganda, and the Republic of the Congo.
Moscow donated a mobile anti-epidemic laboratory to Uganda in 2024 and has supplied similar facilities to several other African countries, including Burundi, Ethiopia, Namibia, and the Republic of the Congo. More than 80 Ugandan specialists have received training in pathogen monitoring, disinfectology, laboratory diagnostics, and biosafety from Rospotrebnadzor’s scientific institutions, the agency said in May.

items.title: Western intervention worsened Nigeria and Sahel security crisis – senator
items.summary: A Nigerian senator said Western intervention in Libya created a security vacuum that allowed armed groups to spread across the Sahel Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
Western intervention worsened Nigeria and Sahel security crisis – senator
Western intervention in Libya worsened the security crises facing Nigeria and the Sahel by creating a vacuum that allowed armed groups to spread across the region, Nigerian Senator Yahaya Abubakar Abdullahi told RT.
Abdullahi, who chairs the Senate Committee on National Intelligence and National Security, said that although the West African nation faced security challenges before the 2011 NATO-backed overthrow of Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, it was able to contain them.
He argued that Western governments removed Gaddafi “without any proper arrangement to maintain the security and unity of the Libyan state,” opening a major security gap across the Sahel.
“Several groups, armed groups, emerged. Some of them with religious agendas, some of them with ethnic agendas, some of them with separatist positions.”
Nigeria has experienced an upsurge in militant attacks, village raids, and mass abductions in recent months, driven by Boko Haram, the Islamic State West Africa Province, and armed gangs known locally as bandits. Officials have also linked the Lakurawa group operating near the borders with Niger and Benin to Islamic State networks in the Sahel. The Nigerian military said its forces killed more than 324 “terrorists and other criminals,” arrested 373 suspects, and rescued 610 abductees in August alone.
Some attacks have specifically targeted Christian communities, including coordinated raids on three churches in Kaduna State in January in which more than 150 worshipers were abducted.
The violence drew criticism from US President Donald Trump, who designated Nigeria a “country of particular concern” last October over alleged violations of religious freedom, and claimed that Christianity faces an “existential threat” in the country. Trump threatened to halt US aid if Abuja fails to stop what he described as the killing of Christians.
Abuja rejected the characterization, saying it does not reflect the country’s reality or government efforts to protect religious freedom.
On Monday, Senator Abdullahi similarly dismissed claims of a Christian genocide, arguing that Muslims and Christians are both victims and that the violence is primarily rooted in economic problems.
“The issue of Christian genocide is more or less a whitewash, and it’s promoted by people who want action in the United States, not to protect Christians, but to protect those Christians in the diaspora who want asylum in the United States,” he said.
The senator insisted that Abuja is willing to work with the US but will not accept “dictatorship or mentorship.” 
“Nigeria is free to choose who its friends are,” he said, adding that it can work with any country that understands its security needs.
He also praised Russia’s longstanding support for Africa’s most populous nation. Soviet assistance during the 1967-1970 civil war helped preserve Nigeria’s unity after some international partners abandoned the government or backed separatist forces, he said.
The senator was visiting Moscow as part of a delegation seeking cooperation with Russian Railways on rehabilitating infrastructure in northwestern Nigeria. He said the proposed long-term partnership could help transform the region into a transport hub serving Nigeria and the wider West African region.

items.title: Tanzanian president loses husband
items.summary: Tanzania has announced that President Samia Suluhu Hassan’s husband, Hafidh Ameir Hassan, died while receiving treatment in Zanzibar Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
Tanzanian president loses husband
Hafidh Ameir Hassan, the husband of Tanzanian President Samia Suluhu Hassan, has died while undergoing treatment for a heart condition in the country’s semi-autonomous Zanzibar archipelago, the government has announced.
Vice President Deogratius Ndejembi said Ameir died at around 8 AM local time on Monday at Emilio Mzena Memorial Hospital. He extended condolences to the president, the bereaved family and the Tanzanian people.
The 80-year-old was buried later that day in Kizimkazi, South Unguja, in accordance with Islamic tradition. The funeral was attended by senior government and religious officials, including Ndejembi, Prime Minister Mwigulu Nchemba and Zanzibar President Hussein Ali Mwinyi.
On Tuesday, President Hassan received a delegation that delivered a message of condolence from Kenyan President William Ruto. Ruto said the Tanzanian leader had lost “a lifelong companion,” her children a beloved father, and the country “a distinguished son.” Rwanda’s Paul Kagame, Zambia’s Hakainde Hichilema, Burundi’s Evariste Ndayishimiye, Somalia’s Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed also expressed solidarity with the president, her family and Tanzanians.
African Union Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf described Ameir’s death as a “difficult period” for President Samia and her family and wished them “strength, courage and solace.”
“For almost five decades he stood quietly beside her, through every season of her service to Tanzania. A companionship of that depth becomes part of who a person is. To lose it is to lose a portion of oneself, and I feel for her deeply,” Nigerian President Bola Tinubu also wrote on X.
Born in Zanzibar in 1946, Ameir married Samia in 1978 and largely remained outside the political spotlight. They had four children, including Wanu Hafidh Ameir, a member of Zanzibar’s House of Representatives. Ameir worked as a teacher before becoming an agricultural specialist. He studied agricultural machinery engineering in Britain and worked for Zanzibar’s Agriculture Ministry until retiring in 2005. He later taught at Kizimbani Agricultural College.
He became Tanzania’s first gentleman when Samia assumed office in 2021 following the death of then-President John Magufuli. Samia became the country’s first female president and secured a second term in a disputed election last year.

items.title: Pope at Audience: Human dignity must always be defended as God’s gift
items.summary: At his Wednesday General Audience, Pope Leo XIV continues his reflection on Vatican II’s ‘Gaudium et Spes,’ and says the dignity of every human person is a permanent gift of God’s love that we must defend. Read all
items.body_text:
Pope at Audience: Human dignity must always be defended as Godâs gift
Vatican News
Pope Leo XIV dedicated his Wednesday General Audience to the dignity of the human person, urging Christians to defend it in every circumstance with âthe light and strength of the Gospel.â
Continuing his reflections on the Second Vatican Councilâs Pastoral Constitution Gaudium et Spes, the Pope said recognition of fundamental human rights represents one of the most important achievements in human history.
However, he warned, humanityâs journey towards the full recognition of human dignity remains incomplete, since old and new contradictions continue to obstruct it.
READ THE FULL TEXT OF POPE LEO'S CATECHESIS HERE
Pope Leo said the Church contributes to this journey by recalling that dignity arises from the very being of each person.
Quoting his encyclical Magnifica Humanitas, he stressed that every human being is âplanned and willed by Godâ for communion with Him, with others and with creation.
âHuman dignity does not depend on a personâs abilities, wealth or position in life, nor on the right or wrong choices made,â he said. âInstead, it is a gift that precedes and transcends each person, endowed by God as an expression of His unfailing love.â
The Pope explained that this infinite dignity is rooted in humanityâs creation in the image of God.
Human beings are capable of knowing and loving our Creator, while the rest of creation is entrusted to our responsible care.
Christ, he added, reveals the ultimate foundation of this dignity by revealing humanity to itself and making known to us our highest calling.
Pope Leo went on to say that human dignity can never be understood in isolation.
âTo be a person means to perceive oneself as a gift to be shared, growing and maturing through acceptance, reciprocity and service,â he said.
Dignity therefore entails both personal responsibility and solidarity with others. It calls for mutual care and for resistance to the many forms of manipulation that distort the understanding of the human person.
The Pope acknowledged that humanity remains wounded by sin and divided within itself, caught in a struggle between good and evil.
Yet, he said, Christians can face this fragility with hope because Christ came to free, strengthen and renew humanity from within.
Citing Gaudium et Spes, Pope Leo also rejected any separation between body and soul, recalling that the human person âthough made of body and soul, is one.â
Treating the body as an object that can be used or disposed of arbitrarily, he said, constitutes a denial of human dignity.
The body must instead be regarded as good and worthy of honour, since it was created by God and destined for resurrection.
The Pope then highlighted intelligence, conscience, and freedom as three essential expressions of human dignity. Intelligence seeks truth, conscience gives unity and meaning to life, and freedom allows people to take responsibility for our decisions.
Pope Leo concluded by recalling that the Holy Spirit frees us from fear and confirms our dignity as children of God.
âCreated in Godâs image, through Christ and for His sake, we have received a unique and indelible dignity,â he said. âLet us commit ourselves to promoting and defending it always.â

items.title: Pope: Emphasis on individual freedom makes us less free to be ourselves
items.summary: Pope Leo XIV tells Bishops associated with the Focolare Movement that our modern emphasis on individual freedom can in reality make us less free to be our genuine selves or follow our highest ideals. Read all
items.body_text:
Pope: Emphasis on individual freedom makes us less free to be ourselves
By Devin Watkins
Pope Leo XIV met on Wednesday with Bishops associated with the Focolare Movement, formally known as the Work of Mary, founded in Italy in 1943 by Chiara Lubich.
In his address, the Pope said the Bishopsâ encounter expresses their collegial affection as friends of the Focolare Movement, noting that they hail from various countries and social situations.
Pope Leo praised their focus on âGiving Witness to Unity,â saying the theme of unity is dear to his heart.
âIn an age sadly marked by increasing polarization,â he said, âour Lord enabled [Chiara Lubich] to give witness to both the sense and service of unity, thus becoming a sign for her own and future generations.â
The Church continues to bear this task, added the Pope, saying he recalls the âprejudice, racism, religious intolerance, and even violenceâ that the Bishops face in their countries.
In the West, he noted, the formerly-stable networks of family, friendship, and community are succumbing to deep fragmentation.
As societies become more marked by individualism, freedom is increasingly presented as âabsolute autonomy,â so that people may pursue happiness âwithout any moral, natural, or even human limits.â
âAnd yet we observe a paradox,â said Pope Leo. âFor all the emphasis on individual freedom, people today frequently feel less free to be their genuine selves or follow their highest ideals, out of a hidden fear of being judged or of not fitting in.â
This loss of openness to others worsens our sense of disunity and indeed takes away our happiness, which the Pope said we find only in communion with the Triune God.
âIn revealing the heart of the Father, Christ shows us the deepest meaning of our existence, of our relationships, and the path to happiness,â he said. âThrough the gift of the Spirit, we have become children of God, sharers in the divine lifeâ.
By embracing our communion as children of God in Christ, we take part in the Churchâs mystery of communion and act as a sign of leaven and unity in our world.
In conclusion, Pope Leo XIV invited the Bishops associated with the Focolare Movement to bear witness to âthis longed-for unity of the human family.â
âThe answer to the sad divisions that plague our world,â he said, âlies not in forming more committees or launching more projects, but in going back to the source of our unity in the Holy Trinity.â

items.title: Thousands of West Africa’s young Catholics meet at first-ever regional youth gathering in Ghana
items.summary: Powerful messages are appearing on billboards across Ghana as thousands of young Catholics from across West Africa gather in Accra this week. Read all
items.body_text:
Thousands of West Africaâs young Catholics meet at first-ever regional youth gathering in Ghana
Gabriel Asempa Antwi â Accra
For the organisers of the first-ever West Africa Youth Days (WAYD) 2026, the meeting of thousands of young people in Accra is a call for young people to become âactors and agents of peace and hopeâ in a region confronting profound social, political and security challenges.
Catholic youth: take courage
WAYD 2026 is taking place in Accra from 7 September to 11 September, with the main activities happening at Achimota School. Nearly 4,000 young Catholics from the countries represented by the Regional Episcopal Conference of West Africa (RECOWA) are in attendance.
The theme, âTake Courage: Catholic Youth as Actors and Agents of Peace and Hope in West Africa,â gives the gathering significance that reaches beyond a conventional Catholic youth celebration.
West Africa is a region where millions of young people are growing up amid political uncertainty, violent extremism, communal tensions, economic hardship, unemployment, migration pressures and an increasingly contested information environment.
In parts of the region, democratic institutions have come under severe pressure, while conflict and insecurity continue to disrupt communities and displace families.
Contemporary West Africa
Against this backdrop, the Catholic Church is asking its young people not merely to pray for peace, but to participate in building it.
For a young Catholic in Ghana, Nigeria, Côte dâIvoire, Liberia, Sierra Leone, Togo or any of the other countries represented at the gathering, peace is not an abstract theological concept. It can mean living alongside people of different ethnicities and political loyalties, resisting hatred online, refusing manipulation, resolving disagreements without violence and finding the courage to serve communities facing hardship.
In that sense, the theme of WAYD 2026 speaks directly to the realities of contemporary West Africa.
A regional Church gathering around its youth
The event is being organised under the auspices of RECOWA and regional Catholic youth structures, with the Church in Ghana serving as host.
The Ghanaian Catholic community has been mobilising extensively for the event. Archbishop John Bonaventure Kwofie of Accra has appealed to priests, religious and lay faithful to prepare spiritually and materially for the arrival of young pilgrims, describing the hosting responsibility as both a privilege and a major task for the local Church.
The Ghana National Catholic Youth Council has likewise positioned the event as a major expression of youth faith, fellowship and service.
Youthfulness and regional solidarity
The preparation has itself become part of the story. Catholic youth groups and dioceses have been involved in mobilisation, fundraising and preparations to welcome participants. The event's visual identity â now prominently displayed on public billboards in Accra â combines Catholic symbolism with Ghanaian and West African cultural motifs, communicating a message of faith, youthfulness and regional solidarity.
The gathering is therefore being positioned not simply as a national Catholic event, but as a regional encounter with implications for the wider West African community.
Beyond five days in Accra
The first West Africa Youth Days is therefore not simply about bringing young Catholics together. It is about creating relationships across borders, cultures and languages â relationships that can help strengthen the conviction that West Africa is more than a collection of neighbouring countries.
